VISE HUMAN HOPE. by four pretty lines at the commencement of the lkitratd of the short poem entitled "Hope," in Lytton's charm- ing treaullation of" The Poems and Ballads of , Schiller " And it is not a dream of a fancy proud, With a fool for its dull begetter; There's a voice at the heart that oclaims aloud— We are born for a something better I " When the world seems weighted with care and sin, And dark clouds pbscure the heaven, And I hear he universal din Of humanity anguish-riven, The thought of Schiller comes like balm , r, To my mind, his grateful debtor, ' L And I breathe the words with a sense of calm— We are born for a something better!" :When I grieve over human littleness, • And the herd of ills that track us, Think how things curse that were meant to bless— How the red Joy-juice of Bacchus May hide a serpent,to sting and slay, Or a fiend the soul to fetter ; ' lam hopeful still, and can cheerily say— ' " We are born for a something better!" ; When I see a Crcesus roll in o'Pld, While the poor beside him hovel When I note how love is bought and sold, And how the millions grovel— The earth to ma seems all awry; • But I read in the stars that glitter, And in the blue of the silent sky— "We are born for a something better!" When in fancy I hear the howl of war, And see man slay his brother, I pine for a sphere where no discords are, Where no camp-fires hearth-fires smother; And I dare to dream of a golden age, For this world of beauty fitter, When the nations shall no longer rage— " They are born for a something better!" When I muse on the woes that afflict the race— Grim Ignorance, Crime, and Error,— . ' In thought I behold them go their ways, By the sunrise smit with terror; • While Love awakens to banish Hate To Hell, and in manacles set her; And earth's night grows bright as I cry elate— We are born for a something better!" Warrington. .N. 41 ARTHUR BENNETT.

I THE BARK OF rirs Pt.:um—The manner in which the bark flakes off in rectangular scales is very characteristic, and is, perhaps, a main reason tor the impunity with which the plane thrives in the soot-laden atmosphere of our metropolis. A copious annual crop of smoothly- polished leaves, readily washed by the slightest shower, and thus affording a large surface to the food-giving Tight and air, and a bark which thus yearly throws off all impurity, constitute an ideal city tree. We can hardly, perhaps, expect the enthusiasm of the poet to be quickly reused by the foreign charms of exotic trees, so that it is naturally the poets of America, the native home of one variety of the plane, who sing its praises. It is to the appearance produced by this shedding of the bark that Bryant alludes when he writes of the Green River:— Clear are the depths where its eddies play,

: And dimples deepen and whirl away ; grelez And the plane-tree's speckled arms o'ershoot • The swifter current that mines its root. ••••From Cassell's "Fahailiar Trees" far October. THE EFFECT OF Srimowers.—Dr. B. W. Richardson, of London, the noted physician, says he was recently able to convey a considerable amount of conviction to an intelligent scholar by a simple experiment.'nThe scholar was singing the praises of the "ruddy bumper," and saying he could not get through the day without it, when Dr. Richardson said to him, "Will you be good enough to feel my pulse as I stand here ?" He did so. I said: "(bunt It carefully. What does it say ?" "Your pulse says seventy-four." I then sat down in a chair and asked him to count it again. He did so, and said, " Your pulse has gone down to seventy." I then lay down on the lounge, and said, "Will you take it again?" Be replied: "Why, it is only sixty-four. What an ex- traordinary thing !" I then said: When you lie down at night, that is the way nature gives your heart rest. You know nothing about it, but that beating organ is resting to that extent; and, if you reckon it up, it is a great deal of rest, because, in lying down, the heart is doing ten strokes less a minute. Multiply that by sixty, and it is six hundred. Multiply it by eight hours, and within a fraction it is five thousand strokes different; and, as the heart is throwing six ounces of blood at every stroke, it makes a difference of thirty thousand ounces of lifting during the night. When I lie down at night without any alcohol, that is the rest my heart gets. But When you take your wine or grog, you do not allow that rest; for the influence of alcohol is'to increase the number of strokes; and, instead of getting this rest, you put on something like fifteen thousand extra strokes, and the result' is that you rise up very seedy and unfit for the next day's work till you have taken a little more of the 'ruddy bumper,' which you say is the soul of man below." Too Close Istrrarrox.—On oneToccasion, while on a journey through Italy, the Pope halted at a small vil- lage, the inhabitants of which resolved to send some of their principal men as a deputation to his Holiftess. The Mayor, who was to head the deputation, proposed to present him with some of, the chief produce,of the coun- try, consisting of pineapples, figs, and cream. It was accordingly arranged that each member should 'carry some figs and cream in silver basins, the pineapples, however, being dispensed with. Before setting out, the Mayor thus addressed his followers: "As you do not very well know how to conduct yourselves before exalted personages, you must watch me closely, and do as you see me do." The procession was formed, with the Mayor stklking majestically in front, furnished, like his fol- lowers, with a basin of figs in his left hand and another of cream in hie right. The door of the room in which his Holiness sat was opened, and the Mayor repeated his caution to those behind him. It so happened that there -was a step down into the room, but the Mayor failed to notice it. He stumbled, and the shock sent his beard and face into the cream basin. Trying to recover him- self, he only made matters worse, for he fell upon his knees with his hands and basin under him, and his creamed face raised imploringly to the representative of St. Peter. The other members of the deputation, think- ing that this was the proper ceremony to observe in the presence of such a distinguished personage, dipped their beards in the cream, threw away their vessels, and' bent down on their knees,' at the same time casting a half-inquiring and confident look at their leader, as if they meant to say, "You see we are all right; we have carefully followed your example." The Pope Was at first astounded, but soon burst into a fit of the most boisterous laughter' while his attendants, thinking that the deputation had come to mock their master. began pelting them with the scattereci figs. The Mayor hobbled 'out of the room, closely followed by his brethren, one of -whom whispered to him, "How lucky it is for us that -we did not bring the Pineapples. -How nicely our heads would have been battered with them." Tax RATS or Loom.—A mile or so out at sea rises a green triangularly-shaped eminence, called Looe Island. Several years since a ship was wrecked on the island, but not only were the crew saved, but several free pas- sengers of the rat species, who had got on board, nobody knew how, where, or when, were also preserved by their own strenuous exertions, and wisely took up permanent quarters for the future on the terra firma of Looe Island. In course of time these rats increased and multiplied; and, being confined all round within certain limits by the sea, soon became a palpable and tremendous nuisance. Destruction was threatened to the agricultural produce • • of all the small patches of cultivated land on the island —it seemed doubtful whether any man who ventured there by himself might not share the fate of Bishop Matto, and be devoured by rats. Under these circum- stances, the people of Looe decided to make one deter- mined and united effort to extirpate the whole colony of iavaders. Ordinary means of destruction had been tried already, and without effect. It was said that the rats left for dead on the ground had mysteriously revived faster than they could be picked up and skinned or cast into the sea. Rats desperately wounded had got away into their holes, and become convalescent, and increased .and multiplied again more productively than ever. The great problem was, not how to kill the rats, but how to annihilate them so effectually that the whole population might certainly know that the re-appearance of even one of them was altogether out of the question. This was the problem, and it was solved practically and -triumphantly in the following manner :—All the j. habitants of the town were called to join in a great hunt. •The rats were caught by every conceivable artifice; and, once taken, were instantly and ferociously, smothered in onions; the corpses were then decently lase out on clean rkina dishes, aid straightway eaten with vindictive 'xlish by the people of Lope. Never was any invention or destroying rats so complete and so successful as this. very man, woman, and child that could eat could swear to ths death and annihilation of all the rats they had eaten. The local returns of dead rats were not made by the bills of mortality, but by the bills of fare; it was getting rid of a nuisance by the unheard-of process of stomaching it! Day after day passed on, and rats dis-. appeared by hundreds, never to return. They had re- sisted the ordinary force of dogs, ferrets, traps, sticks, stones, and guns, arrayed against them; bat when to these engines of assault were added, as auxiliaries, smothering onions, scalding stew-pans, hungry mouths, sharp teeth, good digestions, and the gastric juice, what cersild they do but oiye in? Swift and sure was the destruction which now overwhelmed them—everybody who wanted a dinner had a strong personal interest in bunting them down to the very last. In a short space of time the island was cleared of the usurpers. Cheeses remained intact; ricks were uninjured. And this is the true story of how the people of Looe got rid of the rats! —From The Sea: Its Stiering Story of Adreature, Peril and Heroism." MEDICINES 'ELASTIC STOCKINGS. DEAR FBED,—You will ne sr.-uprisen at receiving a letter from me, but thank G.oi, lam pleased to say em getting better every day. I shall be an glad to breathe tin freell air again It has seemed a dreadful long time to be in bed. You know tWM taken to the Hospital last April to be treated for Bright's,Disease of the Kidneys. Well, on the 31st of July they tapped me, and took away 304 ounces of water. The 'same thing was done again nn the 18th September, and 408 ounces of water obtained. On the 9th October I was discharged from the Hospital as incurable. In Janu- ary this year (the 20th), was again tappsd at home and 380 minces of water taken away. The St. Bar- tholomew's Hospital in London refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Elartholernew'eHospital, Chatham. also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for years, and two local docters gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the Host:alai it took three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an object of misery and despair. After the Hospitals had refused me and doctors given me up. my wife persuaded me to try Hop Bitters, and from he commencement have improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks and can now get down- stairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid . f a few more bottles of the }titters shall be well again. The water has entirely left my body and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wond-rtul medicine. I wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the Hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Sitters eat everything with a relish. The only diffimity is the expense, but must not mind that an long as lam getting well. On a certain pit-heap not a hundred miles fm Cram- lington, recently, while the back shift men were gathered together in the cabin previous to going down into the pit, the conversation turned on suicides, and particularly on committing suicide through love. One of the men exclaimed with warmth, " Wey, lads, aa waddent com- mit suicide for nivvor a woman i' the wand! No, lads, aa wad cut ma throat forst !"

In a continental sea-side watering-place there was a reading-room kept by an English lady, who, on the strength of her position, supposed herself to be connected with literature. Lord Macaulay passed through the town, went to the reading-room, and wrote ,down his name in the subscription book. His money was returned to him with the remark, "No, my Lord, we literary people must not take money from each other." Among so many, can He care? Can special love be everywhere? A myriad homes, a myriad ways, And God's eye over every place? I asked. My soul bethought of this: In just that very place of His Where He hath put and keepeth you, ' God hath no other thing to do !—Whitney. At an evening party Dumley was introduced to a young lady, and after a remark about the weather, he said, gallantly—" And have I really the pleasure of meet- ing the beautiful Miss Smith, whose praises are being sounded by everybody" "Oh, no, Mr. Dumley," the lady replied, "the beautiful Miss Smith to whom you refer is a cousin of mine." "Oh, that's it? Well, I thought there must be a mistake somewhere," said the gallant Dumley. A man going home from his work at a late hour in the night saw that the occupants of a house standing flush with the street had left a window up, and he decided to warn them and prevent a burglary. Putting his head into the window, he called out—" Hilloa! Good peop--." That was all he said. A whole pailful of water struck him in the face. And as he staggered back a woman shrieked out—" Didn't I tell you what you'd get if you wasn't home by nine o'clock ?" Oh l—at this hour when half the sky Is glorious with its evening light, And fair broad fields of summer lie Hung o'er with greenness in my sight; I long to know if scenes like this Are hidden from an angel's eyes; If earth's familiar loveliness

Haunts not thy heaven's serener skies.— Whittier. On one of the nights of ,the last engagement of the late W. C. Macready, when he was to play Hamlet, he was very particular at rehearsal in the disposition of charac- ters at the fall of the curtain. He had selected the most commanding place on the stage,7well down to the lights, and declared that there he intended to die. It so-hap- pened that as the fatal moment was approaching, just after Hamlet had stabbed the King, his Majesty took it into his head to die on the spot selected by the philo- sophic Dane: The poison was burning in Hamlet's veins; he was in the agonies of death; but still he found time to say, sotto toce, to his stepfather—" Back, back; I'm going to die there." The blood of outraged royalty was up, and the stabbed monarch replied—"l'm King, and I'll die where I please; pick out a place for yourself," And Hamlet was compelled to give up the ghost farther up the stage. Mustesr. NerrAemx.—ln the eleventh century Guido of Arezzo first gave to music a definiteness of outline by the invention of notation by lines and spaces. In teacg- ing singing he used the words Do, re, me, fa, sal, la, which are derived from an old monkish hymn addressed to St. John. Previous to this introduction of the use of points placed on parallel lines and distinguished by means of letters, the Greeks and Romans used the letters of their alphabets to show the pitch. This they did, by placing them in various positions. Franco of Cologne invented characters which at once denoted both the tune and time of the sounds. He introduced the four symbols of very long notes, viz., the large, the long, the breve, and the semibreve ; while the invention of the minim, crotchet, quaver, and semiquaver is ascribed to John de Muris, a doctor of the Sorbonne, who made this important addition to notation, and also originated cer- tain characters determining the measure in the year .1338. Still shorter notes have been since introduced. Sharps, flats, naturals, bars, and ligatures were all intro- duced into notation during the seventeenth century. CLIVE AND TIM GANDLER.—CIive was present at the bombardment of Madras in 1746, and became, on parole, the prisoner of La Bourdonnais, and was one of those, as we have said, who were made a public spectacle by Dupleix when he violated the terms of the capitulation. Disguised as a native, he made his escape from Pondi- cherry, and on reaching Fort St. David became a gentle- man volunteer, and in that humble capacity gave proofs of the indomitable courage that inspired him. He once formed one of a party at play, whom two officers by ungentlemanly cheating tried to fleece. The winners were noted duellists, so the other losers paid their money in silent rage; but Clive refused to follow their example. and taxed the players with knavery. He was challenged, went out and gave his fire, upon which his adversary, quitting his ground, put his pistol to Clive's head, desired him to ask his life. Clive did so, but the bully now re- quired that Ye should pay the sum he had lost, and re- tract what he had said. "And if I refuse ?" demanded MT. "Then I fire," replied the other. 'Fire, and be ' hanged !" said Clive coolly. "I still say you cheated, nor will I ever pay you." The gamester, struck with the bold bearing of his antagonist, called him a madman, and threw away his pistol. We must not finish this anecdote, continues Mr. Gleig, without recording Clive's conduct in the sequel. When complimented by his friends, he observed, "The man has given me my life, and I have no right in future to mention his behaviour at the card table; though I shall certainly never pay him, nor associate with him again."—Casselre "Illus- trated History of India." AN INCIDENT OF SPANISH TRAVEL.—At Jaen we had an hour before the train started, and we dined partly to fill up the time,'and we found the landlord as niggardly with his food as he was liberal with his'cbarges, and just as we felt we were beginning our dinner we found that only the bill was to come. Then, in a kind of dram with three horses, we were about to start on our way ''to the station, not so much to avoid walking as for protection from the storm of piteous appeals to our charity—ap- peals we had no means of examining—but just at the moment of starting the proprietor appeared with a tiny piece of paper, stating that three pesetas were charged for our ride. "Why three pesetas? There are only two of us." "One peseta for the luggage." "What lug- gage?" The luggage of this senor." "This senor has no luggage." "Then the luggage of that senor." "That senor has no luggage." Then for the luggage just put on the roof." "-It is not ours." "But here is the bill; three pesetas." "Then alter it to two." "But the luggage?" "Keep it for the other peseta." There was no appeal from this, and we escaped on payment of the right fare—two pesetas. We saved the tenpence, owing- to our experience of a similar oversight at Madrid, where an omnibus-driver demanded and obtained eight' pesetas (six and eightpence) from four of us, though we knew, and he knew we knew, it to be a simple robbery; but the train was just starting, and he was sure we would not put off an eighteen hours' ride for a whole day for the sake of a few shillings, or even to expose a roguery. But here at Jaen we were in no hurry, and could as easily walk as ride; so we were firm, and car- ried off our tenpence.—" Cassell's Family Magazine" for October.

A SUCCESSFUL EXPERIMENT.—A. Scot was shown for sale at the cattle market, Clitheroe, last Monday, belong- ing to Mr. W. B. Dewhurst, Brungerley, without tongue. The Scot, from some cause or other, had its tongue cut out about July, and a.S it could not eat grass was wearing away to a skeleton. An experiment was tried that was I found to answer remarkably. Corn Oil Cake (supplied 1 by the Crown Oil Cake Company, Hull) was broken into large pieces and placed behind its jaws daily. A change for the better was soon observed, and the animal began to thrive so that in about three months it was fit to show for sale as a fat Scot, and it certainly did not shame its companions in the pen. SANDCRAC/C—A good blacksmith is necessary to cure a bad sandcrack. A bar shoe should be applied at once to the forefoot affected, and so carefully set on as to have an even bearing all round the foot. A transverse groove, nearly an inch in length, should be cut to the quick with the rasp, just above the upper end of the crack. A slight blistering of the coronet above this point will fur- ther succeed In promoting an unbroken growth from above. It is sometimes necessary to drive a nail through the edges of the crack, and this should be rivetted so as to hold the edges together. Sometimes inflamma- tion sets in, when poulticing will be necessary. If the crack is very wide, some substance, as gutta-percha, put into it will keep out some grit, and also keep the edges immovable.

EAEL BEAUCHAMP AND HIS TENANTS.—EarI Beauchamp has just issued a circular to his tenants in Worcester- shire, explaining what course he intends to pursue by way of revising his rents for the future. Instead of making returns of '25 per cent. he proposes to arrange a permanent rent, and says it will be better for the future that the landlord should pay the tithe, so that the rent may be fixed at a net sum, instead of the tenants paying part tithe and part rent as at present. Taking these circumstances into consideration, the noble Earl offers the farms to the tenants at a reduction of about 30 per cent. on the present figures, the reduction to commence at the next audit. It is understood that the tenants have all expressed their willingness to continue tenants on these terms. Aonicgurrrizet Hominsos Acr (1883).—" H.C.F." says: "I have read Sec. 33 of the Act ' (1883) carefully, also comments upon it, and there seems to be some difference of opinion upon the point raised, which is, whether 12 months notice is required in all cases of tenancies exist- ing prior to 1883, unless there has since been a special agreement to exclude Sec. 33. The following is the case: 'F' holds a farm under a written agreerfient entered into the in year 1880, which provides for a six months' notice to quit. Does the Agricultural Holdings (Eng- land) Act, 1883, render this agreement void so far as notice to quit is concerned, and make a 12 months' notice necessary, no agreement to exclude Sec. 33 having been entered into by the parties since the passing of the Act ?"—A year's notice, expiring with a year of tenancy, is necessary in all cases, unless the landlord and tenant, "by writing under their bands," agree that a half-year's notice shall be sufficient. Such a written agreement is often entered into by landlord and tenant, and it is the only; legal way of determining a tenancy by a:half- year's notice. TYING UP CArrtn.=-If the cattle are to be tied up in double stalls, there should be 7ft. 61n. between the divi- sions, and a post should be placed in the middle to pre- vent the cattle interfering with each other. The proper width for single stalls is 4ft. Gin., or sft., according to the size of the cattle. The best form 'of tie consists in an iron rod about 2ft. 6in, long, the two ends bent at right angles, so that when they are driven into the side of the stall the rod is about 2in. or 3in. from its face. This is fixed in a vertical or slightly sloping backward position to the division of the stall, the ends passing through and being secured by nuts, a cow chain having been attached to it by a ring, which runs freely on the rod. This chain consists of two smaller chains united together with.two or three stronger links to connect them with the rod, and care should be taken to insert a swivel. The smaller chains are hitched round the neck of the animal by a hook attached to one of them, and the animal is thus confined securely, but is allowed sufficient freedom for its comfort.

LORD TOLLEMACHE AND THE SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.— The Mark-Lane Erpress says—A statement having ap- peared to the effect that Lord yollemache approved of the principle of Mr. Jesse Collings's Small Holdings Bill, and had actually carried out the details on big estate, someone has directed the attention of the noble lord to the subject. In reply Lord Tollemache says:— " I disapprove of Mr. Jesse Collings's Bill," and then goes on to say, in reference to small holdings and allotments, "By far the most effectual and satisfactory way of ex- tending this system is by the voluntary action of land- lords; but if no decided movement takes place on their part in the matter, as a last resource, not only for the comfort and advantage of the middle and labouring classes, but for the protection of the jug rights of landed property generally, the compulsory power you allude to ought, in my opinion,- to be adopted, accom- panied by conditions such as an ample notice being given to the owners anand, with power of appeal, &c." Surely in these words Lord Tollemache endorses the principle of the bill, aind that he has, in effect, carried out its details on his own estate everyone knows. Then, where does the supposed contradiction come in? Land- lords ought to let or sell land in Small holdings, Lord Tollernache says, and if they will not, the law must com- pel them. Probably there are points in Mr. Collings's Bill which do not please Lord Tollemache any more than they or other points are satisfactory to the present writer; but it is perfectly clear that Lord Tolfemache supports the principle of the bill. THE MILK OF THE DEVON.—In a paper read by E. D. Hicks before a Southern Dairy Convention last year, he said: The milk of the Devon Is rich in caseine and butter, yields its cream slowly, and is, for drinking purposes, superior to that of any of the breeds of cattle. In pro- duct of quantity of butter it is second only to the Jersey, and in quality second to none. In some of the Devon herds of this country the value of the Devon as a dairy cow has been overlooked by breeders paying more atten- tion to them as beef producers; but in many herds, par- ticularly in the dairy districts of New York, Pennsyl- vania, and New England, much attention has been given to the dairy qualities. It would be useless to enumerate the cows which have produced from fourteen to twenty- one pounds of butter per week, giving from twenty to twenty-two quarts of milk per day, although there are many authenticated cases on record, not for a single week only, 'but fora long period. For instance, Gem 1,343 produced 315 pounds pf butter in ninety-five days, more than 214 pounds per day, and Beauty 506 pro- duced sixteen. pounds a week when she was fourteen years old, an age at which most of the cows of the butter breeds, so called, have passed to that country where churn dashes are unknown. Devons are-Valuable out- side of their milk and butter producing qualities, and it is not necessary to tell big stories about them. At the Minnesota State Fair in 1882, the premium offered for the best herd of milk Cows, quantity and quality of milk to be considered, was taken by the Devons from the herd of Mr. Baker, of Wisconsin. The strongly fixed repro- ductive power of the Devons is well demonstrated in the New England red cattle; as even there their grades re- produce the Devon colour and form, and their muscu- larity also, to a considerable extent. The hilly pastures of the Eastern States tend to strengthen and maintain their inherited fulness of muscular growth. THE CROPS.—A correspondent of the Manchester Gnar- dian writes :—Want of sun and wind has been much against clearing off the arrears of a harvest which threatens to be protracted far into October unless a , change comes on shortly. In Mid-Cheshire a few days ago I noticed a great number of fields of wheat out, and there were also many fields, of wheat in the haddock in the Wirral Hundred. , In the Little Fylde, between Lan- caster and Morecambe Bay, where there is a great deal of grain grown, there is still too much in the fields. In several instances there are also fields of beans to cut. In the low district lying between Cockerham, Glasson, and Cockersand Abbey there is also a large quantity of grain out. Much of the clover that was lying out a fortnight ago has been gathered in, bnt in very poor con- dition, and there is still some clover out and eddish hay also. The weather has been most unfavourable for this kind of work. The frosty nights, of which there have been many, have put a stop to grass growing, and many poor pastures and meadows are fast assuming the brown appearance of winter. Potatoes have been much cut down by the frost, which, however, has contributed to keep off the disease. The accounts given by gnawers are much less glowing than the promise was earlier on. In the Little Fylde I was informed that the most successful croppers of the Season were magnums and Reeding heroes. The champion was not much planted. The frost has driven cattle into their winter quarters, and as a rule there is not nftch food for them out of doors, the quantity of grass being below the average. I hearmany complaints of cattle and swine disease. Farmers are busy turning over the stubbles, and much farmyard manure has been carted upon the meadows during the last week or ten days. Trimming fences, thatching grain stacks, and work of that kind is being actively pushed forward. In only a very few instances have I met with potatoes being dug and stowed away in "hOggs" for late supply. In spite of the cold, turnips and mangolds keep an excellent colour. NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL NOTE.—During the past fortnight we have had few fine days, and the bulk of the harvest is still standing in the fields, and some has only this week been cut. The chief difficulty this harvest has been that the frequent rains have been accompanied by, high winds, which have blown down the stooks, and kept the hands engaged setting up. So far, I have not noticed any growth in the stooks, but the grain has lost colour, more or less according to the time it has been cut. Root crops have improved by the

rains; but it is now apparent that swedes will not be a I lull crop, never having fully recovered from the insect attack in the leaves, Last week you invited discussion upon the lubject of manures. It has long been my im- pression that here in the north we do not give that at- tention to manures which they deserve. It seems to me that on most of our stock farms, if all was done in this respect that might be done, most farmers would be able to make as much manure as would render them nearly, if not quite, independent of purchased manures. For six months, from Whitsuntide to Martinmas, our cattle and -horses go upon the,pastures the sheep all the year round. One Of the implements of our grandfathers' days, the dung-scaler, is now very rarely seen on our farms. The voiding:: of our live stock are left just where they fall, and the consequence is that our pastures are dotted with great sops of rank grass, rank by the over-richness of the manuring. The other six months, horses and cat- tle are kept in stables and shippons, and pigs are mostly under cover all the year round; the animals are chiefly bedded with straw, and the manure fed out to middens, exposed to rains. Oa very few firms, indeed, is there any provision made for the stothig :and preservation of the urine from the buildings or from the middens ; but on most farms it is allowed to run into some grass field near the house, mostly wasted, and in many instances worse than wasted, bemuse such drainage causes a nuisance to health, and often percolates into the place; where the animals get their supply of drinking water, prejudicially affecting their well-being. There can be no doubt but that many losses and illnesses are directly 'traceable to this cause.—R. • AllTtritlq CULTIVATION.—We have been told, within recent years, that the practice of stubble cleaning and autumn tillage originated in mistaken notions as to the reasons tor stirring the soil, and as to the sources of plant food. Further, that the practice has got its death- blow from observations at Bothainsted, proving the great waste of nitric acid during winter in ground which is not covered with plant growth of some kind or another. In -short, farmer e have been advised to leave their stubbles for fallows untouched AMtil the spring. It is to be hoped that farmers will not be slow to act on such advice, even in a Year like the present, when har- 1 yea Is not only late, but threatens to be unusually Pro- I longed. It is 'true that fertility Is conserved in whiter by keephig the soil covered with vegetation, and that a bare fallow is attended with a considerable loss of ni- trates. 'When we are told, however, that the true way to meet this is to leave the -stubble untouched in the autumn, and to encourage the free growth of couch grass and other weeds during winter, we take leave to reply that, though this advice may commend itself to the slug- gard in autumn, it will bring its own retribution in spring. By all means let us conserve the nitrogen of our sails as far as possible. It is the most costly thing a farmer 'has to buy. But a gold sovereign is only worth twenty Shillings. And in any case, land under a crop which will yield its own profit is as well protected from the loss of vagrant nitrogen as when growing unprofit- able weeds. We must also remember that keeping the soil covered is not everything; for the power of vegeta- tion to utilise the nitric acid in the soil is much dimin- ished if there be a deficiency of available mineral con- stituents. Since the bare summer fallow was discon- tinued, this deficiency, in the case of our poorer soils, is only to be prevented or made good by stubble cleaning and autumn tillage. Let this important work be done early enough, however, to admit of a catch crop, if not a regular winter crop, being grown. The catch crop of trifolium, winter vetches, or rye, &c., will pay well for growing, and the land will be clean after its removal in spring. It will then require comparatively little labour in spring to prepare the soil for the summer crop; whereas, otherwise, the work is so laborious that it is seldom well done, and as seldom accomplished in-time. The right plan is to autumn clear or cultivate all the stubbles, and to winter crop as much as possible. "Clean land and no bare fallow" should be the maxim. Land overrun with weeds should at all times be subject to dilapidations. -

VlLltil WITHOUT GOING TO BED. Mr. EDlTott,—While spending a few days at the pleasant seaside town of Aberystwlth, Oarolganshlre. Wales, I heard relat.d what seemed to me either a fabulous story' or a mar. venous cure.

The story was that a poor sufferer who had not been able to He down la bed for six long years, given up to die by all the Doctors, had been speedily cured by some Patent Medicine. It was related with the more implicit confidence from the circum- stance, as was said, that the Vicar of Llanrystyd was familiar with the facts, and culid vouch for the truth of the report. Having a little curb-81W to know how such stories grow in timelling, I took the liberty while at the village of Ll4nrystvd to ctli upon the Vicar, the Rev. T. Though a total stranger to him, both heand his Wife most graciously entertained me in a halt hour's con- versation, principally touching the case of Mr. 1410, in which they seemed to take a deep and sympathelo interest, having been fareillar with his sufferings, and how rejoined la What seems.) to them a most'remarkable care.

The Viper remarked that he presumed his name bad been cmiiected, with the report from his having mentioned the case to Mr. Jolisn Thomas, a chemist, of Lianon. He said Mr. Pugh was formerly a reddent of their parish, but was LOW living in the parish of Llandd.elnol. He strongly vouched for Mr. William Pugh's eharacter as a respectable farmer and worthy of credit. I lett the venerable Vicar with a livelier sense of the happy rela'im of a pastor and people, feeling that be was one who truly sympathised with all who are afflicted in mind, body, or estate. On my return to aberystwith, I was impressed with a desire to see Mr. Pugh, whose reputation stood so high. His farm Is called Paneom-Mawr, signifying "above the dingle," situ. ated near the summit of a smooth round hill, overl.oking a beautiful valley in which is situated the lovely ivy•mantled Church of Llanddelnol. I found Mr. Pugh, apparently about 40 years old, of medium height, rather slight, with a pleasant and intelligent face. I told him Iliad heard of his great afillc- Von and of his remarkable and almost mirAeulous relief, and ill/it I had come to learn from his own His what there was of truth in the reporta. Mr. Pugh remarked that his neighbours bad taken a kindly and sympathetic interest in his case for main years, but of late their interest had been greatly awakened by a happy change in his condition. What you report as having heard abroad, said he, is substantially true with one exception. I never under- stood that my Me was ever given up as hopeless by any phy- sician. I have been treated by several dGcters hereabfmtra as good as any In Wales, but unfortunately so prescription of theirs ever brought the desired relief. Fifteen years ag.N.he said, I first became conscious of a sour and deranged stomach and loss of appetite, which the doctors I told me was dyspepsia. What food I could hold in my stomach seemed to do me no good, and was often thrown up. with painful retchlngs. Inls was followed after a time with hoarse- ness, and a raw soreness of the throat which, the doctors called bronchitis, and I was treated for that, but with little success. Then mine shortness of breath and a sense of suffocation, es- pecially nigh s, with clammy sweat, and I would have to pet I out of bed and sometimes open a door or window in winter ' weather to fill my lungs with the cold air.

About six years ago I became so bad that I could not sleep in bed, but bad to take my unquiet rest and dreamy sleep sitting in an armch,dr. My affliction seemed to be working downward Into my howrls as well as upwards into my lungs and throat. In the violent coughing spasma which grew more fr-quents my abdomen would expand and colts se and at times it would seem that I should suff,cate All this time I was redneed In strength so that I could perform, no hard la- bour and my spirits were con equently much depressed. Early in this last spring I had a still more severe spasmodic attack, and my family and neighbours became alarmed, be- lieving that certainly. I weed not survive, when a neighbour, who had some knowledge, or had heard of the medictna- sent to Aberystwl:ll by the driver of Lhe Omnibus Post, some seven mile, distant, and fetched a bottieot Mother Biegcl's Curative Syrup.

This medicine they administered to me according to the directions. when to their surprise and delight no loss than toy 1)R11, the spasm ceased, I became at ease, and my S4O- - was calmed., aly bowels were moved a. by a gentle cathartic, and felt a sense of quiet comfort all through such as I had not before realised in many years. I stotd walk around the house and breathe comfortably in a few hours after I had taken the medicine. I have continued to take the medi- cine daily nor, forson ething over two months, and I ran lay down and sleep sweetly at migh's and rave not since had a rrcurrence of those terrible spasms and sweatings. I have been so long broken down and reduced in soy whole system that I have not tried to perform any very bard out-door latottr, deeming it test to be prudent lest by over.e3ertion may do myself injury before my sttength is fully re,tored. I feel that my stomach a. d bowe's have been andt are being thoroughly renovated and renewed by the medicine. In fact I feel like a new man. I have been much congratulated by my neighbours. especi- ally by the toed Vicar of Liahnrystycl, who with his sympa- thetic wife have come three miles to shed tears ot joy on my recovery._ .

A LAuGHING-PLANT, that is, not a plant that laughs, but one that creates laughter, is described in " Vick's Floral Magazine :"—"lts seeds prodace effects like those -produced by laughing-gas. The flowers are of a bright yellow, and the seed pods are soft and woolly, while the seeds resemble small black beans, and only two or three grow in a pod. The natives dry and pulverise them, and the powder, if taken in small doses, makes the soberest person behave like a circus clown or a madman, for he will dance, sing, and laugh most boisterously.and cut the most fantastic capers, and be in an uproariously ridiculous condition for about an hour. When the ex- citement ceases the exhausted exhibitor of these. antics 1 falls asleep, and when he awakes he has not the slightest remembrance Of his frisky doings."

ON THE BANKS OF THE DOUGLAS. I Br J. J. (From The Blackburn Times) Leaving the church, the party proceeded southward along the road for about half-a-mile, when they came to Carr House in the town chip of Bretherton, but in the parish of fools, where, it is believed, Horrocks lived during his brief ministry in the district. Carr Howse is a large, old- fashioned building, three storeys in height, with heavy stone mullioned windows, which are filled in with small diamond. shaped panes of glass, and it has still something of a manorial look, althoagh it is now a farmhouse. Immediately above the entrance to the porch a large stone contains the following inscription :—" Thomas Stones of London, Haberdasher; and Andrewe Stones of Amsterdam, Merchant, bath builded this hoarse of their own charges; and giveath the seats unto their brother, John Stones, London. A.D. 1613. Laos Deo." When the photographers had exposed several plates on the intereeting.edifice, the party were, on application, conducted by the lady of the house, through the building to the room which, Mr. Brickel believed, was occupied by Horrocks. It has been somewhat altered, but In its principal features remains the same as when the "strange unaccountable genius" (so designated by Hearne), used it as a study, and observatory, two hunlred and forty- four years ago. The apartment is directly over the porch, and the bay-window by which it is lighted forms a recess, at one time panelled round, from which there is an extensive view south, east, and west; while, curiously enough, some of the panes are composed of coloured glass. Everything about the house—the mallioned windows, many of them walled up long years ago, to escape the window-tax; the antique 'fire-places; and the oaken floors and staircase, remind the visitor of a bygone age. But the main idea that fills the mind when surveying the house, and especially when standing in the room which has been glorified by the presence of the young astronomer, is the thought that here, in this (then) lonely out-of-the-way place, far removed from all congenial companionship, Jeremiah Horrocks lived and laboured, webbing the moon and stars by night, and the sun and tides by day. Here it was that, haviag calculated the time when the transit of Venus would take place, with ice One near him whom he oonld consult in an emergency, no one to cheer him in his labours, or enoourage him in his studies, he, on the morning of Saturday, the 23rd of November, 1639, "having cleeed the windows against the light, with a telescope through an aperture towards the sun, to receive its rays at right angles upon a paper, on which he had described a circle, whose diameter was nearly equal to six inehes,"—sat and watched all through the day and throughout the night, but without making any discovery. The 24th was :Sunday, and he could not watch eontinuously on that day, because he had his duties as aerate of the village church to discharge, and these under all circumstances he faithfully performed. Twiee, therefore, were his observations interrupted—" Ad majora avocalus, guae ob hoer parerga negligi non decide." "Called away to higher dutiee, which ought not to be neg- lected for these ornamental pursuits." He continued his observations from sunrise till nine o'clock, and from ten till noon. At one o'clock he went to the church, and conducted the service, then returning to his room, he says— " About fifteen minutes past three in the afternoon, when I was again at liberty to continue my labours, the clouds, as if by divine interposition, were entirely dispersed, and I was Once more invited to the agreeable task of repeating my observations; I then beheld a moot agreeable spectacle, the object of my most sanguine wishes, a spot of unusual mag- nitude, and of a perfectly circular shape, whish had already fully entered upon the sen's disc on the left, so that the limbs of the sun and Vanes precisely coincided, forming an angle of contact. Not doubting that this was really the shadow of the planet, I immediately applied myself sedulously to ob. serve it."

At the age of fourteen he determined to study astronomy, although, as has been well said, "There was not one public observatory, not one teacher in either university, not one book in the English language, for either guidance or help," at the time he made the resolution. But undismayed by the difficulties he knew existed, he wr:tes :—"I determined that the tediousness of shady should be overcome by indus- try ; my poverty, failing a better method, by patience; and that, instead of a master, I would use astronomical books." 'When seventeen years of age, he says in one of his letters : "It was a pleasure to me to meditate upon the fame of those great masters of science (Tycho Brah6 and Kepler), and to emulate them in my aspirations." When curate of Hoele, and village schoolmaster as well, at the age of twenty, alone in his lodgings at Carr House, he pursued his astronomical studies until he came before his fellow-men as "the first person since the creation of the world who calculated and observed the passage of the planet Venus over the sun's disc." He was, says Professor de Morgan, "by very far, the greatest English astronomer of his day." He was, besides, a profound mathematician, who not only computed his own tables, but corrected those of others: a Christian philosopher, who while he believed that "the will of God is the cause of all things,' held that "resting in generalities is the death of philosophy;" an exemplary divine who, though "loving science much, loved religion more," and faithful to his truet, Allured to brighter worlds, and led the way; and a poet whose verses, written in Latin, have been com- mended by the Rev. Arundell Blount Whatton—author of a work entitled the "Life and Labours of the Rev. Jeremiah Horror," and the translator of Horrocks's "Venue in Sole Visa,"—who says that "they (the verses) evince a bold im- agination, combined with a judicious taste ;" and who also adds that "the sentiment which pervades his poetry is deli- cate and refined." He was an astronomer, a mathematician, a divine, a poet, and a philosopher, and he died at the early age of twenty-three, when most men are just commenaing to live. intbetrue acceptation of the word: died in the early morning of the 3rd of January, 1641, the day before his contemplated viait to his devoted friend William Crabtree, of Broughton, near Manchester, who shed bitter tears when he learnt he had lost his dearest friend, and his native country one of her most gifted sons. But That meteor-life, soon lost to vision here, Now shines unclouded In a glorious sphere; Yet here its light his bright example gives. And here in fame undying Rorrox lives. Perhaps it may not be considered a digression if we remark en passant, tor the benefit of those who are not very well acquainted with this district, that any person living In Blackburn or vicinity may, by taking one of the West Lancashire trains, which leaves after dinner, travel direct to Much Hoole, enjoy a pleasant walk of a mile through the fields, inspect the church, visit Carr House, and get home again in goed time for tea.

-Leaving Carr House, the party retraced their steps a few hundred yards down the road, crossed a stile on the left, and walked down the bank of a small stream, whose sides were adorned with the scented y arrow, and the yellow crowfoot—the latter being "the tufted crow-toe" mentioned by Milton in his beautiful poem of Lycidas—till they arrived at the Ferry. Having hailed the ancient-looking Charon who has for fifty years been ferryman here at Tarleton Lock, at the imminent risk of gliding into the mud on the one hand, or gliding into the river on the other, the party managed to get into the boat without any mishap occurring, with the exception of Hotspur. who had conceived the idea of ex- posing a plate on the party while amid-stream and he was consequently left ashore. When once fairly afloat, the water poured so fast into the sieve-like craft, that the facetious Alexis deolared "that if Hotspur had only delayed operations a few moments longer, he might have taken boat, boatman, and passengers in the act of sinking." When the party were landed, and had soiled the bank, they found, to their surprise, at least a dozen anglers engaged in plying the gentle art. Horatio, who is of an inquisitive turn of mind, seeing so many disciples of Izaak Walton, Inquired "If there were a lis'aing match taking place." "No," said the knight of the rod addressed; "the fact that there are so many fishing here this afternoon, is due simply and solely to private enterprise." Horatio, in common with the rest of the party, has never ceased from that day to this, to admire the enterprising spirit manifested by the patient ones, who on that particular day, with the hot sun blazing down upon them, spent the whole afternoon fi.ilaing for " snigs" in the muddy Douglas, and In the stagnant waters of the canal, which at this point joins the river. iliThree canal boats,laden with atone waiting for the tide in order to proceed to Preston, formed an excellent subject for the photcwraphers. A few minutes having been spent with the cameras, the party, resuming their journey, walked down the southern bank of the river, on through Lund and Lathom's shipyard, where they were informed, to their sur- prise, that schooners of 200 tons' burden were regularly launched ; and, cressing the fields, they emerged on to the road at the primitive village of Tarleton. Turning to the right, as they strolled leisurely down Hesketh-lane, the atmosphere being clear, thy had a splendid view of the surrounding country for many miles. Parlick Pike, Fair- snaps, and Bleasdale Fells stood out boldly in the distance on the right; the wooded summit of Billings Hill was well in view; Zloghton Tower was seen flashing in the sunlight;. Pendia- Hill loomed out grandly away to the north; the purple ridge of Rivington Pike was finely outlined in the east; and on the left Southport was plainly discernible, laved by the sparkling waters of the ever-changing sea. With ouch a noble prospect lying around, and spread out before them, the party journeyed on to Hesketh Bank. Be- lieving that neither meat nor 1119,93 ever hinderrd work, they halted at the Becconsall Hotel, and in a short time eat down, and did ample just to a substantial, capitally-served tea. The cravings of hunger having been satisfied, Hotspur grouped the party in front of the hotel, and risked a plate on a section of the "Sebtion." This operation over, the party wended their way along the road, and, taking the first turning to the right. prooeeded down a narrow lane, where the hedges were crowned with fragrant honeysuckle wh'ch was

Interwound With the ruddy-tinted roses, breathing scented music round, and the emerald borders of the roadway were enamelled with wild flowers, such as the lilac vervain, with its long, slender stem ; the purple bitter-sweet or woody- nightshade ; and the exqusitely-coloured mallow; while towering over the modest flowers at their feet blossoming elder trees, which at a distance resembled green mounds covered with ours, glistening snow, skirted the way- side. ilesketh-with.Becconsall church stands on a gentle eminence at the foot of the lane, and seems to be about as far removed as it can po.sibly be from the habitations of the people, who dwell in the parish. The fact that the original structure, built in the sixteenth century, was the private chapel of the Becconsalts, of Becconsall Hall, which is in the neighbourhood, accounts in all probability for its Peculiar isolated situation. The present edifice, erected in 1765, is about as plain and unpretentious a building as it is possible to imagine. It is built of brick, has a white- washed front, a small bell turret on the western gable, and is protected on three sides by stately lime trees. Owing to the somewhat unusual circumstance, that the name of the patron :saint has been entirely forgotten, it is generally

styled Becconsall Chapel. There is a varied and extensive view from the churchyard, comprising Becconsall Marsh, Tarletou Moss, Freckleton Marsh, the winding Ribble, and cloud-capped Preston. There are few, if any, old tomb- stones in the burial-ground, at least, if there ere any, they are most assuredly out of sight. The following admonitory lines were copied from a stone dated 1823:

All who come here this grave to see; As we are now, soon you must be. Repent in time, do not delay. For in our prime we're snatched away. After resting for a few minutes among the tombs, and en- joying the noble prospect, the party left the church re. posing in the shadow of the flowering limes, and, turning to the left, a very short lane, almost grown up with nettles and brambles, brought them to the brink of the Douglas, where they were favoured with an exceedingly gorgeous sight. The sari, like a golden argosy, was sailing majestically among light fleecy clouds that resembled islands of silver, floating in a sea of azure, and the fair scene was reproduced in all its beauty in the waters of the calmly flowing Doug- las. Several plates were exposed here on a picture which incinclKl the brown sands, left bare by the receding tide: the tranquil river, several canal boats in the foreground, and the railway-bridge in the distance. By this time, Low walked the sun, and broadened by degrees, Just o'er the verge of day. So the cameras were unshipped, and when the Methodical MAN-who is extremely careful of his photographic app tra- ms, had wrapped each piece of mechanism in its own special habiliments, and put them all in their respective little beds, the party re-passed the chapel, traversed the shady lane, and were just turning their faces station- wards as

The Sun thrmgh heaven descending, Like a red and burning cinder, From the hearth of the Great Fell into the western waters. They had not been long at Heaketh Bank Station, when the 9.14 train draw up at the platform, and departing like Hiawatha

In the glory of the sunset. When the goddess of night wa spreading her mantle over the quiet earth, they were whirled " through the purple twilight," over moss and over marsh, and landed safely at Blaokburn about 10 o'clock. And after having strolled through green fields, traversed shady lanes, travelled over ground where the ancient Britons and Saxons fought many of their fiercest battles, paid their devoir at the shrine of a genius, of whom Lancashire and England may wellbe proud, the party separated at the station, all thoroughly delighted with their sojourn on the banks of the Douglas.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

The frost on Saturciay nightand the early part of Sun- day night, when &leg. were registered by 11 p.m., has been sufficiently sharp to injure the leaves of the French Beans and the points of the Scarlet Runners are slightly affected. We were, however, pleased to find at an early hour on Monday morning that the frost had entirely dis- appeared. Should we be spared another early visit from "Jack Frost" these vegetables will continue to yield a supply for two or three weeks hence. Should the tops be further injured by frost it will he advisable to gather all the beans as they will keep a week on the stone floor of a cool room. French Beans are also fre- quently preserved in earthenware vessels with a layer of salt between each ftyer of beans till the vessel is filled, when it may be' covered over. They will keep good for • months. When taken out for use they will require to be soaked in water for 12 hours and the water changed two or three times, or they may receive a good wash and then be allowed to stand ins fresh lot of water for some hours, and when cut up previous to boiling they shoUld be allowed to drop into another lot of clean water where they may remain an hour or two. Our fear respecting potatoes has been realised. The disease has made its appearance in several places and secondry growth or supertuberating is prevalent, which., if possible, is more disastrous than the disease. The latter gives but little outward indications of its presence and the miscluef is not discovered till the crop,br the expected one, comes to be dug up. Every opportunity should be seized upon to pack soil round celery in order tohleach it, as well as protecting the leaves from ben'," damaged by the wind. Sticks that are so thick as not to'be conveniently grasped in one hand while the other is placing soil should have a loose band tied round them till the soil is pecked round. It is necessary to take this precaution more especially on stiff lumpy soils in order to prevent the lumps finding their way on to the heart of the plant and spoiling it by preventing its upward progress. All onions, except those having thick necks, should be pulled up and left on the surface of the ground for a day or two, or what is better taken into an open shed so as to get them thoroughly dry before they are stored. It will happen, that the stems of some are perfectly dry and' shrivelled' while others are still green. These should be picked out: before they are carried in, and placed on hamper lids or something of the kind so that they may be carried out- side on dry sunny days to be further harvested. They should also be the first to be consumed because they will not keep so well as those that have been properly ma- tured. • -

THE FRONT GARDEN.—The rain ;and wind have robbed the majority of the plants of their beauty for this season, and in some localities the frost has destroyed all the tender things, whilst in some gardens such tender subjects- as dahlias and heliotropes are scarcely touched. Michaelmas Daisies are the brightest flowering plants we have at the present time, and they will defy all weathers for the next two months. )The prevailing colours of the many varieties are the various shades of blue,, and the fhwer heads of the variety Versicolour are white and reddish purple. These herbaceous Asters are perfectly hardy, and grow from one to three feet high, but the tallest even need little support. Flora's gifts in Novem- ber and December are so few that we gladly welcome these &les of daisy-like flowers. Coreopsis lanceolata (Lance-leaned Bug-Nut), with its yellow-rayed: flbwers, will be conspicuous for some time yet, as they are unaffected by the weather. Anemone-Japonica in two varieties—one white, the other rose-red—are the most useful hardy herbaceous plants for supplying.cut bloom at this season of the year. The white variety,like -other white fibwers, get stained after being open a day or two, but this drawback is made up by others daily expanding. THE WINDOW.—Few window plants will be safe- out- side after this date, so it is as well to wash the pots and take them indoors. Fuchsias that have done flowering, if turned on their sides, may remain out for another week or two, and should be turned up occasionally if they get dry. All Pelargoniums should have the soil shaken from their roots, and the fourth part—and in case of large plants a third—of the roots should be rereoved before they are re-potted, which should be, done into smaller pots in a mixture of loam, leaf-mould, and sand. The pots should be thoroughly cleansed inside; and per- fectly dry at the time of potting, or it will. be a difficult matter to turn the plant out when it needsa larger pot in the spring.

Hope never affords more joy than in affliction. It is on a wat,ery cloud that the sun paints- those beautiful colours of the rainbow.

Every man has some peculiar train of thought which he falls back upon when alone. This,, to a great degree, moulds the man.—Du paid Stewart. "James, did you divide your paper of chocolate with your brother?" "Yes, certainly, mamme.;. I ate the chocolate and gave him the motto—he is. fond of read- ing, you know." There is sanctity in suffering when meekly borne. Our duty, though set about by thorns, .may still be made a staff, supporting while it tortures. Cast it away, and, like the prophet's wand, it chanqs.to Ft snake. , Patient the wounded earth receives- the plough's sharp share And hastes the sweet return of golden grain to bear, So. patient under scorn and injury abide,— Who conquereth all within may dare.the world outside. The largest bar of gold ever seen in Nova Scotia has been brouvbt to Halifax from the New Albion Mines, at Montague. It weighed 1,054 k ounces, and is valued at 20,618 dollars.

Content to keep the upper windows of his mind open to the holy winds and the pure .lights of heaven, and the side windows of tone, of speech, and behaviour open to the earth to let forth upon his fellowmen the tenderness and truth those upper influences bring forth in any region exposed to their operation —Macdonald. When Southey was offered a half-share in two news- papers—the Morning Post arld tho Courier—by which he could probably have secured £2,000 a year, he replied, "I will not give up the country and the lazy reading of old folios for two thousand times two thousand pounds ; in short beyond £350, a year, 1 consider money as a real evil."

The visit of the Margais of Hartington to Belfast has been fixed for the first week in November. His lordship will then 'formally open the new Ulster Reform Club. CARNATAVON BOROUGHS —Mr. ;Edward Swetenham, of the North Wales Bar, has been selected as Conservative candidate, for the Carnarvon Boroughs, in opposiVon to Mr. Jones Parry. WOLVERHAMPTON, S.—A rumour having been circulated that Mr. F. A. Homer, J.P., of Sedgley, would oppose Mr. C. P.Williers, he was on Monday waited upon, and an- nounced that the report was not correct. FINIHITRY (CENTRAL).—Ott Monday, Sir John Bennett received a deputation from the Liberal Organisation Corn- mittse inviting him to address a public meeting with a view to his adoption as a candidate. Sir Joan Bennett complied. THE Uurrgrt LIBERALS. —The programme of the Liberals of Ulster is now almost completed. They have decided to contest nineteen seats. Up to the present there has been little excitement in !Ulster in connection with the general election, but matters will .now no doubt soon be- come animated. _ _ _ .

'Remits DIVISION.—On Monday afternoon a deputation waited upon the Hon. Alfred Egerton, at the offices of the South-East Lancashire Registration Association, Manches- ter, asking him to become a candidate in the Conservative interest for the Eccles Division at the ensuing election. Mr.'Egerton at once consented to do so. His opponent in the Liberal interest will be Mr. V. K. Armitage. Met • CIIAIIIMELLIN AND ALLOTMENTS —Mr. Chamber- lain having been asked by a Glasgow correspondent whether he carried into practice his theories on the land question, writes that be is the owner of some property in the neighbourhbod of Birmingham, and has tested his theories by letting some land at the lowest possible agricul- tural met in the district for the purpose of allotment and cultivation. NORFOLK, N.W.—There seems to be every probability that Mr. Joseph Arch will succeed in his candidature for "North-West Norfolk. The most serious difficulty in the way hat been money, but now his expenses have been guaran- teed, fie is opposing Lord Henry Bentinck, who him much influence in the district, but it is believed that the Liberalism of the newly-enfranchised labourers and the secrecy of the ballet will defeat all attempts at interference. Moe EDWARD, CLLEKE AND Mn. CHAMBERLAIN.—Mr. E. Clarke; Q.C., M.P., at a meeting held at the New Swindon Railway Institute, on Saturday, said the recent straight- forward proposals of lelr. Joseph Chamberlain stood out in brilliant relief to the obscurity of his great leader's alrnoet forgotten manifesto, and it had cleared the air, for Mr. Chamberlain was as•wise as he was courageous, and he had mimed a most remarkable opportunity for asserting his right to be the neatirremier. I GOSCHEN'S ADDRESS —Mr. Gr6SCherl's I.address to the electors of the Eastern Division of Edinburgh was issued on Monday- Referring to schemes of local go- vernment and localGriance, he states that with a reasonable freedom as to details he cordially approves of Mr. Glad- stone's programme. Notwithstanding the recent severe depression of trade and agriculture, he is°, opinion that the sound sense of the great majority of the people will reject ail remedies, however specious, which imply a return to any form of ,protective duties or the adoption of illusory schemes of adjustment. THE GOOD TEMPI:ARS AND THE GENERAL ELECTION.— The Grand Lodge of England, of which'Mr. Joseph Moline, of Birmingham, is the presiding officer, has formed a "Good Templar Parliamentary Fund Committee," for the purpose of educating the electorate in Temperance Politics' and for the carrying out of the resolution of the Grand Lodge atits last annual session, which expressed the desirability of send- ing to Parliament members of the 'Order. The committee, coneisting of ,66 members, comprises officials of the Order in 31 counties, with power to add to their number. A general conference of Good Templar politicians is to be con- vened without delay. REM-7110ES OF CATHOLIC PRELATES.—The Irish ItGelibil Catholprelates have adopted a number of important re- solutions on-the social, political, and religious situation of Ireland. ' The resolutions reassert the right of the Boman Catholics to share in the public endowments for University and intermediate education; denounce anew the Queen's Colleges and Trinity College, Dublin; appeal to the Irish Parliamentary party to press forward the grievances of their Church in these respects; and condemn the violence and intimidation which are being resorted to iv. some parts sif the country, which cannot fail, it is declared, to bring down the angeref God on those who are guilty of them and dis- grace Ireland, in the eyes of the civilised world. div.p: WE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1885.

be withdrawn, and the party of progress will at once take it for their cry. While there remains a large body of Liberal Churchmen sternly set against Disestahl ishment, so long we may hope tleat the Liberal party (as such) will hesitate to pronounce in its favour. The party of progress is sure to beth 3 party of the long future. Let us try to make it plain that Disestablishment means not progress but retrogression. Such is the shape that the matter has ultimately taken for me.—Ever faithfully yours, C. J. VAUGHAN." Stu CHARLES DUKE AT CHELSEA. On Tuesday even- ing, a vast number of the electors of Chelsea assembled at Preece's Riding School, in the Fulham-road, to hear an ad- dress from Sir Charles Dilke. M.P. The building, capable of accommodating about 3,000 persons, was densely crow- ded half an hour before the commencement of the proceed- ings, and the interval was enlivened by the singing of " bongs for Liberals." Sir C. Dilke was greeted with en- thusiastic and prolonged cheers. The Conservative party,. he said, were engaged in carrying oe and carrying mit the Liberal policy (cheers) though the Liberals naturally thought that they could have dons it better. The mission of Sir H. Drum- mond Wolff to Constantinople, which was trumpeted about at the moment it was undertaken as constituting a sort of half step towards a new departure, had produced no more result than might have been produced in London by a con- tinuance of the conference between the Foreign Office and Hussem Fehin Paslaa. He regretted the failure, both upon public and upon personal grounds, but it had formed no new departure to the Conservatives. They had carried oat the agreement to which the Liberal Government had come in regard to Egyptian finance ; they had evscuated all the places in Egypt which the late Government intended to evacuate, and they had carried through the Afghan frontier negotiations upon the basis their predecessors had laid down. The only difference he recognised was that they took very quietly the flogging of a British Consul's clerk assistant, with regard to which probably a Liberal Govern- ment would possibly have shown a little more spirit. As regarded German annexation' it was eifficult to reconcile the howl against the late Crevernment with reference to British interference in Angra P(quina and the North New Guinea question with Tory acquiescence in the disregard of British inteiests in Zanzibar. The tearing up of Lord Salis- bury's treaty of Berlin had been taken very quietly by the Conservative party. (Cheers.) THE EARL OF.TDDESLEIGH ON THE LIBERAL PROGRAMME. —The Earl of Iddesleigh addressed a Conservative meeting at Sherborae Park, on Saturday. His Lordship described the present as a time for caution and prudence and for depend- ence upon our own firmness and integrity. He did not claim exclusive credit for the Conservative party in passing great measures, for many had been passed by the Liberals. But it should be remembered that Liberals advocated the disestablishment of the Church; the upsetting of the House of Lorels, and the crushing out of landlords. Because they , did not advocate these measures, Sir William Harcourt said I they bad no policy. Whatever might be the particular measures they took up they were determined to give a de- cided negative to proposals for uprooting and destroying the fundamental institutions of the country. Mr. Chamber- lain's proposal was to parcel out the land in holdings ot two or three acres, but-he saw insuperable difficultiesin the way of its accomplishment. He agreed with a system of allotments and security given to the labourer, but be re- minded them that the money to purchase great tracts of land for purposes of sub-division would have to tome from the taxpayers, and he wanted to know why a million opera- tives in the textile trades, for example, should be taxed in orderto give land to a million agricultural labourers. Did they think that the people who were holding out these pro- mises had no views of their own? Did they suppose these men did not-intend themselves to make a good thing out of it? Not a hit of it. They bad a very good reason far what they did. He wished to know, if a man chose to put his money into the purchase of land, why he was to be leas protected than if he put it into a cotton mill? With regard to the Education Act, he contended that the Liberals could not have carried it to so complete a success had it not been for the help of the Conservatives. They ought to be careful before abolishing school fees, though he was pre- pared to see the educational system still further estinded. In ,conclusion, he referred to the Royal Commission on Trade.

did net think "local option" a bad thing where the thing to which it was to be applied was perfectly legitimate. It was admitted that the closing of public-houses on Sunday where it was according to the views of the population was a legiti- mate act, but to give to localities the power where the number of non-thirsty souls exceeded the number of thirs y souls of saving that the thirsty souls should have no drink seemed to -him to trench upon the elementary liberties of mankind. He should be prepared to place the power of licensing in the banes of the local authorities to the extent to which magistrates rave it now. If any unfair encroach- ment was made on the industry of the publicans or others fair compensation undoubtedly must be given, and the local authority would have to provide that. As to Ireland the traditions of his party were clear and dis- tinct and they would not be departed from. They looked upon the integrity of the Empire as a matter more import- ant than any other political consideration that could be named. He did not in the case of Ireland see any plan or suggestion that gave the slightest ground for anticipating that it was in the direction of "Imperial Federation" that a satisfactory solution of the Irish problem would be found. To maintain the integrity of the empire must be their first policy. As to the present condition of Ireland, for which, it was said, the Government was to blame because the Crimes Act was not renewed, he asked, first, if it was quite certain that the Crimes Act would have prevented what is now taking place, and, secondly, if it was in their power to renew the Act. There were difficulties in dealing with "boycotting," but the Government were doing their best to cope with the evil. On the land question Lord Salisbury said the Conservatives desired more than any party that the transfer of land should be made cheap and easy. The Lord Chancellor believed Vial with a complete and compulsory system of registration of titles the transfer of land could be made cheap and easy, and the experiment was to be tried. If Mr. Colling's proposals were to be tarried it would have the effect of doubling the cost of the transfer of land. He should like to see facilities given to clergymen and ecclesiastical and chari- table corporations to sell at a fair price the land on which their income depended, for they would be much happier and better off if their incomes were in Consols. By this means they would bring into the market a large quantity of land peculiarly suited for gardens and allotments, which would suit agricultural labourers if they desired to become small farmers. Coming to the question of education, the noble Marquis said he should like to see the law made more liberal on behalf of those upon whom the present law pres- sed with undue severity, but he should shrink very much before he gave to every subject of the Queen the right to have his children educated at the public expense. Ile saw in the proposal for free education a desire to get rid of religious education. Referring to the statement of Mr. Gladstone in his manifesto on the question of Church Establishments, his Lordship said this latest avowal meant that the time of ultimate and supreme conflict was at hand, that the danger they had foreseen was at their doors. He was astounded at the action of some Liberal Churchmen who, by now supporting the Liberal party after the declara- tions that had been made, were supporting the machinery which was to destroy that which they held most dear. A vote of coufiderice in Lord Salisbury concluded the pro- ceedings.
