This committee recommended that the following estimate of expenditure by this committee for the helf-vear Ending 25th March, 1888, be approved :—luspectors' salaries, £9B 108 ; maintenance of boys at industrial schools, £4O; sun- dries, £l5; total, £153 10s. On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, the minutes were adopted. , .

div.head: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.
div.p: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

I This committee recomtnended that the following estimate of expenditure by this committee for the half-year ending 25th March, 1886, be approved :—Wages, £900; cartage, £250; macadam, £900; tiles, £160; cubes, £5O; paving Bridge-street, Haydock-etreet, Heath-lane, and Market- street, £750; cleansing and flushing sewers, £150; tools and suLdries, £5O; total, £3,210. On the motion of Alderman KEAN, seconded by Councillor TAYLOR, these minutes were confirmed.

. - THE BATHS, ETC. The minutes of the lowa Hallo Park, and Baths Com- mittee contained a report by the Surveyor as to the exten- sion of the Baths, in which be estimated one of the schemes of extension proposed would cost about £1,700, and the other about £2,600. The committee recommended estimates for the ensuing half year as follows ;—Town Hall depart- ment, £202 178 • Bauk Park department, £972; Baths depart- ment, £612 Os ico. Alderman WEBSTER moved, and Councillor J. PIERPOINT I seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor LITTON, referring to the report of the Borough Surveyor, said it seemed to him they were going to spend a lot of money on the Baths. He protested against this ex- tension of the Baths, which, be thought, a great deal of people did not appreciate. He saw that for the four weeks ending in September the receipts were £l9 7s 2d, as against £32 Us 6d in the corresponding period last year, which was not very encouraging, and yet they proposed to spend money on the Baths. He considered it was a waste of time discussing the question of the Bathl, because he did not think the proposals would be carried by the Council. Councillor J. PIERPOINT pointed out that the minutes merely referred to the printing and submitting of the re- port of the Borough surveyor to the Council for their con• sideration, and not to the approving of plans. He might tell them that he was thoroughly opposed to any additional outlay on the Baths until he was thoroughly convinced they were going to reap the benefits. Cooncillor LtrroN: The Council will not be pledged to anything. Councillor J. PIERPOINT : Certainly not.

Councillor Bovros criticised the &talon of the Baths Com- mittee. The Babe, he said, had been built by a lot of gen- tlemen, but the former directors did not make them pay; it became a white elephant to them, and consequently they were handed over to the Corporation, and they had been a white elephant ever since. They were so badly constructed that they did not answer the purpose for which they were intended. He thought the Baths were going to be a second Longford. (Laughter.) Councillor BURGESS did not think it was worth while discussing the question. as it was not before the Council. , Councillor ROBERTS thought tbe speech of Councillor Bolton was both irregular and absurd from beginning to end. The report presented to them that night was a direct outcome of the instructions given by the Council to the committee. The report was only presented for the purpose of further consideration, and be could not understand how any man could be so absurd as to attempt to cast ridicule upon what had been authorised and sanctioned by himself and his colleagues. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Strron thought everybody must admit the desirability of having good baths in the town, and he thought that it was to a great extent the fault of the com- mittee that the people did not appreciate the baths more. He did not believe they gave that encouragement to the public they ought to give, and which would make the baths /successful from a monetary point of view. Whenever there had been a swimming club in the town the receipts from the baths had been very good indeed, and if the committee would encourage a swimming club he thought the baths would pay very much better than they did at present. He should not like that question to be thrown over, as good bathe would be a great benefit if they coald•get them with- out going to too much expense. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CROSFIELD did not approve of Councillor Bol- ton's sneer at the gentlemen who were originally engaged in the formation of these baths. He remembered that it I was the late Alderman Smith who was the prime mover in the matter' and he came to him (Alderman Crosfield)— ' Councillor BOLTON said he did not sneer at anybody. Alderman CROSFIELD said if it was not a sneer it was something very similar, and it sounded so to him. Coma- cillcm Bolton said those gentlemen went and formed the bathe, and when they found that they dird not pay they got rid of them. It was as much as to say that they entered into a commercial speculation to make money. It was nothing of,the kind. (Hear, hear.) When the baths were formed it was from a desire to do some good to the town whether they pain or not ; it was not a question of making money. They all knew that the baths did not pay, and half the money that had been spent on them was accepted when they were handed over to the Town Council. He thought all would admit that a town like Warrington ought to have its own baths, but he must say he was rather astounded at the amount of money the report mentioned as likely to be spent. It ap- peared that £2,700 was sadly too much money to spend on the baths, and he should say to the committee that they had better moderate this expenditure and reduce it very considerably or else be did not think the Council would be willing to sanclon the amount. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BROADBENT thought that when they came to see the plans they would not consider that the additions to the baths were at all too great for a town of the size and importance of Warrington. Be believed it would be found that the plans were so judicious that it would be advisable to adhere to them, and if they were not prepared to spend the money immediately they might wait till they were prepared. Councillor Litton had said that the Baths were not appreciated, but be (Councillor Broadbent) had heard it said that in the summer months the bathers were so numerous that the water could hardly be seen. (Hear, hear.) ,Councillor DIXON recommended that they should pro- vide other baths as well as swimmihg baths. ' Councillor JOLLEY said that to ascertain whether the alterations were required it was simply a question of whether the baths were crowded out or not. Alderman WEBSTER said that the town was now so pop- ulous and the Baths 60 much appreciated that they did not answer their purpose. In the summer months they were crowded to excess. Councillor Surron asked whether the committee had con- sidered the question of a public laundry. The CHAIRMAN said he thought that was mentioned. Councillor Scrron remarked that there were a good many people who thought that a public laundry would be beneficial in Warrington, and that it would be a source of revenue to the Corporation. The minutes were then confirmed. MARKETS COMMITTEE.
Councillor LITTON proposed, and Councillor linpmateledx seconded the adoption of these minutes, which recommended an estimated expenditure of £755 6s for the ensuing half

year. Councillor W. PrErtrotarr, referring to the recommendation of the 28th September, "that the tender of Mr. John Nor- bury for the erection of the Market Inspector's office, at £222 10s, be accepted," remarked that to him that appeared a large amount of money for the purpsse. He had had an office built that suited his requirements, and would suit those of the committee, at a cost of £4O, and should like to know why in this case it was proposed to pay so large an amount. Couocillor PIIION said that the trade in the market ren- dered a good office necessary, and he had no doubt that when Councillor W. Pierpoint had seen the office it was pro- posed to build, he would be satisfied. Councillor Ram PIERPOINT said that the smallest space they could do with for the office of the inspector was 22 feet long by 16 feet wide. Perhaps that space would hold four of the offices of Councillor W. Pierpoint —[Councillor W. PIERPOINT : It would not bold one.]—Fhen there was another room Of the same size, which would probably hold another. (Laughte.r.) As the Office was to be erected in the centre of tha market, it w4uld naturally be more costly than if built in a correr. There was nothing unduly elabor- ate about the plans, and it would be a pity were they to attempt to reduce it. Councillor st2rosr said that he was not aware that the office was going to be such an expensive affair, and should like to ask bow much space it was going to occupy. Councillor LITTON : Councillor Pierpoint has just told you 22ft. by Itift. Councillor Surros thought that they should be chary in taking space for an office in the beet part Of the market ; t it might be so situated as not to take up so much valuable space. Councillor Immonr said that the office was to be placed in the centre of the market, so that the inspector could have a good view of what was going on all around. Thu minutes were then adopted.
GENERAL PORPOSES COMMITTEE,-THE USE OF THE ROOM
IN JOHN-STREET.

The CnentatiN proposed the adoption of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee. There was one reselution which, he hoped, would commend itself to the best judg- ment of the Council, and that was the one recommending the letting of a portion of the buildiog in John-street to a number of ladies and gentlemen who had banded themselves together, as he understood, to improve the condition of the female population of the town. They had agreed to let It at a nominal rent of 2a61 per month. A letter had been , received from Mr. McTurk, in which he said that he pro- posed to attend that meeting, and would, if necessary, give any information regarding the objects for which it was de- sired to use the room. The letter added that they hoped to secure the use of both the upper and lower rooms. He (the speaker) was afraid that they could not accede to the re- quest as regarded the lower room, which was occupied with property belonging to the Corporation. Councillor Surrox seconded the resolution. Councillor BOLTON thought that, if the recommendation orthe committee was pissed, it would be dealing unfairly with the two Welsh gentlemen, whose request to use the room for religious purposes had been refused by the Coun- cil. He thought that they should not favour any one par- ticular sect. The room was now required for a philanthro- pic purpose, and he thought that as a Council they bad no- thing to do with it. He thought that they should sell the property, as they could do nothing with it. The Welsh gentlemen who applied for the use of the room were trying to improve their countrymen, and the present appli- cants bad a laudable object in view in trying to 0-Trove

another class, and be thought that to grant the rewst would be making fish of one and flesh of another. He should move teat the Request be not entertained whether he got a seconder or not, as a protest a;ainst the whole trans sc- tion.

Councillor SUTTON thought that it was a very foolish thing to refuse the loom to those who applied Ipr its use be. fore—it was a selfish thing to keep the building useless— hut two wrongs did not make one right. (Hear, hear.) It was now applied for for a good object, and he certainly said that they should now let it. He did not think that the room should be left useless if it rould be made of benefit to anyone in the town. Until they could make a better use of the building they should not refuse the request now made.

Councillor BROADBENT had no donbt that the resolution would be passed, because the General Purposes Committee consisted of all the members of the Council, and it was hardly possible for it not to be. He thought that a mistake had been made in refusing to let the room to the Welsh gentlemen referred t; but be agreed with Mr. Sutton that that WAS no reason why they should continue to keep the room in uselessness. He thought that the feeling of the Council would te one of great thankfulness to the ladies and gentlemen who intended to devote their time and ener- gies for a purpose the very best that could be done in War- rington at the present time— that of finding innocent re- creation, and amusement, and teaching for the young girls of the town. He should be glad if they could see their way to allow the use of both rooms.

Councillor JOLLEY asked if it was not somewhat irregular to let the room for 2s 6el a month, considering the responsi- bility of the Corporation to pay ground rent and make the street? He had no objection to the people having the rooms, but thought that they should be consistent in deal- ing with the finances of the ratepayers. Councillor SUTTON: It is better than nothing. Alderman CROSFIELD agreed with Councillor Bolton to the extent that he would not be a party to favouring one denomination at the expense of another. He believed that the reason the building was not let to the Welsh gentlemen was because they were goirav to make it into a place of worship. It was now required for a different object. It was to be used for the purposes of a ladies' mission, and was not to be confined to any particular denomination. He WM' pathised strongly with those who were undertaking the work, and thought it was the duty of the Corporation to grant the request. It would be shabby indeed to prevent these people succeeding in a good object. He took it that the rent of 28 63 was merely a nominal one, and that it was not intended to get anything to cover the ground rent. He hoped the Council would be unanimous in passing the resolution. Councillor W. PIERPOINT accorded the recommendation his heartiest sympathy, and quoted a previous resolution of the Council, from which it appeared that the nominal charge for rent was made on the basis of a former charge. The minutes, which also recommended an estimate of expenditure for the ensuing half year of £778 Be, were then adopted.

div.head: FIRE_ ENGINE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FIRE_ ENGINE COMMITTEE.
The minutes of this committee, which recommended an expenditure of £l2l for the half year ending March next, were passed on the motion of Councillor W. PIERPOINT, seconded by Councillor HUTCHINSON.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

This committee submitted estimates of expenditure, of which the following is a summary :—Borough rate: Sep- tember, 1884, £3,456 3s 4d; March, 1885, £4,309 193 3d: September, 1885, £4,709 us Id. Improvement rate: Sep- tember, 1884, £9,272 19s 2d; March, 1885, £7,602 4s id.; September, 1885, £8,230 9s Id. General sewers rate: Sep- tember, 1884. £BOl 15s sd; March, 1885, £707 49 3d ; September, 1885, £625 2e sd. Total : September, 1984, £13,520 17s lid; March, 1885, £12,619 7s 7s; September, 1885, £13.565 2$ 7d. The CHAIRMAN proposed the adoption of ;he minutes, and called attention to the financial statement for the en- suing half year. The total amount of expenditure esti- mated on the borough rate was £4,709, as compared with £3,456 for the corresponding period of last year. That was a considerable addition, which arose horn circumstances dealt with by various other commit'ees, and which the Finance Committee had nothing to do with. They proposed a borough rate of Is 3d in the £. There was also an esti- mated expenditure of 2d in the £ on the sewers rate ac- count. There would be a surplus left for that, ar,d they expect-d that next year they would only have to ask for a rate of id in the Z. Alderman WErisrEn seconded the motion, which was car- ried, and formal resolutions fixing the improvement rate at is 3d, and the general sewers rate at 24 in the Z. were passed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Alder- man CROSFIELD. THE PAVING OF BRIDGE-STREET.

Alderman WEBSTER moved—" That it be an instruction to the Paving and Sewering Committee, as the necessity arises, to re-pave Bridge-street with wood, instead of the or- dinary granite sets." When the new buildings in that street were completed, he said, necessity would arise for the repairing, at any rate, of the lower portion. The question was an important one, and one affecting the ccmu3ercial interests of the town. The noise and inconvenience that at present existed did seriously interfere with business, and people went to other towns to make purchases to escape the inconvenience. He thought that the success that had at- tended the paving of Sankey-street was such as to be con- vincing that it was decidedly the host kind of pavement. He thought there was no ground for objection on the score of expense, that it would be a great sanitary improvement, and that it would be of advantage to the commercial in- terests of the borough. Councillor Dixox seconded the resolution.

Councillor WRIGHT said that as a committee they felt that upon sanitary grounds setts were the best and most economic. The cost as given him by the Borough Surveyor some time ago of the maintenance of the streets was £t37 per annum, as against £lB3 for wood, for a given portion of ground- Alderman DAVIES remarked that at the present time the Paving and Sewerage Committee felt that their work was inadequately done on account of the absolute wart of funds. They had a great desire to do what they could with the money at their disposal, but beyond that he thought it un- fair to press extra expense upon them. Councillor BROADBENT thought the Council would be unwise to in any way tie the hands of the committee—in whom they had confidence—as to hew they should do the work. He thought Alderman Webster, who had now had an opportunity of stating his views, would do well to with- draw his resolution. He had no doubt that the committee would give the views of the Alderman every proper coat- i sideratien. and it might be that they would see their way to adopt wood pavement. At all events, he should certainly recommend the Council to leave the committee free. Councillor JOLLEY hoped that Alderman Webster would see his way to withdraw the motion on the score of expense alone. If it was done in Bridge-street, how could they re- fuse the same paving to the other streets? They were all narrow streets, and if wood paving were adopted in one they would probably have to carry it out throughout. Wood pavement would inert, three times the expense. Alderman KEAN said it was intended to take up the setts throughout Bridge-street and to put down new Bette, calcu- lated when properly 'laid to be almost noiseless, and he thought it would please Alderman Webster almost as well as wood pavement. He thought that with such a gradient horses would frequently fall in Bridge-street if there was wood paving. Councillor FRANCOMB thought that the matter might well stand over for the present. Alderman CROSFIELD said he should be glad if Bridge- street could be paved with wood, but he was afraid that the 'gradient of the street was too severe to make it safe. The lower part of the street was pretty level, and wood paving might be introduced there with comparative safety. It was entirely a question of expense, and the arguments Alderman Webster had used about Bridge-st. held good in regard to the other streets, and until they were richer and less pressed upon with expense he was afraid they would have to wait for that happy day. Councillor W. PigaPorter said he should have preferred that a proper estimate of the cost should have been sub- mitted. Ho thosight that, so far as the gr.dient was con- cerned, wood paving would be quite safe in Bridge- street. Alderman DAVIES asked if Alderman Webster wmlil be quite satisfied if the committee gave an asiurance that they would lay before the Council the two acne:nes. Alderman WEBSTER having again eprilren, th 3 diicussion dropped, it being understood that he agreed '0 accept tba suggestion of Alderman Davies. This was all the businels.

ALARHING TRAP ACCIDENT, An alarming trap accident occurred in Bridge-street, Earlestown, about half- past three on Thursday afternoon. A poi.y and trap owned by Mr. William Chambers, draper, Bridge-street, were stand- ing near the back entrance to his premises in Bock Market- street, when the animal suddenly took fright. It ran along the narrow passage into Market-street, and thence turned up Bridge-street, round the corner shop of Messrs. Evans and McClure at a great speed. The sh irp turn and the speed of the pony caused the trap to trwerve to the opposite side of the road_ In the trap was James Alfred Chambers, four years of age, son of the owner, and as the vehicle was tbrown completely over on the footpath, near the shop of Mr. Stirrup, hair dresser, it WAS feared ty the alarrn.:(l spectators that he was seriously injured if not killed. He, however, escaped alnmst miraculously. When the trap was over-turned the child was violently pitched head foremost into the door space of Mr. Stirrup's shop, otherwise the trap would have fallen upon him if not crushed him to death against the wall. As it was he sus- tained a severe bruise on the forehead, and tbe skirt was also torn. As quickly as possible he was carried into a ntigh- bouring shop, where his injuries were attended to. When the trap was thrown over the animal strimWed, but quickly disentangled itself from the reins and tracings, and was making off when it was caught hv a pasaiiog man. At the moment the trap ran on the footpath and overturned two children were passing, and they only escavd laY a few Inches. The accident created considerable excitement.

div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

—lt is stat—ed that Nov—emoer fixed for the dissolution of the present Parliament. At Oldham County Court, f,i) Tuesday, Joel Foeter, builder, was committed for tlial for perjury committed in that Court.

Henry Norman, aged 31, convicted of the murder of hie wife by stabbing he: with a dAgger, was hanged at eight on Monday morning. The Council of the Yorkshire Miners' Association at Barnsley, on Monday. decided to apply to the employers for an advance of 15 per cent. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone attended early service at Hawar. den on Tuesday morning Mr. Gladstone walked through the village in the afternoon. _
At Tu'n.stall, Staffordshire, on Saturday night, the wife of a carter named Mark Hopkinson, living at Tunstall, gave birth to four children, all seas

The Earl of Erne died at Croom Castle, County Ferma- nagh, in his 83rd year. He is succeeded by his son, Viscount Crichton, member for Fermanagh. A verdict of wilful murder was returned at Clapham on Monday against the mother of two girls who on Thursday were found dead in bat suffocated. The woman is said to be insane.

At Greenwich, on Wednesday, Martha Howard, of Forest Hill, was committed for trial, charged with the murder of her daughter, aged rive months, whose head the prisoner almost severed from the body by a stroke with a chopper. Cries of murder were raised on Saturday morning in a lodging-house in Candleriggs-street, Glasgow, by Marv, wife of Robert Miller, who has since been apprehended on a charge of throwing at her a bottle of vitriol or some cther acid.

The annual conference of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants was opened at Leicester on Tuesday after- noen, under the presidency of Mr. McLiver, M.P., who gave hie inaugural address, in which he demanded shorter hour 9 of labour.

At a meeting of traders and merchants of Cork on Sat- urday, resolutions were passed affirming the great import- ance to the community of the starting, on a strong founda- tion, of the Munster and Leinster Bank. Fifty thousand shares have been subscribed for. CABINET COUNCIL.—Tbe Cabinet Connell sat from noon to half-past two on Tuesday, soveral Ministers waikingaway in a drenching downpour. It is understqod that the princi- pal matters considered were the position of affairs is Bul- garia and Bournelia, and the condition of Ireland. Lord Derby presided on 6atnrday at the proceedings in- cident to the opening of the session of Cambridge College, Liverpool, and distributed awards to the students. Be be- lieved that as Victoria University became better known the number of its Students would continually' increase and its bold upon the confidence and support of the public would be strengthened.

sEarors CIIIRGE AGAINST A TRAVELLEII.—Henry Geo. Dunohoe, a respectably-dressed man, stated to be a traveller for a leading wholesale jeweller in Birmingham, was brought up at the Chippenham Police Court, on Saturday, charged with assaulting Annie Mortimer, twelve years of age. The girl described the assault, and swore positively to the ac- cused, who, however, denied the charge, saying he had never seen or spoken to the girl till he was apprehended. The magistrate committed the accused for trial.

THE CHURCH CONGRESS opened at Portsmouth in the presence of about 2,000 visitors. On Monday night the Bishop of Newcastle presiged over a meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society, and said they were fighting against tendencies in human nature and a great trade, and in his mind moral suasion was not safficient without legis- lative efforts, which must find an echo in the hearts of the people. A meeting was also held, presided over by Earl Nelson, in favour of free and open churches. THE DAPT/ST Ile annual meetings of this Union were commenced at Swansea on Monday night. The Union way presented with a very cordial address from the clergy and ministers of all denominations, beaded by the Vicar. Suitable responses were made the President of the Union, Ur. S. G. Green, of London ; the Rev. C. Williams (vice-president of the Union), of Accrington ; and represen- tative ministers of Swansea and Cardiff. A resolution in favour of the extemion of tbe Sunday Closing Act to Eng- land was carried with unanimity. MANCHESTER DETECTIVES STRUCK BY LIGHTNING.—Two members of the Manchester Detective Police were walking Ashton Old-road, Bradford, about 11 a.m. on Monday,. when they were struck by lightning. The umbrellas they were carrying were struck from their bands. One of the officers named Gibbons was rendered insensible, and re- mained in that position for fully half an hour. His corn-- panion, Sergeant Girdharn, sustained very little injury, and was able to walk to his borne. A woman and a horse were also thrown to the gonna by the same flash.

SINGULAR AFFAIR NEAR' Wnnxirsiu.—A shocking dis- covery was made at Bedwell stud farm, near Wrexham, on Saturday night. A groom going into a shed which had not been visited for some time was horrified at Ending an em- aciated and apparently dyiag man. The poor creature was taken to Wrexham Workhouse, where means for his resuscitation were taken successfully. The man declared he had been lying there for a fortnight, during which time he had nothing to eat. He has been identified as James Edwards aged 50,a married mar, bat living apart from his wife, who resides at Birkenhead.

ATTACK ON SALVATION ARMY LIFE GUARDS. The Salvation Army Life Guards, who have been making a tour in Yorkshire, were the victims in Leicester, on Monday, of what appears to be a most unwarrantable attack. On ar- riving in the town on their way to London they were met by a large mob, by whom they were very badly treated. One of the officers was thrown from his horse and assaulted, many of his companions were also injured, and the accou- trements of the guards were flung about in all directions. Great excitement prevailed, and the police seemed powerless to stop the disturbance. Two arrests were made. TRK COMMISSION' ON THE DEPRgSSION OF TRADE Win be a kind of travelling inquiry. After taking evidence in Lon- don, it will visit Manchester, Sheffield, Leeds, Hull, Liver- pool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Glasgow. Dundee, Aberdeen, Belfast, Dublin, Cork, and, if the progra:nrne be carried out, will subsequently take leading ports in the South and West. of England. At the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, on Monday, the Chairman saiet anyone would eee at once how difficult it was to answer the questions asked by the Com- mission satisfectorily, but special meetings of the Council had been held to consider them, and it was heped that in a few (Inv, suitable replies mrght be given to some of the most important. At a meeting of the Agricultural Engineers' Association, at the Memorial Hall, London, it was resolved to give no answers to the questions, but to leave the matter. to the individual members.

MARRIAGE OF SIR CHARLES DILKE —The Right HOB. Sit C. Wentworth Di' lke M.P. for Chelsea, was married on Saturday to Mrs. Mark Pattison, at the Pik;-iSh Church of St. Luke's, Chelsea, by special licence. The ceremony was arranged to take place at half-past twelve. Precisely at noon Sir Charles Dilke arrived, accompanied liv his son, Master Wentworth Mike, the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P., who acted as best man, and Mr. J. E. C. Bedley. The bride arrived a few minutes before/ the appointed hour, accompanied by her brother, Colonel Strong, who gave her away, her brother-in-law, Mr. F. Winn Pattison, and Mrs. pattison, her sisters, Mrs. Neale and Mrs. Tnckwell, and her nieces, Miss Tackwell and Miss eitirke. The service was, immediately commenced by the Rev. Gerald Blunt, M.A., rector of Chelsea. No invitations were issued except to a few near relatives, but among the large crowd which nearly filled the body of the church were Mr. Westlake, Q.C., and Mrs. Westlake ; Mr. Firth, M.P. (Sir Cnarles Dake's col- league), and Mrs. Firth; M. Gennadius, the Greek Charge d'Affaires ; M. Catalani, of the Italian Embassy ; Mr. May.. cock and Mr. Female of the Foreign Office ; Mr. Black, of the India Office ; Mr. M‘Coll, editor of the Athenteum ; General Kent. and Mr. Osborne, president of the Chelsea Liberal Association. The register was signed by Mr. Cham- berlain, Mr. Pattisan, Colonel Strong. Mrs. Bodley, Mrs. Tuckwell, and Mrs. Neale. On the conclusion of the cere- mony, the bride and brideeroom, who were loudly cheered as they left the church, drove to the house of Mr. Frank Paitisen in Berwood-place, and later to the afternoon pro- ceeded to Oaklands Park. During the day congratulat :ry telegrams were received from Major Dilke, of Maxstoke, from diplomatic representatives abroad, members of the liause of Commons, and many other friends. The bride was dreessa it: a cream-coloured stalactite velvet dress, trieened with peiat d'Aleecon, with bonnet to match. THE LATE I,RD SHAFTES.Bnint.—At a delegate meeting of the miners ef the Rhondda and Ogtnore Valleys on Mon- day, at whice 16,000 men were represented, a resolution was passed expressing profoand regret at the death of Lord Shaftesbury. The delegates stood with their heads un- covered while the resolution was being put. The coffin containing the remains of the late Lord Shafteebary Was tes. moved from his lordship's late residence to &temente Station on Monday afternoon for conveyance to London. A funeral peal was rune, and the Mayor and CorporatiOn witnessed the remains depart. The funeral service was held at Westminster Abbey on Thursday morning. The remain, of the deceased nobleman were conveyed from his town d* residence, in Grosvenor-square, followed by the chi mourners, Lord Shefteeteury, the lion. Anthony Evelyn and Lionel Ashley, Lord Templeton, aud other immediate relatives of the late Earl. The Abbey was filled in all parts, all classes of society, include the congregation representing ing many members of both Houses of Parliament, and numerous clergymen. The Dean and Canons met the cor- tege at the west door, and the procession eves formed to the, lantern, beneath which the body, laden with wreaths, wee deposited. A solemn funeral service followed, and the choir sang Handel's anthem, " Weer, the ear heard himr and Spahr's " Blest are the departed:" The Archbishop of Canterbury. the Marquis of Lorne, Sir Richard Cross, anda many notables were amongst the congregation, the Queen and Prince of Wales being represented. After the service the coffin was conveyed to St. Giles, Dorsetehire, for inter- ment. The coffin was taken from the iiikey to Waterloo Station, followed by a number of deputatiom At the sta- tion, and while the coffin was being placed in a carriage, a hand played the funeral march. Large crowds bad assem- bled at the station at a quarter past two, the time of the departure of the train. At the Congregational Union at Hanley, on Thursday, and at the Baptist Union at Swansea, resolutions of sympathy with the relatives and friends of the late Lord Shaftesbury was unanimously adopted. div.p: CREWE is a railway town, and it has a 'railway candidate in the person of Mr. 0. I, STEPHEN, a director of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Some 7,000 work-people are employed at the Com- pany's works; and they and their families may be said to constitute the town of Crewe. But, while the director-candidate for the representation of Crewe is a Tory, the rmajority of the workmen—three-fourths, it is estimated, are Liberal. There is a wide field for intimidation, and, if report speaks truly, intimidation is being practised. It is not perhaps the sort of intimidation that can be brought within the reach of the law; but it exists for all that, as the workmen too well know. Recently a special correspon- dent of the Daily News has been on the spot investigating the facts, and he is very em- phatic in his testimony. "Terror," he says, prevails on the gigantic scale." The work- men who are supposed to hold Liberal Opinions dare not say their souls are • their own, whilst "the Tors, hands can spout their politics as they like, and canvass as they like." There are only four working-men on the local Liberal Committee, whereas "the number of work- ing-men members should be eighty at least," at the time of a Parliamentary election. Ex- cellent workmen have been discharged with the view, it would seem, of striking terror into the hearts of the rest. In another col- umn we give the statement of one of them who is now living in Warrington ; and we ask any flir-minded man who reads it if he balieves an artizan of this stamp would have been discharged if he had not been a Liberal. Mr. G. W. LATHAM, the popular Liberal can- didate, has challenged Mr. STEPHEN to de- clare that the men at the works are at liberty to vote as they like, without fear of suffering for acing in accordance with their political convictions; but he has not met with a re- sponse to this appeal. Dr. ATKINSON, who is a railway official, was chairman of the meet- ing at which Mr. STEPHEN was formally ac- cepted as the ToryCrewe candidate. Referring to the fact that Cwe "Unless the candidate chosen has the influ- ence of the Railway Company behind him, I believe we shall have a hard struggle and an uphill battle." "The influence Cf the Rail- way Company ! ''—" there's the rub." The men are to be used as so many machines to work out the redemption of the Tory party. There is the ballot, of course, but the ballot is of little avail to men who have been turned on the street because they dare to keep a conscience. These men are asked to pay a terrible price for their honesty; and it is the duty of their comrades to avenge them. But how ? it will be asked; and the answer is—by going straight at the next election, and let- ting Mr. STEPHEN see that he has played a bad game—and lost.

--------- THE Anti-vaccinators of Earlestown have rnade:an impression on the Liberal candidate for the Newton Division, if they have not wholly Itnade a convert of him. He was waited upon r.ome time ago by a deputation, who pressed -upon his attention the question of compulsory vaccination; and he promised that he would give the matter his special consideration. He has been as good as his word; he has "read the literature they had left and since sent him," and he frankly confesses that his views on the subject have "quite changed." He is now in favour of doing away with the -compulsory clauses; but deems it prudent not to pledge himself, so that, if returned to Par- liament, he may feel free to listen to the arguments on both sides of the question. The Anti-vaccinators may congratulatq them- selves on the progress they have made; for Colonel MCCORQUODALE now takes a stand which is considerably in advance of the majority of Parliamentary candidates. Sir CHARLES Drum when questioned on the subject on Tuesday evening, said he was in favour of" abolishing cumulative penalties so as to prevent anyone from being punished more than once for not complying with the Act." He thought that was as far as the next Parliament would be likely to go, and .expressed himself as being of opinion that if it had been put to the vote during the last session he would have been beaten on a divi- sion.' We quite agree with Sir CHARLES DILKE that cumulative penalties ought not to , be inflicted; but it is another thing to say that the State should case to interest itself in vaccination.' It cannot be doubted that a per centage of children suffer terribly from 'diseases superinduced by vaccination, and yet it may be that a larger per centage are . saved from the ravages of smallpox. There can be no sudden reversion of policy; the issues at stake are too grave to be lightly treated. There is a mass of evidence, which 'is constantly accumulatingt as to the merits and demerits of vaccination; and it must be left to Time—since Doctors disagree—to separate the wheat from the chaff.

SIR. HENRY PONSONEY, the QUEEN'S pri- vate secretary, has been good enough to open the eyes of the public as to the supposed wealth of her MAJESTY. He has given a flat i Contradiction to the rumour that has been n circulation to the effect that the QUEEN had lately invested [1,000,000 in the purchase of ground rents in the city of London. .Sir HENRY states that the Queen, as an indivi- dual, "has bought nothing and possesses no- thing in the City of London, that she has in- vested no money in ground rents; and that she does not possess a million to invest." As to the Crown lands, which are in the hands of the Commissioners of Woods and Forests, ~, H. PONSONBY thinks it most improbable that any of the revenues of the woods and forests are invested in ground rents. It would seem, however, that he is mistaken as to this, though that does not much matter, it being the concern of the Commissioners rather tha ?f the QUEEN. It is gratifying to find that ft! .MAyasTv is not indifferent to the °Pinion which her people may have 4.3 tp how she disposes of her royal revenue. -AR Interchange of this kind is good alike for

sovereign and subject; it will stimulate loyalty to the throne. But what if her MAJESTY had been a millionaire? She would have still have been far behind some of her subjects in the matter of personal wealth. Sir THOMAS BRASSEY (engineer) is reputed to be worth £5,500,000, and Sir F GOLDSMID (banker) £10,000,000. If we cross the Atlantic, we find a JAY GOULD (broker) with the reputation of being master of £20,000,000, and a VANDERBILT (railway director) stated to be worth £36,0c0,000 When we read of such vast sums, we begin to fear that we shall hear next of her MAJESTY being reproached with her poverty There are people who will say she ought to be a millionaire—for the credit of the nation.

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH BAZ %AR, WIDNES. —The sum realised by this bazaar, held last week end, is £lO7. CIRCULATION OF THE BLOOD.—Dr. McCambridge, of Widnes, on Wednesday evening delivered a lecture upon this subject to the members of St. Bede'e Young Men's Society. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—The members of this society were en- tertained by a magic lantern exhibition on Thursday. M. lon, ef Liverpool, WAS the manipulator, and the Vicar occu- pied the chair. Sr. MICHAEL AND ALL ANGELS' CHURCH, RUNCORN —llll'. Guest, quarry owner, Runcorn, has offered to give half of the stone required for the purpose of building a boundary wall round this church. CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—Last night week Mr. J. D. Jones read an able paper, entitled "Les Miserable& or Outcast London," to the members of this class, at Runcorn. An interesting discussion took place. Rowconx PARISH CarEcn.—The harvest festival was continued on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. T. M. Armson preached, and in the evening the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., of Frodsham. The edifice was crowded at the evening service. FORTHCOMING CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The annual concert of the Runcorn Volunteer Band will take place on Tuesday evening next. Several popular vocalists and in- strumentalists have been engaged, and a capital programme has been arranged. A NEW Wxsrow POINT Sznamnia.—The trial trip of the new steam tug *• Emulator," built to the order of the Wes- ton Point Steam Towing Company, took place on Wednes- day, and WAS very satisfactory. The tug accomplished the trip to Liverpool in an hour and fifteee minutes, having two loaded barges in tow as far as Garston. THE FORTHCOMING LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUN. CORN.—The arrangements for the visit of Mr. H. Gladstone, M.P., to Runcorn, on the 20th inst., are now complete. Twelve hundred tickets of admission to the body of tbe hall and the gallery will be distributed, and an additional 100 tor the gallery. There will be 50 places reserved for ST. Palm's Cwrracn, Wirms.—Large congregations assembled in this church on Sunday, when the harvest thanksgiving services were continued. The Rev. W. Pres • ton (Runcorn) and the Rev. J. W. Rhodes, vicar of St. Chad's, Liverpool, were the preachers. On Monday even- ing, the Vicar of Widnes, delivered a sermon. The collec- tions amounted to £4O. FARE WORTH PARISH CHTIRCH.—The annual harvest fes- tival took place on Wednesday evening, when the edifice was tastefully decorated with fruit, flowers, and cereals. The Venerable A rchde icon Bardsley preached a sermon from the text, " Neither say they in their heart, lot us now fear the Lord our God that giveth rain, both the former and the latter in His season: Re reserveth unto us the appointed weeks of the harvest." A collection was made on behalf of the curates' fund EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.—An explosion of a serious nature occurred at the works of Messrs. T. Snaps and Co., on Sun- day. Two plumbers were at work filling up with mortar the intention in a vitriol chamber, when the imprisoned gas acquired such force as to buret two sides of the struc- ture, and the lead and wood work Was scattered about. For. tunately the men were standing at the sides of the hamber that retained their position, and escaped injury. The dam- age is estimated at £2O STABBPD BY A BOY ATI WIDNES.—On Sunday night last, Richard Smith, son of a furnaceman living in Margaret street, and James Matthews, son of a labourer residing in . . . . . .

Carollue-st.,were playing tegether,when Matthews flourished a penknife, and with a tragic air struck his companion on the right breast. The blade penetrated the boy's clothing, and inflicted a rather serious wound, which is, however, now healing nicely. It is thought that the boy was animated by the heroism of the "penny dreadful " order. WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOL.—The winter session was commeneed this week, and conforming to the custom of last year the capital library of the school will be open to the public on Saturday evenings. Magazines, period- icals, and newspapers are provided. On Tuesday evening next the annual distribution of prizes takes place in Lace's. street School, and the proceedings will be made additionally interesting by a lecture on the Transit of Venus by the Rev. S. J. Perry, F.R.S. Full particulars in our advertia. ing columns. Rtmccons IRISE Nevrorrausys.—At the weekly meeting of the Runcorn branch of the Irish Nationalists on Tuesday, Mr. Edward Hill presiding, it was resolved " That this ' meeting of members of the Runcorn branch of Irish Na., tional League do call on the Irishmen of this district to put themselves at once into line with their countrymen in Ire- land by organising themselves for the coming Parliamentary elections." Mr. John Fallon read a piper OD the rising at Wexford, and the President recited a poem. " We're Irish everywhere." THE THEATRE ROYAL, Rinccontt.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, Mr. T. H. Hitchen, solicitor, made an application on behalf of Mrs. James, the proprietress of the Theatre Royal for the renewal of the license to that build- ing. Mr. W. R. Waldron, lessee, made a similar applica- tion, and produced an agreement showing that he had leased the theatre for three years.—The Bench fixed the 19th inst fer ths bearing of the application.—The county surveyor has inspected the tteatre and expressed the opinion that the alterations made have made the building a suitible one. I GOOD TEMPLARISM AT WIDNES.—The Samaritan Lodge held its weekly session on Monday evening. There was a large attendance of members, and Bro. Machin, W.C.T., presided. After the usual routine business had been gone through, an enjoyable entertainment of songs and readings was glven by Sister Smith, and Bros. Parker, Machin, Wrie,ht, Fairhurst, Piper, and Webb. The members of the Widnes Excelsior Degree Temple held their monthly meet- ing on Friday last week. Bro. Machin, T.D., presided, in the absence of Bro. Galilee, D.T. The ceremony of initia- tion of third degrees having been performed, the Sisters provided a fruit banquet and ice-cream, and the proceedings were enlivened by songs and solos rendered by Brothers and Sisters. NARROW ESCAPE OF THREE MEN AT RUNCORN.—By the last train from Lime-street on Saturday night, Edward Doyle, Patrick Carty, and William Thomas, Irishmen, ar- rived at Runcorn railway station, having forgotten to alight at Ditton, where they are employed as labourers at the works of the Liver Alkali Company. They were directed how to reach Runcorn Bridge' but in the darkness they rambled into Dute's Field and fell into a "gut." Luckily there was not much water in the channel at the time? and they cried loudly for assistance. Albert Povey, dock con- stable, and P.C. Boson appeared on the scene, and by means of ropes rescued the men from their uncomfortable and dangerous position. All three men were much ex, hansted, and were taken to a lodging-house in Mersey- etreet. Thomas and Carty were able to walk to Ditson on Sunday, but Doyle was so injured that he was unable to move, an he was attended by Dr. Mangan. WIDNES REVISION COURT —The labours of the gentle- men engaged at this court have been most arduous. The sitti.gs commenced on Friday morning last week, and were continued morning and evening (Sunday excspted) until Thursday night. On Wednesday night it was approaching midnight when the court rose, this prolonged application to duty being necessary in order to finish by the Bth inst, which is the last day fixed by the Act. The business was concluded at seven o'clock on Thursday evening, and the representatives of the political parties and the Revising Barrister (Mr. Cottingham) appeared thoroaghly "fagged out." The woik has been of an almost entirely routine character. Mr. H. B. Shores and Mr. T. G. Middlebrook, who have conducted the revision for the Liberal party, have been especially active, and when the results can be fully ascertained a very large preponderance of Liberal voters will be shown nanc.Gralins FOR HEALTH.—Sanitary Importance of Washing at Home.—This can be done with ease and economy and the clothes made beautifully sweet, wholesome, lily-white, and fresh as sea breezes by using Hudson's Extract of Soap, avoid- ing all risk of contagion with Infected clothes at Laundries, or where the washing is put out. A RUNCORN VAGRANT.—Edward Johnson, an old offender, was sentenced to a month's hard labour by the Runcorn magistrates, on Thursday, for sleeping in the stable of Mr Samuel Crosby, Top Locks. ROBBERY BY BOYS AT WIDNES —Michael Evoy, Michael Ford. Michael Burke. and John Ford. hays, were charged at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, with stealing a quantity of timber, value 61, from a fence in Warrington- road, the property of Mr. E. V. Bibby, Gannon Copper Weres. The boys had made statements to P.C. Pitt which incrimieated each other, and they were each sentenced to I receive six strokes with the birch rod. ASSAULT AT RUSCORN.—At Runcorn Police Caurt, OD Thursday, Thomas Gandy, a young man, pleaded guilty to assaulting Margaret Bramble. About eleven o'clock on the previous night the 'young woman was in King-street. when the prisoner met her and knocked her down. He kicked her whilst in that position. Her screams brought P.C. Pinney on the scene, and the prisoner was apprehended.— The prisoner, who said he was far gone In drink, was fined 20s and costs. RIVAL FISH DEALERS AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Jane Drury, fish dealer. Cooper. street, was summoned for assaulting John Morn., also a Ash dealer, for whom Mr. Lake appeared. On Tuesday, the 291 h ult., Morris was hawking fish in Cooper-street, when the defendant used violent language to him, alleged his fish was bad, and then struck him with a fish. She al-o aimed several stones at him. The defendant pleaded guilty, and she was fined 55 and emits, total 24e, or a fortnight's hard labour. Arraex ON FEMALES AT WIDNES.—At Whines Petty Sec. Moss, on Wednesday, James McGurl, a young man, was charged with assaulting Annie Welsh. It was alleged that about half-past eleven on Saturday night Welsh and another girl were passing up Aiidwood-etreet, when the prisoner and several other young men commenced to push them about. At length the prisoner threw them to the ground and kicked them.—The defenoe was a direct denial, the prisoner stat- ing that the prosecutor bad a knife in her hand.—A fine of 105 and coats was imposed. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT Woex.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the following persons were sum- moned for neglecting to send their children regularly to School :—Jemes Gorst, James Simpson, Hugh Jones, John Kinsella (two cases), Thomas Dunne, Charles McKenna Robert Rosy, and John Hoolighan. Mr. Denby appeared on behalf at the School Board, and the cases were proved be attendance officers Joynson and Rowe. The usual line of &s was imposed. Martin Holland, an incorrigible, was sent to St. George's Industrial School, Liverpool. A DISSOLUTE FELLOW AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. W. Banks at Runcorn Police Court, on Seturday, Matthew Heffern, shoemaker, Frodshem, was brought up under a warrant charged that he being a person able to maintain himself and family did on the 19th Sep- tember leave his wife and family chargeable to the common fund of the Runcorn Union, after being convicted as an idle and disorderly person.—Mr. Houghton, collector to the Guardians, said the prisoner had been twice previously be- fore their worships for deserting his family, whom he never recognised.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.—Mr. Handley re- marked that there was no doubt the prisoner was an idle dissolute fellow who did not intend te maintain his family. —He was sentenced to three months' hard labour. RUFFIANISM AT RUNCORIC.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, William Morrell, a youth, was charged with ' cuisine an obstruction to the footpath. He pleaded guilty. P.S. Neild sail on Sunday night, the 13th September, the I defendant and five or six other lads were running against people and wrestling with one another on the footpath in Church-street. The defendant put his arm round the neck of a young woman and would not release her until the ser- geant came up. He then refused to give his name, and be took him to the police station. People could scarcely get along the street on a Sunday night through lads like the defendant.—Supt. Leah said these boys were a very great annoyance to people leaving church or chapel. The de- fendant was very impudent and abusive when caught —Mr. Campbell characterised the defendant's conduct as teneal and ruffianly. He was fined £1 and costs 9s 6d, or 14 days' hard labour. Bwrgestea. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY—This *society cominenced its meetings for the winter session on Wednes- day night, R. Wyllie, president, in the chair. After the usual preliminary business had been gone through, the Pre- • aident proceeded to deliver his opening address, giving a digest of subjects of interest for mutual improvement so- cieties. He drew attention to the importance of giving due , attention to the cultivation of a good sound ployecal con- stitution, as being important for the support of a powerful working mind. Then having treated OR the means of attain- log knowledge by instruction, observation, and experience, I be proceeded to chew that knowledge, simply as knewledge, *as of little use to a man, unless it was digested and the principles drawn thereupon, appropriated, generalized, and applied. The successful application of knowledge was the I greatest of the talent and individuality of a man. The pre- , sident proceeded to illustrate how the various subjects of science, art, literature, and theology may be taken up as subjects of essay, debate, or for thegenersl acquisuion of knowledge. He concluded his remarks by reminding those present of the saying of Lord B icon, that reading maketh a full man, conference a ready man, and writing an exact ' man.—The Rev. J. D. Thomas proposed a vote of thanks to the president for his address—The motion Was seconded by Mr. George Lacey and unanimously carried. HOLY TRINITY Y.M.C.A., RUNCORN. The inaugural meeting of the 12th session of this society was held at Trinity schools, on Monday evening. The proceedings com- menced with a fruit banquet, followed by a miscellaneous entertainment., at which the chair was occupied by Mr. W. H. Verdin, the Conservative Candidate for the division.— Mr. A. Cunningham, the secret: ry, read the annual report ' of the committee, which was of a very encouraging charac- ter. The Chairman delivered a brief address in which he referred to the advantages of Young Men's Christian Asso• ciations. Through these societies a young man could make many friends with tastes similar to his own, and he would to a great extent avoid the evils of bad companionship. The following programme was gene through :—Pianoforte solo, Miss Tomlinson ; song, " Love of home." Miss Pres- ton ; recitation, Miss Tyrie • song, " Madoline," Mr. C. Pownall; duet, Miss Edwards and Master Cook • clad- Quetta solo, Mr. Jones ; song, "Auntie," Miss Lord (Wid- nes); pianoforte solo Miss Isherwood ; song, Mies Preston; duet, Rev. George Preston and Miss Preeon. On the motion of the Rev. W. Preston, seconded by Mr. W. Han- Wiest). a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman. A similar compliment was paid to the president and vice-pre- sidents of the association, and to those ladies and gentlemen who bad taken part in the evenieg'a entertainment. A WIDNES CONTRACTOR HEAVILY FtSTED.— }lobed Smithson, publican and contractor, was charged at Widnes IPetty Sessions, on Wednesday, with cruelly illtreating a horse. P.C. Bruce said on Tuesday evening, the 22nd, he saw a mare attached to an empty lurry, standing before the Horns Inn, Farnworth. The animal was covered with sweat. The defendant came out of the inn and shouted to the man in charge of the horse " All right, Bill, I'll make the go. I've a Tip- perary rifle here," at the same time flourishing a thick stick. In a few minutes be emerged from the inn again, and drove off in the direction et Moorfield-lane, striking the animal twice with the stick. Near the Black Horse Hotel he ordered the break to be put on, and he hit the animal across the ribs, the right shoulder, and on the legs, causing it to fall down twice. The constable interfered, and the defendant attempted to run the waggon over him. Later the same night Inspector Wood and the constable examined the horse in the defendant's stables. There was some skin knocked off the knees of the fore legs ; the inside off bind leg was cut and bleeding, and there were several small lumps on the off shoulder. The horse was trembling, and appeared to have sweated very much. He could see where the sweat had been running over the hoofs. The defence was that the mare, which was a valuable one, had been out to grass for three months, and was very "collar proud." In the afternoon she plunged, jibbed, kicked, and threw her- self down, eventually smashing the trap. In the evening he put her in the lorry, and she got her leg over the shaft. He denied striking her more than twice. A fine of 40s and costs, 15s, was imposed. Gaskell, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Wall, a young man, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a pony by working it whilst in an unfit state. Wm. Furness, provision dealer, Warrington, was sum- moned for allowing the animal to be worked.—On the 24th September, Wall was driving the horse in Widnes, and noticing that it appeared to be in pain, be examined it. Under the saddle he found a raw wound about the size of a crown, from which blood and matter was oozing.—A fine of and costs was

imposed. Mn. GLADSTONE AND THE LITE GoVERN3rENT.— Mr. Gladstone and Lord Richard Grosvenor have written giving an unqualified contradiction to a statement recently made by General Sir Alexander Gordon, at Fraserburgh, Aberdeenshire, to the effect that the late Government had sought their defeat, that at the Cabinet Council on the afternoon of the day •on which the Ministry fell three members of the Cabinet tendered their resignation on the Irish question, and that Lord Richard Grosvenor unsuc- cessfully urged the Government to adjourn the de- bate. The reports that Mr. Gladstone intended to speak in public previous to delivering his election addresses in Midlothian next month have been dis- posed of by the right hon. gentleman himself. He was invitea to attend a Liberal meeting in Chester, but declined on the ground that he is compelled to husband his strength for the coming campaign. At a meeting of the Midlothian Liberal Association on Wednesday resolutions were adopted expressing satisfaction that Mr. Gladstone had consented to lead the Liberal party in the new Parliament, and approving of his recent manifesto as indicating a scheme of present action on-which all sections of • Liberals could unite. • COAGIILTNE —Cement for Broken Artleles, 6d. The money was paid. Mn.. CHA.S.IBERLAIN'S VISIT TO HAWARDRE —Mr. Chamberlain paid a visit to' Mr. Gladstone on Wed- nesday. Mr. Gladstone had arranged to accompany Sir Thomas Brassey to Hawarden School during the evening, where the genial baronet had arranged to deliver a lecture to men only on Manliness and Faith. ' At the last moment, however, Mr. Gladstone felt himielf unable to leave the castle, and, for the remainder of the evening, was closeted with Mr. Chamberlain. ' The dinner party included Sir Thos. and Lady Brassey, Mr. Chamberlain, and Alderman Robert Frost, ,president of the Chester Liberal Asso- ciation, Mr. Chamberlain-remained over night at Hawarden Castle, and left on Thursday afternoon. Ile drove to Broughton Hall Station, on the Chester, I Mold, and Denbigh line, and proceeded to Chester, leaving by the 4-20 express for Birmingham. Mr. I Chamberlain was recognised on Chester platform by the crowd, but there was no demonstration. Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain had a conference at Hawarden Castle on Thursday, occupying the greater part of the morning. • LIBERAL V. TORY FINANCE.—With the object of refuting some of the claims put forward by some I (...4 the Conservativearthe National Liberal Federa- tion of Birmingham have published a coloured dia- gram in the form of a leaflet dealing with .the rechic- tion of the National Debt. The diagram illustrates in a manner` not likely to be' mistaken the fact that between 1868 and 1874 the Liberals reduced the , debt by £27,289,639, and that in the succeeding six years of Conservative rule the reduction waano more the.* £1,080,310. The Liberals, again at the end of 1884 had made a second reduction of £29,645,137. A simple calculation thus shows that during the last sixteen years for every 4kd of debt paid off by the Conservatives the Liberals have paid off 20s. The National Press Agency has also issued a number .of leaflets on finance. -The diagrams show at a glance "Annual increase of National Debt," "Increase and Decrease of Unfunded Debt," "Taxation Itetnitted," and" Surpluses and Deficits?! No Tory will offer to make a stand on the question of finance against Liberal provided with these leaflets. • . Sin RICHARD CROSS AT BARNSLEY.—Sir Richard Cross, on Thursday afternoon, opened the Barnsley , Conservative Club, and in'the-evening addressed a crowded meeting, at the Public Hall. The question, he said, which the country had to consider was whether they would again entrust the Government " to those who during the'last five years had brought upon it discredit, disgrace, and disaster. If the Liberal party obtained a majority, the Radicals had given plain warning that they would not join the Ministry unless they could have their way, and therefore it was necessary for the electors to be I aware of moderate men, as they would inevitably be dragged into the Radical net. As to foreign affairs, the desire of the present Government on the East, erttßoumelian question had been to act with the! other Powers who were parties to the Berlin Treaty, and he was sorry that some Liberal speakers had spoken with some exultation of a breach of treaty which had caused great anxiety to European states- men. ' Upon domestic matters, he claimed that a , very decided programme had been put forward by Lord Salisbury, and that the Conservative party had done as much as their opponents for the working- men, without setting class against class. THE SHIP CANAL PROSPECTIIS.—The preliminary iprospectus of the Manchester Ship Canal Company Tins been issued. This first appeal is being made in what has been spoken of as a semi-private. manner —that'is, it is not being made through the profes- sional channels by which investors in similar un- dertakings are usually approached. The promoters have adopted this plan because they desire as far as possible to confine their subscriptions at the outset to the district which the canal is designed to serve, and to keep the stock out of the hands of specula- tors. The prospectus is accompanied by an elabor- ate map showing not only the route of the proposed canal, but the towns and manufacturing districts ,Which it is likely, to serve, and the existing railway and canal connections therewith. ludging from the special information given on this map, the de- I velopment of a coal traffic is looked forward to as ! likely to he a very important feature. The share capital is fixed at £8,000,000, and in the estimates we find that allowance, is made for interest on £1,800,000 of loan capital, which the promoters hope to obtain at 4 per cent. The time likely to be re- quired for the construction of the canal is estimated to be four years, and the time reckoned as sufficient for the ' largest vessels to traverse the canal from Eastham toManchester is eight hours. It is proposed to raise the £8,000,000 of the capital by the issue of 800,000 shares of £lO each—lOs per , share being payable on application and 10s on allotment, and the remainder at such periods as may be found necessary. It is thought that the revenue of the Bridgewater Canal undertaking will. enable the directors to pay interest at the rate of £3 per cent per annum upon all capital which it will be necessary to call up during the first twelve months. The following are by the Act appointed the first directors of OW company :—Mr. Daniel Adamson, C.E., J.P.; Councillor-Henry Boddington, jun. ; Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P.; Mr. Wm. div.head: MARRIAGE OF mit. T.__r. MATHIBSON, OF
div.p: MARRIAGE OF mit. T.__r. MATHIBSON, OF
WIDNES.

On Tuesday, Mr. Thom is Train Mathieson, eldest son of Mr. Neil Mathieson, of Beactffield, Prince'a Park, Liver- pool, and chemical manufacturer. Widnes, was married to Miss Mary Gertrude Robinson, third daughter of the late Mr. Peter Robinson, J.P., of Warrington. The ceremony was celebrated at St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington, near Lynam, and the sacred edifice contained a large number of relatives and friends of the bride and bridegroom. The officiating clergy were the Rev. J. Collin, M.A., and the Rev. S. Wilkinson (vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington). Miss Robinson, the younger sister of the bride, was the brides- maid, and she was adorned with a beautiful diarnone neck- lale. the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. Douglas Mathieson was the best man. The service was full choral. As the happy pair left the church they were greeted with a heavy shower of rice, and many were the good wishes expressed for their future happiness and welfare. The breakfast took place at the house of the bride. The presents were very numerous and costly, amongst them being a han.lsome and valuable silver tea and coffee service At Widnes the interesting event was celebrated with con- siderable rejoicing. The works of Messrs. Mathieson and Co. were gay with a hundred coloured emblems, the ship- ping in the docks were decorated with flags and bunting and tugs were displayed on many buildings in the town. The employes of Messrs. Mathieson had a half-holiday, and in the afternoon were entertained with an excellent tea. The building known as the Glycerine Shed had been con- verted into a dining ball, and decorated with flags, greenery, plants, and mottoes presented a very bright and comfortable appearanc.. The top wall had been very tistefullv adorned, the centre piece being the sentiment "Lone life and happiness to the Bride and Bridegroom?' "May every biassing agent them," "God bless the happy pair," " Prosperity te N. Mathieson and C 0.," and " Suc- cess to the chemical trade," occupied positions in ether parts of the building. About 450 persons sat down to the tables that ranged the length of the room, and they ap- peared to enjoy heartily the excellent repast provided by Mr. Parkes, of the Central Hotel. While thus engaged Mr. and Mrs. N. Mathieson, accompanied by a number of wed- ding guests entered the room and received a perfect ovation. Mr. Douglas Mathieson, on behalf of the newly-married pair, thanked those present for the most beautiful present they had made to them. It was all the more gratifying to them because it was unexpected. (Cheers.) Mr. •Mattbieson (the father) said that glad and happy assembly had something of sadness in it. It reminded him that he was getting into the " sere and yellow leaf." It was unlikely he would see such another gatherieg as that in the works, and he must reconcile himself to the fact that !se must pay the debt of nature or leave Widnes before very long. He had been very much impressed by their kindness in giving his son so handsome a present, which was all the more appreciated because it was unexpected. Of all the gifts he had received, theirs was the one he prized most of all. (Cheers.)—Mr. Robert Morris (son-in-law) made a jocalar speech appropriate to the occasion, and cheers were given for Mr. D Mathieson, Mr. W. W. Gossage, Mr. IL S. Timmis, Mr. W. H. Busbby, and Mr. A. F. ferupdrit, all of whom were present, and they all responded with a few appropriate remarks. After the tables had been cleared away a concert took place, those present being supplied with refreshments. THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. The members of the Town Council who retire this year are :—North-West Ward: Messrs. G. Dakin (L) and Wm. Pierpoint (L); North-East Ward: Messrs. F. Dixon (L) and James H:ritter (L) ; South-East Ward: Messrs. W. Br.s.lton (C) and Thomas Hutchinson (C); South -15 est Ward: Messrs. W. J. Burgess (C) and T, Litton (C) ; Latchford Ward: Mr. Joseph Taylor (C). We understand that it has been arranged between the two parties in the town that, in view of the coming Parliamen- tary election, and in order to avert the turmoil and expense of a contest, the representation should remain as at present. All the retiring members of the CALAncil, we have reason to believe, will be re- elected.

div.head: NEW BOARD SCHOOLS AT
div.p: THE NEW BOARD SCHOOLS AT

GREAT SANKEY. Ott Tuesday afternoon the foundation stone of the new Board Schools for Great Sankey was laid by the Rec. E. S. Jackson, the vicar. The site of the new schoo!s is eitua, ted a short distance from the church on the Warrington side, and when built they will front on to the Liverpool. road. In the schools there will be a large room capable of acc-mmodating 200 children, and provided with a recess 32 feet by 17 feet. There will also be two classrooms, each 20 feet by 18 feet, allowing accommodation for BO boys and girls. Cloakroom, lavatories, boardroom, and a dining- room, for the accommodation of the scholars who carry their dinners, will be provided. The style of the building will be Gothic, the front elevations being constructed of brick, with sandstone dressing. The coat of site, schools, teacher's residence, boundary walls, and laying out of ward is estimated to be £1,640. The building will be heat-it by means of hot water pipes and open fires. The weather on Tuesday afternoon was very =propitious, there bring a heavy downpour of rain during the whole of the ceremony. This considerably marred the attendance, but, notwith- standing, there were several persons present, including the following members of the School Board—Messrs. Turner (chairman), Kerfoot, Ridgway, and Cook Mr. S. Sutton (the clerk). and. Mr. Nodal (architect), Mr- Rama- bottem (Pendleton) builder, and others. The school chil- dren were also present and sung hymns. The Rev. E. S. Jackson was presented with a silver trowel by Mr. Turner on behalf of the Board, and with a mallet by the builder, Mr. Ramsbottom.—Having engaged in prayer. the Rev. E. S. Jacksoti declared the stone to be laid. He said he had great pleasure in being present at that cere- mony. He believed his good friend beside him—Mr. Tur- ner—suggested his name to the Board, as he was one who lived among them and was, perfectly irrespective of any' feeling of party or clan, always ready to do anyone a mood turn when he could. He was not *al ways -able to do it, but he was pleased if he conic'. Ida hoped that all who were educated in that school would be made good and capable citizens, be able to look forward to a better world than this when th.iy had • finished. He spoke as a clergyman, and he was very glad the Board had taken care of religious teaching in their school, for no matter how good secular education might be in itself, if it were not tempered with religion nothing good came of it. (Haar, hear.) He felt as a clergyman of that parish that he must thank the Beard for the way in which they had taken the matter in hand. Re also said as a rate- payer that he considered the Board had done uncommorly well for them, and he Was glad to hear their chairman say that they should have a lees rate to pay. Ile thought the Board was most efficient, and he begged to thank the mem- bers on behalf of the ratepayers for the way they had managed affairs in tbe past, and he was sure they would go on managing them well. (Applause.) The scholars having sung a hymn, Mr. Jackson pronoanced. the benediction and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY. Lord Salisbury's speech delivered at Newport list ! night was eagerly looked for, alike by Conservatives i and Liberals. The one wanted to know what they i were to fight for, the other what they were to fight. I Sir M. H. Beach is reported to have said that there j was no need for the issue of a counter-blast to Mr. i Gladstone's manifesto, because the policy of the ; Conservative Ministry 'was made known in their I speeches. This, if said at all by the Chancellor of j the Exchequer, must have been said with his tongue ' in his cheek. There was certainly nothing in his I own speech indicative of a policy, and Lord Ran- dolph Churchill being otherwise engaged, has for a month been silent. With the exception of Lord Salisbury, there was no other member of the Govern- ment with authority to set forth a programme. As a matter of fact, there was, up to last night, nothing before the country in the shape of a declaration of Conservative policy, and these utterances of Lord Salisbury were looked forward to with exceptional interest. The Marquis made a speech of prodigious length before a carefully selected and enthusiastic audi- ence. Infinite pains had been taken by the man- agers of the meeting to keep out all disturbing elements, and thus Lord Salisbury was permitted, as every public man should be, to address the meet- ing without interruption. The speech will not rank among the brightest and most incisive efforts of the Conservative chieftain. Lord Salisbury is best in attack. Weighted with the grave respon- sibility of his position and embarrassed by the knowledge that he had no clearly defined plan to offer to the waiting country, he beat about a good deal. The only points on which he was absolutely clear was in declaration of the Conservative com- monplace about the union of Church and State, in his denunciation of Mr. Chamberlain's proposal for small allottments, and in his declaration against 1 free ed.neStion. For the rest he rather hinted at pos- sibilities of further conversion to Liberal principles.' He was in favour of extension of the ptinciple of ! Local Government, though apparently with the main object of easing the rates on houses and lands, and throwing a larger proportion upon the wage- earning arid professional class. He announced him- self as a convert to Sir W. Lawson's Local Option proposals, though, afraid of going too far, be would have the bx.periment a temporary one. He was in favour of simplifying and cheapening the transfer of land, proposals for which have long been before Parliament in the hands of a Liberal Lord Chancel- lor. As for Ireland, the point on which his declara- tions were more closely watched, his speech will convey much encouragement to the Parnellites, who now openly avow their desire for the separa- ation of England and Ireland. Lord Salisbury is not ready for this yet: But, to use his own words, " We should be holding out false expectations if we avow a belief which, as yet at all events, we cannot entertain ;" that is to say, Conservatives are not yet ready to make open cause with the Separatists. But Lord Salisbury says to Mr. Parnell "for goodness sake don't desert us at this junctin e. Tide us over the General Election. Sustain us in power in the House of Commons, and then we'll see what we can do in the way of bringing about what we will call Imperial Federation." This speech will not do much to enliven the elec- toral battle which is now drawing near at hand. There will be more speechmaking next week. But until Lord Randolph Churchill joins in the fray no- thing particularly lively may be looked for. Mr. Gladstone has issued a long manifesto. Lord Sal- isbury has made a speech nearly twice as long. Issue has been joined; but no heated feeling has been aroused, such as that which throbbed through the country in 1880. The reason for this is obvious. It takes two to fight, and the Conservatives have already thrown up the sponge. They have no policy such as they were wont to go into battle with in 1832 when they fought the Reform Bill, or in 1845, when they tried to keep the cheap loaf from the hand of starving workmen. Their policy has hitherto always been one of negation. The Liberals have proposed, the Conservatives have, opposed. Now that role is abandoned. All they can do is to dress themselves up as nearly like Liberals as pos- sible and promise Liberal measures with the hope of being permitted to introduce into them as strong . a tincture of Conservatism •as the House of Com- mons will allow. In these circumstances the strug- gle is for men, not measures, and the battle cry of the Conservatives in the coming contest will be • "Salisbury," whilst Liberals will once more rally , to the cry of "Gladstone." . The death of Lord Shaftesbury has elicited a profounder and wider burst of regret than has the loss of any other public man for many years. Lord Shaftesbury had his failing, inasmuch as he was inclined to take a narrow view of theological matters. But that named, there remains nothing to be said to lessen the beatify and completeness of his character. Though generous, he was shrewd and of an eminently practical mind. Many men who have a reputation for charity are sometimes ' imposed upon by worthless people. But this did not often happen to Lord Shaftesbury. As an in- stance of the practical business-like way in which he dealt with affairs is the story of his dealing with the East End clergyman who some years ago wrote to him in despair, declaringth at he had done all that in his power to keep his parish going, and that he was now at the end of his .tether. Lord Shaftes- bury's answer was short but to the point. " I will come and be your guest for a fortnight," he wrote. lie went to the vicarage, lived its home life, and went about with the vicar through all the high- ways and byeways of the parish. The result was that he gave help liberally and judicially, and the parish is now one of the most prosperous of its class. The new earl is a man hitherto little known, so little that I have heard many people indicate the belief that Mr. Evelyn Ashley, a well-known mem- ber of the last Administration, would succeed his father in the title. Amongst the other delights which Mr. Gilbert has for guests at his charming house is a private hearing of the Mikado. After dinner the host leads the way to the telephone room which is connected directly with the Savoy Theatre. Applying the telephone to the ear one can hear quite plainly what is going on at the theatre, the music, the spoken words, the songs, and the applause. It is of course faint, but quite distinct, and the identity of the performers can be recognised as easily as if one' were looking down upon them on the stage. Mr. Gilbert is just starting for Egypt, where he will spend his holidays and perhaps pick up some , notions for a piece to succeed the Mikado, which in

To my own know- ledge, honest loyal men who stood out successfully against 1 the and League have lately succumbed to the National ; League. such men are joining ovary day. Boycotting ! has no longer a sensational character; it is carried out, 88 a Leaguer said at Lioterick. it should be, 'without proclama- tion or bell.ringing, silently and judiciously.' If our British rulers make full inquiry. they will no longer cry 'peace' where there is no peace."
