NOTES 1W THE WAY. Halifax journeyed to Broughton to oppose Broughton Rangers, but the Yorkshire men had to retire beaten by two tries to three minors scored by Halifax. Both teams were strongly represented, and a grand game was the result. Swinton were far too good for Sale, this fixture being played on the Sale ground. The home team was hopelessly defeated, not scoring a single minor, against five tries and six minors scored by the :r opponents. Swinton evidently want a _pal kicker.
The Warrington and Broughton fixture was pleasantly contested, but Warrington were defeated through the want of a referee, as the try scored by Fairfield Turner was un- questionably a legitimate one.

Salford took a trip to Bradford to oppose the crack York- shire club, the match being witnessed by something like 8,000 persons. Bradford won by, two goals and four minors to Salford nil. This is now the third successive win of Bradford, who have previously defeated Rochdale Hornets and Broughton. The off side play of S Mord was very noticeable, and they had to pay the penalty twice. Liverpool easily defeated the Gymnasium at Sefton Park, by three goals and four minors to nil. Neither side scored the first half.

Manchester had a practice game, the first sixteen oppos- ing the next twenty--six, and the sixteen won by one goal and one try to one try anti nine minors. This club play their first fixture to-day, when they oppose the Free Wan- derers.

Runcorn have had a tour, opposing Llanelly on Satur- day, and Cardiff on Monday, but in both matches they suf- fered defeat. I think they had under-rated the playing powers of both Llanelly and Cardiff. Widnes went to Oldham to play the first fixture of the season between these clubs, and, after a well-contested game. Oldham were declared the victors by two tries and one minor to one try and two minors.

St. Helens received a visit from Sutton, but the home team were too strong for the visitors, who suffered defeat by two goals, four tries, and nine minors to three minors. Wigan met Ulverston on the ground of the former, ani won by too goals, two tries, and three minors tl nil. Batley met their first reverse of the season, at the hands of Wakefield Trinity, being easily beatsn by two tries and seven minors to nil.

div.head: UNIYA.WFIh POSSESSION OF 108 RA:BBITS.
div.p: UNIYA.WFIh POSSESSION OF 108 RA:BBITS.
EXTRAORDINLRY CiSE•

Ai Rundern Petty Sessions, on Monday, before the Rev. E.A. P. Campbell and Mr. W. Bankes, James Rigby. of Frodsham, was summoned to answer a charge of being sus- pected of coming from land where he had been in search Of. , game. and of being unlawfully in possession of 108 rabbits. The defendant was also charged with aiding and abetting divers other persons in poaching and being in possession of 108 rabbits.—Major Hamersley, chief constable, was present to watch the case nn • behalf of the police.—Mr. Dreaper, solicitor, Chester, defended.—About midnight on Sunday, the 20th September, P.C. Ygerton visited Field Farm, Sutton, occupied by Thomas Bate. Through an aperture he saw a large number of rabbits hanging over a rail in the granary, and he concealed himself in the fog. man's cabin on the railway, and watched the building all night. About seven o'clock on Monday morning the defen- dant drove up with a pony and cart, which contained three empty hampers. Half an hour later he left the place, and the officer followed and called to him to stop. The defen- dant thrashed the pony, but the officer succeeded in catch- ing it. In reply to neestions, the defendant said he had only fruit in the hampers, bat the constable discovered that they contained 108 rabbits. The hampers were addressed, 'Wiliam Pickles, fruit and potato dealer, Belton." The constable seized the rabbits. and subsequently visited Bate's granary. The rabbits had disappeared from that building. —Wm. Johnson. farm labourer, Mary Meredith, servant, de- posed to the defendant coming to the farm on Monday morning.—Thomas Bate, the farmer, said on Sunday, the 20.11, he was awakened about five o'clock in the morning, and he was told there were some men who wanted to leave some rabbits. Ho said he knew nothing about them, and did not want to have anything to do with them. He ow not see the men, and did not know who they were. He went away from home that day, and on returning at night he went in the granary. There were some bags there. He never saw any rabbits.—Mr. Dreaper: Didn't you supply these rabbits to Rigby? I never did.—l believe it is a fact that you have received rabbits from people before? Never in this world.—William Bennie's, station- master, Halton, said on the 21st the defendant brought two hampers to be despatched to Wil- liam Pickles, fruit and potato dealer, Bolton. He said they coutai, ed plums, but afterwards stated ,the con- tents were rabbits.—P.C. Darrock deposed that the defend- ant had a raboit warren at Belle Monte but there were no wild rabbits whatever upon the land —George Rigby, second gamekeeper to Sir Richard Brooke, said be and the head keeper on Sunday morning, the 20th ult., went over the land. They could track where a gang of about a dozen poachers had been, and they could see the peg holes and footrnarke. They traced the footsteps in the direction of Sutton.—Mr. Dreaper contended that there was not the slightest eYidence against his client.. The whole case, he rested upm the merest thread of suspicion. There was not one atom of proof that the game was obtained un- lawfully. From the evidence and Oa manner of Mr. Bate, it was evident that he was an accessory to the crime, if one had been committed.—The magistrates retired .to consider their decision. On returning. Mr. Campbell said they had decided to convict upon the second summons, and dismile the first. They had no hesitation in saying that Mr. Dreaper's remaiks with reference to Mr. Bate were scarcely justified, and were damaging to the character of any respect- able man. There was no evidence at all that could call them forth, and the Bench were sorry they had been made, —Mr. Dreaper said he should certainly apologise were be not aware of other things behind. He would, however, apologise to their worships.—Mr. Campbell : Very much obliged.—A fine of £3 and costs, £3 14s Ad, was imposed, and the rabbits were ordered to be forfeited.—Mr. Dreaper asked for a case to be stated in the ordinary course.—Rigby asked for time to pay the money, but the Bench declined to do so, and gave him the alternative of two months' im- prisonment.

div.head: REIGN OF TERROR AT
div.p: THE REIGN OF TERROR AT
CREWE.

A special correspondent of the Doily News gives an account in Tuesday's issue of the " reign of terror" at Crewe consequent upon the sort of in- fluence which is being brought to bear upon Liberals employed at the works of the London and North. Western Railway Company to vote for Mr.. 0 L. Stephen, a Tory director of the company. We give extracts, which tell their own tale : And now for some illustrations of the Crewe " scare." The following one was given to me at the Mayor's dinner by one of the aldermen who was present :—" I was on my way last night," said he, " to our Liberal club, when a workman came up to me, and we walked on together. At the club door the workman looked up and down the street, and round about him. Are you looking for any- body'? I asked. No,' replied the workman ; but I would not have (an active Tory, holding a good position on the Crewe Works) see' me enter the club —not for fifty pounds.' " The alderman, who is one of the ablest,7mose."upright, and most popular men in the town, can give a surprising number of similar in- cidents. Not long ago another workman complained to the vice-ehairman of the Liberal Association about his inability to attend the political mee'ings. " I have six children," he said. " I am no longer young, and I am not particularly strong ; and if I am turned away from the works, what are we to do? You must not think any the worse of me if I stay away • from the meetings l if I attend them lam sure to be spotted." Now, I may as well state at once that if it were desirable to do so—and if the ormnpetent author- ities guaranteed that no workman should suffer on account of his testimony, a necessary condition— scores of witnesses could be brought forward to prove, not only that the scare is universal in the Liberal ranks, but also that the scare is anything but ground- less. I may state at once, too, that none of the work- men atttribnte exercise of unfair pressure to any of the directors, or to Mr. Moon, strong Tory though he be, or to Mr. Stephen, the Tory director who is con- testing the division. What the Liberal workmen do complain of, and bitterly resent (in private), are the hints abont "your bread and butter," the significant looks, the warning nods of the head—the indications not easily definable—which are conveyed to them by certain of the local officials, chiefly by " under-strap- as they call them The leaders of the Liberal Association will, under the guarantee mentioned above, most gladly and readily bring forward crowds of witnesses to :prove that the scare is by no means unintelligible. lam authorised by them to say so, They are ready to prove that Liberal shopkeepers—some of them ex- operatives—who. on being discharged from the works, have tried to make their living on petty trade—have been boycotted by Tory spies. There is a milkman here' a Liberal, who has just been told by some of his customers that they have reason to be afraid of its becoming known to certain parsons that they are dealing with him. Mr. Richard D tle, a first-rate workman of more than twenty years' service at the railway works, a. man who by his excellent character has won universal respect, is ready to come forward as a witness without any guarantee whatever. He was discharged some time ago. He now lives in Warrington, where I have been to interview him and, as he says he has nothing now to he afraid of, he has no objection to the publication of his name. "When I was in the works," he says, " I used to get frequent hints, in a quiet way, about the danger of my politics. Of course I am a Liberal. Well, to cut a long story short, I was discharged, and my foreman, who was really sorry for me, told me he did not know why, though I suspect he guessed the reason. I wrote respectfully to the superintendent, asking him why I was discharged, and calling his attention to my long service; he never 'gave me an answer. I think he might at least have given me one, for he must have known that the gang of which I had charge was one of the steadiest and best in the forging department. Being a total abstainer myself, -I had induced some of them to give up drinking, and, though I say it. I think I did the company a great deal of good by getting so many of these men to join the Blue Ribbon Army, of which I was then one of the local leaders. I took a little shop in Crewe, and in about two weeks after I heard it re- ported about that any workman who cave me his cus- tom would perhaps find his bread and butter gone. There was a man who used to pass up and down in front of my shop He was employed in the works, and I used to see him take note, with his papor and pencil, of the people who came to my place. My neighbours often looked up and down the street to make sure they were not watched, before venturing to come in. One of them, who has a good berth in the works, would come in at night, hut he would not look at ma in the daytime. If plitics have nothing to do with this kinl of thing, what else can it be? What was I to think when I saw, as I sometimes did, that from a batch of newly-dischargsd men, a

drunken ne'er-do-well got taken back almost at once, and that that man was known to be a Tory. It is not right to say that the Tory workmen and tlae Liberal workmen are treated alike." I took down Mr. Dale's statements in full; but the above specimen of thero will suffice. The Liberal candidate has cbal. longed his Tory rival, Mr. Stephen, to declare publicly end in his capacity as railtray director, his dis- approval of and interference with the free opinion of the operatives. Why has not Mr. Stephen promptly accepted the challenge? No one dreams of thinking that Mr. Stephen would knowingly profit by unfair pressure, A word from him would have done much to restore the confidence which, I am hound to say, has vanished from the Liberal ranks. Nothing re. mains but to make an appeal to the whole body of directors and of the company's shareholders, and to public opinion throughout the criuntry. This Tam requested to do, through the _columns of the _Daily .21-e,cs, in the name of the Crewe Liberal leaders and of the majority of its voter..

THE MORLEY COMMON FOOTPATH. REMOVAL OF THE OBSTRUCTION. Two or three months ago it was made known through our columns that the footpath leading from Walton Arches across to Morley Common had been stopped up. As this footpath afforded a very pleasant stroll through fields, and shortened the walk between Warrington and such places as Wal- ton and Daresbury, considerable feeling was aroused by what was generally deemed to be an unneces- sary and an illegal interference with the rights of the people of Warrington and district. The obstruc- tion was erected upon land in the possession of the Birkenhead Joint Railway Company, but, as it was known that Sir Gilbert Greenall had shooting rights over the ground in that neighbourhood,: a belief was very widely entertained that he had been at the bottom of the closure of the footpath. This belief was confirmed when it was made public soon after that • Sir Gilbert Greenall's agent had written to the Railway Company as to the footpath, and that his gamekeeper had turned back and threatened people who attempted to cross the land. In order, therefore, to assert the rights of the public in an ?pen manner, and, if possible bring the dispute to an issue, a party of men numbering between thirty and forty, met on Saturday afternoon at the point where the path has been closed for the :purpose of breaking down the obstruction. Promptly at three o'clock they set vigorously to work to pull down the rails which had been put up to stop passengers, and in a very short time this was done in the most complete manner. Only these rails, however, were pulled down and thrown to one side, theostile being allowed to remain in its original condition. The stile having been re-instated. in its old condition three hearty cheers were given, after which those pre- sent resolved themselves into a meeting, over which Mr. John Walker was elected to preside. The CHAIRMAN said it was a fair question to ask why they were there. He thought they were all agreed, from the action that had already been taken, and tram further eerier' that they were prepared to take, that they were 'there to assert what they believed to be a right, and to make a pro- test against what they believed to be a piece of selfiehness and tyranny. (Hear, hear ) He thought that they hau right on their side, but if not they were doing a serious wrong, and were breaking the law. As to the right: in the first place, a footpath such as that would belong to the public through being what was called an ancient footpath. That was, it could have been dedicated to the public for their use from time immemorial. Land of that sort was lust as much the lend of the people—it was as much the property of the public, and as sacred to them, as the land that was paid for on both sides of it. Assuming that that was their land—as part and parcel of the community—they must assert their right to it and preserve it. Their conten- tion was that this was purely and simply an ancient foot- path. But he thought that they might go a step Nailer, and say that they had a right to the footpath, through its dedi- cation in anether way. The owner of a piece of lend, which had no footpath across it might, by permitting people to go across it for a certain time, dedicate it to public use, and thus it might become a public footpath. Assumliag that they had not an ancient right to the footpath, he held that It would have become dedicated to the public by the nee that had been permitted and made of it. They had been told that day of some who had gone over the footpath for over twenty years ;-and they were told on the authority of !dr. George Croefield, whose word, in a matter of that kind, was looked upon as beyond dispute, that before he came to Walton Lea that footpath was in existence—(beer, hear,)— and that be made use of it for a number of years before he became a director of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company. That being the case, the idea that that footpath, as bad been said, was made for the coevenience of Mr. Crobfield was incorrect; if it was in use by him years before he became a director it could not have been made for him as a director. (Hear, hear.) They had the fact that the path had been used by the public generally. There was a stile there; it had been open at the other eud where there was another stile; and in face of these facts they were en- titled to say that even if there was not an ancient footpath it had by usage become dedicated to the public. He might say, after looking up the law on the subject, that a foot- path et! this kind might become dedicated to the public by something like six, eight, or ten yaars' use. Tnere were cases that showed that if a landowner allowed a footpath to be used for a number of years, and did not oncea year bar the way, but allowed a stile, then the road became a public road. He thought in this Case they were fairly entitled to say that that footpath belonged to the public—FA voice: We will have it.] —As far as the Railway Company were concerned they had no feeling in the matter as a body. It was te the in- terest of the company as well as tho public that the path should be open, for the company had customers at Walton and Daresbury, and other parts on that side of the river, who, of course, wanted to take the nearest way to the rail- way etagere. He thought they might assume that the Pail- way Company had no strong feeling in the matter, from the feet that it was only recently that they took any measures to protect any rights they might have. He was told that an inspector came there after receiving a letter from the agent of Sir Gilbert Greenall, and that he had to ask where the footpath was. Then as to the protest. Sir Gilbert Greenish, who owned so much of the land in that part of the country, had shooting rights over that strip of land. Having these rights, he wanted to dispossess the public of their rights in order that his few birds, his snipe, might breed in comfort, and that he might pop them off at his own convenience. But they were there to say that they would assert their right to that footpath. (Hear, hear.) He thought when they saw what had been done they should mekrea protest against what they believed to be, at the bottom, the action of Sir Gilbert Greenall and his game- keeper. (Hear, hear.) They must remember that so far as they knew, in not one instance, had the Railway Com- pany attempted to stop people from going across that foot- path. They knew that Sir Gilbert's keeper had stopped people, and they knew that the agent of Sir Gilbert Green- all was the man who in the first instance wrote to the Railway Company as to the footpath. It had been stopped, but it was again open, and they were determined that they would keep it open. They might coogratulate themselves on having done a good afternoon's work. He would sug- gest that they should make a point of traversing the path as , Oftkn as they could-keep it open now, give no one an excuse to say that they were trespaseing, and in that way they might pres.erve their rights and Bet any one who opposed at defiance. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. WHITHAM, who was called on, said that the ch air- man had gone pretty fairly over the whole ground of the matter, and dealt with it from all points of view. The ob- struction had now been cleared away, and he thought that they were determined that it should not be replaced. They should so arrange now that whenever it was renewed they shonld as soon as possible visit the place and clear it off. There was another point that should receive notice. That woe, if Sir Gilbert had law on his side,' the proper course for him to take was to assert his right, and institute pro- ceedings against one or two. If he was in the right he would gain a verdict, and if in the wrong he would lose it. The same thing was going 'on all over the country. There was scarcely a landed proprietor in the country—more eepecielly if he happened to be one who prided himself as be- longing to the Constitutional party—but filched pieces of land whenever he could. They were adding to their acres , at every opportunity ; he thought that the attention of the ! people should be kept well alive on this point, and that I they should insist upon their rights. (Hear, bear.) He was glad that they had cleared the obstruction away, and hoped that they should stick to their guns and clear away any future ones. It would be well, if the obstruction was placed up again daring the week, that they should again Visit the place at three o'clock the next Saturday afternoon and clear it away. He thought also that eutlicient notice should be given of that intention, so that it Sir Gilbert Greenall thought fit to replace what they had removed, he could be prepared for them removing it again. (A voice: It will give him a chance.) He weuld make a mo:ion to that effect. (Hear, hear.) The motion was seconded by Mr. Huasr, and supported by Mr. BURTON. The CHAIRMAN: I would just say that so far as any pro- ceedings are concerned Sir Gilbert Greenall has no power, being only the tenant, to take proceedings. Any proceed- • ings that could be taken would have to be instituted by the railway comp my. Of course he would be the man to incite those proceedings as far as this bit of land is concerned, as it is being preserved in his interests. He has already palled the strings, and he may perhaps try io pull the strings again. Let him pull, and we will pall on the other side. (Hear. hear.) I will pot the motion that we meet here next Saturday with a view of clearing any obstruction that may be Put in the way. (Applause.) The resolution was then put, and unanimously carried. Mr. EDWIN Waite= wished, before the meeting dispersed, to make a suggestion. Some years ago, he said, a Footpath Vigilance Society was in existence in Warrington, under the guidance of the Rev. Philip Carpenter, of Cairo-street, and it was well known that much good work was done in the way that they bed been doing that afternoon. When they came to take Into consideration the great amount of filching that had been done, especial:y during the lest fifty yeirs, by the Enclosures Acts that bad been passed for the selfish aggrandisement of a few, he thought that it was high time that the working-men of the country should protest, and earnestly, against such conduct. (Hear, hear.) As regarded that one particular question, the incitement t) stop the road could only proceed from a mean mind, that was Green—all the year rounds (Laughter.) The Cwitarilx thought they might pass a resolution in favour of forming a Footoaths Preservation Association. as, if such a one was formed, it might be a means of debarring landowners from taking advantage. The cost would only be a trifling matter, and, when the organisation was formed. the public would be on their sich, should a case wise. Mr. Bcarrosr said he knew -from his own experience that there was a footpath leading from Appleton to Hatton, —(A Voice: Through the Deena.)—over which he bad passed many times, that was now closed. Why should it be so ? It happened to be where there was game. fie proposed that they should form a society as suggested. Mr. WRIGHT seconded the resolution. The resolution was then unanimously carried. Mr. Burnrox proposed that Mr. Walker be appointed president of the society. The CHAIRMAN thought the meeting had better elect 'someone else, but in answer to Mr. Burton eaid he would agree to take the position pro tem. On the proposition of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. Buurox, Mr. Henry Whitham was elected vice-president

SHIP CANAL DEMONSTRATION AT MANCHESTER. On Saturday, a general holiday was observed in ManchesP ter in honour of the passing of the Manchester Ship Cana- Bill. The rejoicings took the shape of a great procession of trade societies and other organisations, and several public meetings. The trades union societiee ass irt'eled in front of the Town Hall to the numb3r of about 21,000, accempenied• by numerous bands of music and flags and society banners. As the weather on the whole proved favourable, the pro- ceedings were characterised by great enthusiasm. At BOOn. the procession commenced to move from the rendezvous In the direction of Belle Vue .Gardens, where a monster meet- ing was held, The procession WAS several miles in length, and the arrangements were conducted on such a scale as to make it as effective a display as possible. Those of tke processioniets who cou.d not rendezvous iii Albert-square met in Stevenson-square, and joined the main body en route, and eventuilly walked to the Pomona Gardens, where a demonstration was held as at Belle Vire. The various tern- persons societies and organisations met in St. Ann's- equare, and marched to the Alexindra Park, where a meeting WAS held. The streets all along the routes to the various destinations of the liff :rent contingents were profusely decorated with flags, and bunting was dis- played in the main streets of the city, which were crowded. Spectators flocked into the city from all the neighbouring towns and from distant places, and it is estimated that over • half a million witnessed the proceedings, which, as far as could be learned, passed off without any serious casualty of any kind. Mr. Adamson, CE.. the chairman of the pro- visional committee, and Mr. Pember, Q C., the leading counsel for the promoters. as well as the local members of Parliament and other gentlemen of influencs, participated in the demonstration, and were enthueieetically cheered. The following were the occupants of the first seven vehicles:— First carriage: Mr. Daniel Adamson. CE., J.P., Mr. E. H. Pember, Q C., and Mr. E. Leader Williams. sewed car. rine : The Mayer of Stockport, Mr. George Hicks, Coun- cillor Boddington, and Mr. J. Saxon. Third carriage: Aldermen Bailey and Hosband, Mr. William Fletcher, and Mr. Marshall Stephens. Fourth carriage: Alderman Walms- ley. Dr. Mackie, Mr. Richard James' and Mr. Thomas Brad- ford. Fifth carriage: Mr. Henry Whitworth, Mr. C. L. Samson, Mr. Edwin Guthrie, and Mr. Frederick Moss. Sixth carriage: Mr. H. C. Piherstone, Mr. C. H. Wade, ME. Clement Wallersley, and Mr. J. W. Harvey. Seventh carriage: Mr. Paul Gariel, Mr James Johnston, Mr. Melton Prior (Illustrated London News), and Mr. A. H. Whitworth. At Belle Vue an immense crowd of people assembled on and near the outdoor dancing platform and were addressed by several gentlemen from the balcony of the grand stand over-looking it.—The Mayor of Manchester, who presided, expressed the hope that the undertaking would be brought to a successful issue.—Mr. Adamson said he was quite eure that Lancashire would find the means for constructing the proposed waterway, and no would reap ,the profits of the undertaking. He was sure that before six months were over they would have another gathering for the purpose of cutting the first sod, and beginning the work of excavation with ten thousand navvies.—Mr. Panther, who, like Mr. Adamson, was enthusiastically cheered. said that in this matter the whole population of Lancashire understood what was their interest, and the project was supported not by the few but by the good sense and clear sense of the many.— Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., remarked that they were met to celebrate a victory which had cost no blood and done no harm to anyone, and the results of which would bring no inconsiderable advantages to their commerce and industry. —Mr. Houldsy•-ortb, M.P., said no one, after the demonstra- tion, could doubt that Lancashire was in earnest about the matter—Resoletions were unanimously passed congratulat- ing and thanking Mr. Adamson, Mr. Pember, and others who had laboured on behalf of the bill, and pledging the meeting to support the committee to the utmost of its power by taking up shares in the Ship Canal Company,—eimilar resolutions were passed ley the gathering in Alexandra Park, which was also addressed by Mr. Adamson and Mr. Pember. MEETING IN THE FREE TRADE HALL. The enthusiasm of the inhabitants of Manchester with regard to the Ship Canal project was again manifested on Monday evening, in no unmistakable manner, at the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, where a great meeting in its fur- therance was held. To ensure that the proceedings might be conducted "decently and in order," or rather to prevent the inconvenience which must always arise from overcrowd- ing. admission to the greater p ation of the buildine, was by ticket. The hour fixed for commencing the proceedings was seven o'clock, but by half-past six de or nearly all, the reserved seats both on the floor an i in tee galleries were filled. At seven tbe doors were thrown open to all corners, and in a few minutes every part of the hill WAS crowded. The primary object of the meeting was to afford the sub- scribers and friends of the great enterprise an opportunity of seeing and hearing Mr. Pember, Q C., the leading counsel, to whose skilful advocacy chiefly the passing of the Bill was secured. Mr. Daniel Adamson, chairman of the Pro- visional Committee, presided. To his right, and in the front row of chairs on the pl Worm sat the mayors of seven neighbouring boroughs wearing their chains of office, which rendered them conspicuous, and ceit alnly lent a decided pietureequenets to the scene. On the other side were Mr. Pember, Q.C, Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P., Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., Mr. Hopwood, Q C., M.P., Mr. Arnold, M.P. The following gentlemen from Warrington were a'so on the platform: The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Harrison). Aldermen Davies and Pickmere, Councillors Dr. Mackie, Jolley, areening, Marsh, Francomb, and John Pierpoint, the Borough Surveyor (Mr. T. Lone:din), Mr. Geo. Woods, and Mr. William Fairhurst. Mr. Admison, and the gentle- men who entered the hall in company with him, were greeted with ringing cheers, and the proceedings throughout were characterised by the greatest enthusiasm. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said that the risk in the case of the ctnal Woo reduced to a minimum. 1 Before it had been opened a year it would be paving 6 per cent., in another year it would be 8 per cent., and before five years were over, 16 to 20 pr cent.. and it would be impossible to prevent it. He was prepared' to risk all he had in the undertaking. (Cheers.)—Mr. Pember delivered a speech, in which he reviewed the his- tory and main features of the scheme as presented b<fore the parliamentary committees. Mr. Reuben Spencer moved, Dr. Mackie seconded, and the meeting unanimously adopted a resolution expressing confidence that the canal would secure immense advantages to the district and prove re- munerative ts the shareholders, and pledging the nieeting to assist by every means in its power in raising the n,cessa:7 capital.—Aniongst the other speakers were Mr. H. M. lgtanley, the African explorer; Mr. Jacob Bright, ;`4.P., and Mr. Houldsworth, M.P. Mr Houldsworth intim tted that after full consideration of the ereject he threw his lot In heartily with it. COLONEL 111000RQUODALE AND THE
ANTI-VACCINATORS.

. _ It will be remembered that some time ago an influential deputation, representing the Newton and Earlestown branch of the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination Society, waited upon Colonel McCorquodale, the Liberal candidate for the New- ton division ot South-West Lancashire, to ascertain his views on the vaccination question, and to urge him to pledge himsslf in favour of the principles of the society. A second interview took place at the Colonel's residence, The Willows, Newton-le-Willows, on Monday evening, when the deputation consisted of the following gentlemen : Messrs. Benjamin Harrison. Wm. Davies, Wm- Pearson. Richard Evans, and Wm. Gilmour.—Addressing the depu- tation Colonel McCorquodale said his sympathies were with them, and he was of opinion that compulsory vaccination was wrong and unjust. In his present way of thinking he would vets against the compalsory clauses of the Act, but be did not wish to pledge himself. He thought they might safely trust him, and he would be quite conscientious in the matter. He would like to go to the flouee of Commons free to listen to the arguments on both sides of the question, but he was certain'7 of opin- ion that there ought to be a commission of inquiry on the subject. Prior to the previous interview he thought vac- cination was right, but he had since gone into the matter, and haying heard their arguments and read the literature they had left and since sent him, he might say his views on the questien had quite changed. These were his present views, and what he had told them be would be free to re- peat in the House if elected.—ln thanking the Colonel for his candid expressions, the deputation said they were cony he could not give them a specific pledge as ta the compul- sory clauses, because that was a point on which they felt sore. Many people who sat leisurely in their armchairs, and never gave the subject their consideration, thought the views of the anti-vaccinators were mere crochets; but to those who had had practical experience in the working of the Act the compulsory clauses pinched them sorely. How- ever, after receiving such a measure of Colonel McCorqao- dale's sympathy, thee were content to leave the matter in his hands, and to fully trust him for future action on the question. Meanwhile they could assure bins of the support of their party, and as indiviattals he might rely on them doing all they could to ensure his retarn.—The deputation then withdrew.

A dress does not make a woman, but often bretks a man. A little girl described nervousness as "just being in a hurry all over." What kind of man gives his wife the grist reading of the daily paper ?—A blind man. Ddr. Howard Paul, when asked in what part of Switzerland he felt the heat most, replied, "When I was going to Berne." Wr,y does the "girl of the period" make the best house- keeper ?—Because she makes so much bustle aboat a little waist.

Professor: Mention an oxide.—Student: Leather.—Pro- fessor: Oxide of what ?—Student: Oxide of beef.—Exit professor. Hungry guest: How is this? I ordered a steak and a poached egg. I see the egg, but where is the steak ?—Sable attendant: " Dat's all right, sah. De steak am under de egg. As a college-examination a professor asked, "Does the question embarrass you?" "Not at all, sir," replied the student—" not at all. It is quite clear. It is the answer that bothers me !"

Nasmyth tells us in his autobiography that be used to think one of his friends had a charming and kindly twinkle, till one day he discovered that he had a glass eye. "Is anybody waiting on you ?" said a polite salesman to a young lady from the country. "Yes, air," replied the blushing damsel. "That's my young man outside; he wouldn't come into the shop." A DISTINCTION WITHOUT A DIFFEHENCE.—SeerIe--Glas- gow Agricultural Society s show-grounds. Jock, after silently admiring a stalwart Clydesdale: Mann Sandy, that's a fine animal !—Sandy: What—that an animal? Awa', ye ignoramus, dae ye no ken a horse when ye see% ? Scene—Country house; time—after dinner. Old friend: You ought to be proud of yeur wife, Joe—Host: Yes.— Old friend: She's a most brilliant talker.—Host : She ought to be t—Old friend: I could listen to her for a whole night. —Host, wearily: I often do! A young woman, in leaving an omnibus, dropped a ribbon from her bonnet. "You have left your bow behind," said a lady traveller. "No, I haven't; he's gone a-fishing !" inno- cently replied the damsel. First Scotch farmer, selling: " It's a gold horse; but I mann tell ye it's got as fant—it's a wee gi'eu to rin awa' wi' ye." Second Scotch farmer, buying: "If that's a', it'll dae fine! Man, the last horse I had was gi'en to rinain' awa' withoot me !" _ _

RUDIMENTARY SMARTNESS.—Scene—School-playground; first day of term. Old boy : "Oh, your name's Leo, is it ? What, Leo, a lion ? What a beastly name! Why didn't you object to it ?" New boy: Well, you see when I WrIS christened, I didn't know enough Latin to decline it." WHAT A SHIRTLESS ONE ACCOMPLISHED.—" Little boy, do you uudcrstand what is meant by energy and enter- prise ?" "No sir, I don't think I do." Well, I will tell you. One of the richest men came here without a shirt on his back, and now he has millions." "Millions! How many does he put on at a time ?" English grandmother, wishing to instruct a little daugh- ter of Erin in something useful : " Come here, child, and I will teach you to know the clock." Molly, who would much r Aber not learn to know the clock just then: "Sure, granny, I needn't be learning English time when jam going home so soon!"

I "Yon don't say that Tom Russell is going to marry Miss Mollie Penderby." " Yes, that's what they 7ay." " Why, she's a perfect inanity; she hasn't got a mind of her own." " That's just the reason he's marrying her. ; He loves a quiet life, and as she hasn't got a mind of her I own she can't be eternally giving him a piece of ,it." A Board School inspector, finding a Wass hesitating over answering the question, "With what weapon did Samson slay the Philistines ?" and wishing to prompt them, signi- ficantly tapped his own cheek, and asked, " What is this?" , His action toucbing "the chords of memory," the whole class instantly answered, "The jawbone of an ass !" . .- - .

A SLIGHT MISUNDERSTANDING.—Irate Individual : What did you mean by telling Smith that I had been in jail? Calm Individual : I did not tell Smith that you had been in jail. I simply said that you ought to be in jail. Irate Individual (calming down) : I beg your pardon. I must have misunderstood him. PROFESSIONAL CONSOLATION.—FamiIy Physician: Well, 1 I congratulate you. Patient (excitedly): I will recover. Family Physician : Not exactly, but—well, after con- sultation we find that your disease is entirely novel, and it I the autopsy should demonstrate that fact we have decided to name it after you. How HE Was SAVED.—Perkins: " Snifkin failed ! Well! I had a narrow escape yesterday. He tried to borrow ten dollars from me." Ponsonby :-" You didn't lend it to him ?" "No, indeea. I suspected there was something wrong, and—and—" Well ?" "The fact io, I didn't have the ter. dollars." POT ON THE Brawl' Taacx.—A. Parisian wine merchant or rather wine manufacturer, was recently condemned to a heavy fine for adulteration. After the sentence, he asked the chemist how he could have been so positive that the wine was a fabrication. "Because it did not contain an atom of bitartrate of potash, which is to be found in all natural wines," replied the man of science. "Thanks for the information," returned the tradesman ; " the next time you analyse my wines you will find some." SHE Toox ONE.—" Are the fall styles of wall paper in yet ?" "Yes'm." That Was ten o'clock in the morning. At one o'clock in the afternoon, after having 234 eamples displayed before her on vie rack, she tenderly iy.quired: "Have you any more?" "No'm." "Are you sure these are the very latest fall styles ?" "Yes'm." "Then—then I guess I'll take a roll—one for two shillings. I want to paper a trunk."

4ETTING AT THE FACTS. Koscinsco Murphy recently passed his examination, and is now a member of the Austin bar. His strong card is getting the truth out of witnesses. The following is a sample of his system of examination "Are you a married man ?" "No, sir; lam a bachelor." "Will you please tell the court and jury how long you have been a bachelor, and what were the circumstances that in- duced you to become one?"

Young artist, to a friend who has recently furnished bachelor's chambers : "Charley, dear boy, I admire your taste. I see you have a Mae thing of mine hanging there." Friend : "No! Did you paint that ?" Young artist ‘i yes ; I'm proud to say it's from my brush. By-the-way, Charley, if it is a fair question, what did the dealer charge you for it?" Friend: "Well—er—to tell you the truth, old man, the dealer threw that picture in. A gentleman was lately inspecting a class of some sixty children in a London Board-School. In the course of the lesson the little ones had some small sticks in their hands, and he asked the children where they came from. They replied, "Trees." He asked who had prepared them. They answered, "The carpenter;" and on further asking, "Who cat down the trees for the carpenter?" he was astonished to hear—instead of the reply he expected, " A woodcutter "—a general shout of "Mr. Gladstone!" • They tell a good story of a lawyer "out West." A client charged with stealing a hog admitted his guilt to his counsel. The latter was noted for his honesty in private life. After thinking the matter over, he said, "John, cut that hog exactly in half, and bring one half to me." John obeyed. The evidence for the prosecution was weak, and, when the counsel for the defence arose, he won the case by saying to the jury," Gentlemen, I can hold up my hand to fleaveu and say that the defendant has no more of the hog than I have!"

-- • - • A convict at a French penal settlement who was under- going a life-sentence desired to marry female convict, such marriages being of frequent occurrence. The governor of the colony had no objection, but the priest proceeded to crass-examine the prisoner. "Did you not marry in France!: asked the clergyman. " Yes." "And your wife is (led ?' "She is." "Have you any docurnents.to show that she is dead?" "No." "Then I must refuse to marry you. You must bring proof of the death of your wife." There was a pause, during which the prospective bride looked anxiously at the would-be bridegroom. Finally, he said, "I can prove that my former wife is dead." " How can von prove it ?" asked the priest. "I was seat here for killing her," an- swered the convict.

DISAS rito u S FIRE IN LONDON.

A fire broke out at 3-30 on Thursday morning on the premises of Messrs. Flint and Co., 18, Charter- house-buildings, Clerkenwell, London, and Messrs. Barnes and Sprengers, adjoining. The firemen from Farringdon-street were promptly on the spot, but though aided brother engines they were unable to prevent the flames spreading. Within half an hour from the first outbreak 15 large warehouses were on fire, and it became evident that no portion of Clerkenwell-buildings could be saved. The light of the conflagration was visible for several miles round, and the time could- be seen by St. Paul's , clock. Meanwhile the police had broken open the doors of Nos. 8, 10, 12, 14, and 16, Clerkenwell- road, which were threatened with destruction. Some of the inmates seemed unwilling to leave; one old lady, sixty years of age, was removed in a half-fainting condition. The flames from Charterhouse-buildings speedily extended to the other siqe of the thoroughfare, Nos, 112, 14, and 16 being attacked, and the flames com- municated themselves to Wilson-street, Groswell- road. Police-constable Coe rescued a woman and several cnildren from No. 14, Clerkenwell-buildings. As the firemen were playing on a portion of Char- terhouse - buildings, facing Clerkenwell - road, the front wall was seen to rock, and the front of four warehouses fell with a loud crash. Happily no one was hurt. The damage can be but partially estimated. Most of the warehouses in Charterhousc-buildings, which were almost entirely destroyed, were occupied by importers and light manufacturers, but a few were empty. In all, about ten warehoused in Charter- house-buildings and four houses in Clerkenwell- road have been almost totally destroyed, while the rest of the premises in Clerkenwell-buildings wer very seriously damaged, together with some ten houses in Clerkenwell-road and a few others in Goswell-street. The cause of the fire is unknown, and the watchman on the buildings states that no sign of it was perceptible five minutes before the outbreak.

_ A later telegram says :—Throughout the whole of the day several engines have been pouring water upon the ruins in Charterhouse-buildings and Clerkenwell-road. The officers of the Salvage Corps who were engaged in making a survey were con- stantly coming upon fresh damages, and it may be safely stated nearly every house within a radius of 200 yards from the original seat of the fire has been more or less damaged. At three o'clock in the after- noon the fronts of the gutted buildings in Clerken- well-road gave way. Various estimates have been made as to the money value of the damage done by this great conflagration, some authorities placing it as high as £2,000,000 sterling.
WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarket-street, Warrington, on Wednesday evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. W. Marsh, and there was a large attendance of members.—The minutes of committee meetings, which contained memorials on the rent, farm land assessment, and the Manchester Smithfield Market space questions, were read, and a discussion ensued—Mr. John Derbyshire approved of the send- ing of a second rent circular, as, he said, the present season was likely to be more disastrous than had been the eight preceding seasons. They were all aware that they could do but little with regard to inducing landowners to lower their rents, but every little they could do was needed very much. They were also aware that there were many farms the rents of which did not require lowering, but there were scores of others that did require it, and that was one of the things that they must look to. Fle instanced a case in which there had been 150 applicants fer a vacant farm as proving, not that rents were low, but that there were 150 farmers who wished to leave the farms now occtipied.—Mr. Davidson, in the course of a few remarks, said be thought that farmers' clubs were bearing fruit, and they shonld be encouraged to go forward in their work.—Mr. William , Derbyshire also spoke, and Mr. Stelfox, senr., said that he thought there was •a little preju- dice on the part of landed proprietors against a club of that description. When it was formed it was with- out prejudice to anyone. Its object wee to bring be- fore the notice of landed proprietors that there was an urgent neceesity that something should be done to benefit the tenant farmers in Lancashire and Cheshire. There were only three things remained open to them, one was the reduction of rents, the second higher price for produce, or thirdly, starvation. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) The prosperity of the tenant far- mer was that of the landlord, and they should assist and not pull to pieces each other.—lr. T. Stelfox having made a few remarks, the mre'ing confirmed the minutes of the commietee.—Mr. John L Stelfox then read a paper entitled " An explanation and criti- cism of the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1853, and the Ground Game Act, 1880," which he followed by a statement of the demands of tenant farmers. With regard to the Agricultural Holdings Act, Mr. Stelfox said that it was an intricate one and did not deal with the whole question—it did not make provision to give compensation for all improvements, and in respect of the improvements for which it did give compensation it did not do so fully. Besides, it was badly worded, difficult to construe, and the farmer could not get the benefit of it without running the risk of a law suit. With regard to the Ground Game Act, it was on the whole a very fair one; but it should be extended so as to include winged game. Speaking generally, he made allusion to the want of courage on the part of farmers in not avail- ing themselves of the privileges of the Ground Game Act in not killing hares and rabbits now that they had power to do so. No doubt in many cases they feared a notice to leave as the consequence. Following upon that it was clear that farmers required better security of tenure, so that they might avail them- selves of their legal rights without fear. He thought that to some extent farmers might deal with the rent question by combination, so that they need not out- bid each other, and give rents which did not admit of farms being made profitable. The demands of the tenant farmers, as explained by Mr. Stelfox, were, briefly, the establishment of land courts for the fixing of fair rent; the abolition of tithe so far as agricul- tural land is concerned ; the re•adjustment of taxa- tion on agricultural land, the income to be taken as the basis rather than the rental ; and the reduction of railway rates for farm produce. In view of the troublous times that had overtaken agriculture, Mr. Stelfox implored all tenant farmers to cast aside feelings of jealousy and unite in efence of their ancient calling, which was threatened with even more troublous times in the immediate future. He recom- mended mass meetings of farmers at central points, conferences of farmers, and the passing of resolutions calling the attention of the Government to its neglect of agriculture in the matter of education. The coun- try would not occupy itself with the needs of farmers unless they were strongly placed before it.—On the motion of Mr. Bennett, seconded by Mr. Baguley, and supported by Mr. Derbyshire, Mr. Stelfox was cor- dially thenked for his paper.—This was all the business.

IRE RAILWAY SERVANTS' gONORESS.—At the Railway Servants' Congress, at Leicester, on Thursday, the question , of direct representation in Parliament was discussed, and a resolution, from Sunderl Ind, authorising the Executive to make the necessary arrangements, and asking for a con- tribution of sixpence yearly, was passed. FATAL FIRE AT GAINSBOROLIGIT.—A fatal fire broke out on Thursday morning in a solicitor's office over a chemist's I, shop at Gainsborough, The chemist's assistant, who re- sided on the premises, succeeded in removing the wife and I family, but failed to awake the maid servant, who was suffo- cated. Strenuous efforts were made to rescue the girl. CONGREGATIONAL UNION OF ENGLAND AND WALES.— This Hnioa opened its annual meeting on Monday night at Hanley. The Rev. Dr. Parker, London, preached the, annual sermon. Afterwards, a temperance meeting was held. It was reported that the number of abstaining ministers in the denomination was not exactly known, but 200 were stated to be such. In the denominational college them were 353 students, only 50 of whom were not abstainers. On Thurs- day, a paper by Dr. Fairbairn on "The New Puritanism "
-- led to the adoption of a resolution declaring that the rapid growth of sicerdotaiism in the Established Church involved danger to the religious faith and moral character of the people.

. - Two HUN:DRED AND FIFTY LOVE LETTERS.—In a breach of promise case heard at Warwick, on Saturday, the plaintiff, Miss Mary E Tattoo, a dressmaker, of:Birmingham, produced 250 letters which she had received from defendant, Donald McQueen, a Scotch draper. Defendant wrote fervently to plaintiff, but described himself as " a wretch created to repine," an " a deformed good-fornothing little cad," akd " such a funny defermed little devil she need never be jealous." lie spoke of plaintiff as his " morning star whom he loved to smother with kisses," and that he wanted no other heaven or paradise except to live with her.'' He was ordered to pay plaintiff £lOO. LINSEED LOZENGES, solidified linseed tea, laxative and de- mulcent, 6d ; postage 2d. Ray, Brothers, Stockport, and all chemists.—Advt.

MR. SAMPSON'S CHALLENGE. Sir,—The proposal made by my friend in your issue of ' last week seems ingenuous, but is really ingenious. It would doubtless he a very gratifying matter to the Conser- vative party if by any means, however plausible, they could discover the secrete contained in the Liberal agent's brief. For the present, at any rate their curiosity mast remain un- satisfied. If the Conservative party—numbers of whom were present at various times during the recent revision— are satisfied that they have made even the small gain that Mr. !lampoon claims, then we have no cause to complain. I do know this, that several Coneervativee have unhesita- tingly expressed to myself and to other Liberals that they were not "in it;" and it is quite sufficient for me and the members of the Liberal party to know that harieg sub- mitted my statement to members at my committee for ex- amination they are convinced that the figures given are substantially correct.—Yours faithfully, El. ROBERIS, Liberal Agent.

this matter are not in favour of local government ? I have always had my doubts about your affection for local government, but I hardly expected you would fall into so palpable a /mare as this. I think, sir, here you have dis- tiuctly made a slip. There is nothing further in your article that I need notice except the challenge at the end— We will discuss this matter with him en a public plat- form." I don't know who the" we" is, or what the pre- cise points you would have so dismissed. I have given ample opportunity in time past for the public discussion of education matters. having myself introduced theta at the old Debating Society. As far as you are concerned, I think you are lulls competent to dismiss your side of the ques- tion, and to make the most tif the opportunity your paper , affords. If your article last week was a little weak, need- ing this little flourish at the end about the public discus- sion, I would simply recommend pox t 3 try again before . you give op and attempt any new method.—l am, sir, b yours faithfully, E. C. E. CARLETON. Portsmouth, October 7th, 1885.

[We had written the leader which appears in another column when the above letter came te band ; and it will be noted that we have dealt with the chief points which it raises. We may add by way of brief rejoinder that we do not care to quibble about terms; "free" or "gratuitous." it will 'be all the same to those who are relieved of paying school fees. As to remission of fees in denominational schools, why does Mr. Carleton charge the Liberal party alone with declining to yield on this matter, when he knows that the Tory party have taken precisely the same ROUTH Mr. Carleton wants poor parents to apply to school managers for remission of fees instead of going before Boards of Guardians: but Mr. Chamberlain ;would save them the humiliation of applying to anybody, by doing away with school fees. We certainly object to the statement that " Mr. Chamberlain's scheme would give a fatal blow to denominational teaching ;" and re-affirm that it would not touch denom- inational teaching: creeds and catechiams eould be taught under it just as much as at present. Mr. Gladstone is by no means in agreement with Mr. Carleton; the ex- Premier thinks it would be" premature " for him to is- dude" gratuitous education" in bin programme ; but admits that there are " obvious arguments" in favour of Mr. Chamberlain's plan. Mr. Carleton seems, to have re- alised at last that Mr. Chamberlain's proposal does not mean "universal School Boards." There is hope for him; he may distinguish next between the income tax and a local rate, and, without turning his back OR local govern- ment, accept, as we are prepared to do. Mr. Chamberlain's scheme as the one that will least divide the nation, and u the easiest and quickest way of freeing the schools'. With regard to the suggested discussion, it may be stated that the "we " is the editor of this journal—until re- cently a member of the Blackburn School Board, and pre- sumably acquainted with educational matters. The "precise points" to be debated are those arising out of Mr. Chamberlain's proposal. Mr. Carleton attacks it ; we are prepared to defend it, not from any consciousness of weak- ness, but because we have faith in a just cause, and believe with Milton that truth will not be " put to worse" in a "free and open encounter."—ED. Ex.]

THE NATIONAL FOOTPATH PRESERVATION SOCIE I Y. Sir,—Allow me to draw attention to the great necessity in these times to preserve public rights, such as ancient foot and bridle paths, vacant spaces, village greens, roadside slips a lend, &c. As with the insurance of a house or furniture, people are apt to neglect such an important step until some- thing comes home to them forcing them to do it, so people are indifferent to the value of footpaths and other public rights until an attack is made on them, or a ftveurite walk is actually lost. 1 could mention numerous localities where the process of encroachment or stopping fostpaths Is going on. Cannot you rouse the people in y-•ur district to bestir themselves? Is there no gentleman to be found who will come forward and form a local satiety for the preservation of public rights? No other country in the world has such charming and useful walks, and surely we should greatly value them. I shall be most happy to assist in any way, and have printed rules for such society. I bear a footpath has been closed over Morley Common. Mr. Walker, who took some part in opening the path, should communicate with us.-1 remain, dear Sir, yours obediently. HENRY ALLNUTT, 42, Essex-street, Strand, W.C. Secretary.

HOW TO GET ue A CIRCULATION. Sir,—A short time ago I was waited upon by a dapper little fellow, wit° solicited an advertisement for a certain newspaper. In very eloquent terms he descanted to me on ice advantages of advertisisg, and finished up by stating that their charges were very low, in fact, .‘ extremely low ;" something like the paper thought I, but I did not say se. I replied that it was hardly worth while advertising with them. as the circulation of their paper was so small. " Is- deed," said he. "von are mistaken, we publish 5 000 or 43,000 twice a week." " Well," said I, " that's very funny, for I beard from a friend of mine in the trade the other day that they had three &ten copies from your agent and returned all nneold except three copies ; but perhaps the .5.000 or 6,000 include all the copies you give away ?" That is quite a mistake, sir," be replied, 'we do sot give any away." "Then." said I, "to whom am I indebted for the copies that have at various times been put under my door? lam quite certain I never pay for them." "Oh !" he re- plied, "we have an arrangement with the Club by which they take a certain number of copies from us every week for gratuitous circulation:" I need hardly say that this little bit of information, so innocently divulged, caused me much amusement. I leave the story to point its own moral. —Tours, MAX.

At the conference referred to it was stated that there are in the United Kingdom 590 Liberal, and only 379 Conservative papers, and of "enemies in disguise" yet called neutral, there were 1,200. Strange , this and to our Conservative friends somewhat puzzling; more so when it is known that these Liberal papers are not • eubsidized, but are, in the words of Mr. Byrom Reed," con- ducted upon much stricter business principles " than are Conservative papers. No wonder at this ; men will not bay rubbish, and yet this is what Tories expect them to do. Mr. Reed puts the question—" Where can one find a good London letter in a Conservative daily paper? " No Satis- factory answer can be given to this question, but we are justified in saving that this accounts for the inane stupidity that exists to such a great extent in the so-called Conservative working man. Yet, sir, the climax Is reached when you read in a Conservative review the following:—" When, may I ask, and where, are we to find Conservative Cowen—or, may I add, a Conservative Lucy ? " A Conservative Journalist," writing ou the subject of the establishment of Conservative newspapers, says: "The anxious Conservative politician who is deploring the state of the Conservative press in the provinces will ask—What about the politics? I answer, the less the better. What you have to dole to give the grocer the Cork batter market with accuracy and regularity, the Liverpool produce %nat.- ket, and the price of cheese. You must tell the farmer the prices fetched at the Colonial wool sales in the City sale rooms, you must give the beet tip for the race of the day, and, if possible, all the tips of all the papers each day. If you do this, and if your politics are not violent, they will be accepted, because the grocer who gets a proper view of the butter market will swallow everything else. He may grumble at your politics, but he will buy you." Such teachings as these I call fraudulent, and if Conservatives depend upon them, they must not be surprised if working-men turn to journals that lay before them well-written leading articles. Conservatives are agreed that of the two parties they have been "remiss and lethargic." A Conservative writer, whom I much admire, says" Politics are a duty, not a pleasure, and no good man can well abstain from engaging in them." But how can you expect Conservatism to take the position naturally belongiag to it, if, systematically, efforts are made to beguile simple-minded men into the Conservative camp by dangling before their eyes the " best tips on the favourate horse of the day." Conservative writers know well that Liberal newspapers have always been at the front when the people's riehte were in question. The only Conservative " Monthly "that ap- pears gives its readers the following : " It must be remembered, too, that until 1872 the Liberals were the active, moving, and aggressive party, and that in the course of their ascendency they took up, as one of the main objects of their policy, the removal of the stamp and advettisement duties, and, subsequently, the repeal of the paper duty, with the avowed purpose of increasing the num- ber of newspapers devoted to their interests. In fact, as soon as the stamp duty was repealed, they set to work to establish such organs." Such a confession as this, coming from a leading Tory journal, speaks volumes, and all we can hope for is that this candid spirit may be imitated, and that Conservative speakers and writers may from now, take the advice given by the wiiter referred to, "be scrupulously fair." CLIFFORD DIX.
GREENALLISM AND DISSENT. AT WALTON.

SlN—The letter which appeared in last Saturday's Examiner has caused no little excitement in the t ill age of Walton. The only copy of your paper which was " get-at- able " has been borrowed and re-borrowed so many times from "mine host" that it is nearly falling to pieces through excessive use. Many of the villagers are very much pleased that the matter has been so spiritedly taken up, and, while they dare not publicly avow their satisfaction. they none the less rejoice at the exposure of this piece of petty tyranny.—Yours, MORLEY COMMON.
SIGNS OF THE TIMES. Oh cruel fate! Tories of late Have had to change their cry; At Walton school 'tis now the rule— No Wesleyan need apply."
-ED. Ex.

div.head: PASSENGER.
div.p: A PASSENGER.
Warrington, 7th October, 1885. ALDERMAN MCI:MERE AND THE LIST OF VOTERS.

Sir,—This matter has caused no little talk in our town, and sal am anxious that, at any rate, the Liberals of War- rington should know the truth, I venture to submit the whole case to your readers. A great deal of abuse has been showered upon me, bet as every public man is a target for the envious and uncharitable. I do not expect to escape either hostile or malicious criticism. As regarda Alderman Pickmere, I say that the Tory party, and they alone, are rerponsible for his name being struck off the list of voters. ; No man, either in the Town Council or out of it, has a warmer personal regard for Alderman Pickmere than I have, and no one regrets more sincerely than I do that he has ceased to be qualified for an office which he so thoroughly adorned. What, then, are the facts of the case? Simply these. The Liberal agent did not object to Alder- man Picktnere. The overseers, presumably because they believed that he had ceased to possess the necessary quali- fication, left his name off the list of votere, and the Con- servative agent duly sent in a new claim for him. Now it has been the custom of the agents of the two political parties for years past to exchange an equal number of claims and objections, the object being partly to save the time of the Revision Court, and also to enable each party to retain the names of any persons whose qualifications are perhaps not very sound, but who, from various reasons, it is in the interests of the respective parties, and of the public, that they should still be voters for the borough. Such cases oc- car every year, and such a case was Alderman Pickmare's. This year there were two meetings between the party agents, at each of which a considerable number of claims and ob- jections were exchanged. Knowing that Alderrnan Pick- mere's claim was a very doubtful one, I was greatly aston- ished to find that the Conservatives preferred to take the risk of proving his claim in court instead of taking the more prudent course of squaring it outside. Even in court I would willingly have let the Case slip through my fingers, but the Revising Barrister himself took up the examination of Major Pickmere, and it was upon the facts so elicited that the claim was disallowed. It therefore comes to this, either the Conservatives knew that Alderman Pickmere's qualification was a doubtful one, or they did not. The very fact of his name being left off the list for the first time ought to have suggested the possibility of his qualification being considered bad by the overseers; and that being to, I am not surprised at the rumour which is fast spreading in the town that certain of the Conservative leaders, who have for some time been much chagrined at Alderman Pickmere's independence of action, have been only too willing to allow him to drop out of the Town Council in order that a man who would be more subservient to the ring of the party bell might take his place. If, on the other hand, those who are responsible for the registra- tion of the Conservative side did not know that Alderman Pickmere's qualification was doubtful, then any blame which which may follow such ignorance does not attach to the Liberal agent. In conclusion, while I deeply regret the position of affairs, I emphatically deny that lam in any way responsible for it; but on the contrary I assert that the whole matter has been broeght about by the negligence, wilful or otherwise, of the Conservative party.—l am, your obedient servant, HENRY ROBERTS, Liberal Agent.

div.p: FREE EDUCATION.-REV. _E. C. E. CARLETON'S

_ REPLY. Sir,—Will you kindly correct the statement you made in your article last Sat ur day that my " letter WAS in opposition to Free Education." My second letter renders this, of Course, the less necessary; but, nevertheless. when an errone- ous statement is made, it is better to have it set right by those making the mistake. Mr. Chamberlain's Free Education is Free Education without freedom ; and I observe that Mr. Gladstone in his manifesto uses the less equivocal expres- sion " gratuitous education " in reference to Mr. Chamber- lain's scheme. In opposition to Mr. Chamberlain, we want Free Education with freedom. . .

I am glad you object to our poor people in Warrington having to go before the Board of Guardians in order to ob- tain remission of their children's school fees ; but remem- ber your party has all along objected to relieve us of this hardship in places like Warrington, where there is no School Board. If we had a Board it would be different ; and this is one of the manv inducements held out to us to saddle ourselves with a School Board. Our Roman Catholic friends don't need telling that I am not a Romon Catholic, but in this cause I go with them heart and soul. It strikes me that the Roman Catholics and ourselves, in view of the Secularist tendencies of the age, and of the Secularist attitude assumed by many Nonconformists, will have many a campaign to fight together in the future. You object to my statement that Mr. Chamberlain's scheme would give a " fatal blow to denominational teach- ing." If you doubt that you bad better read Mr. Glad- stone's manifesto again and yen will see that his opinion is not different to mine. You seem to say that Mr. Chamber- lain's scheme does not mean universal School Boards. Are we to understand then that you and Mr. Chamberlain in

PARK HOTEL BOWLING CLUB, ASTITON.—The members bowled their annual sweepstases to close the season on Saturday. Joseph Cunliffe and James Billing bowled off for the first prize, and the former won by two points. After the bowling an excellent tea was provided. Mr. Henry Lowe (captain) was called to the chair, and Mr. Thomas Jones to the vice-chair. The chairman gave the prizes to the winners. Songs were given during the evening.

F RODSH AM.

HARVEST FESTIVAL AT FRODSHAM PARISH CREECH —A thanksgiving service for the bountiful harvest was held at Frodsham Parish Church, last evening week, when the 1 church was filled to its utmost capacity. The decora- tions were on au extensive and elaborate scale, and com- pared fayourabiv with the artistic productions of previous occasions. The restored churcb, with its noble proportions and carved oak stalls and screens, is a sight worth seeing on ordinary occasions, but when lighted up on Friday evening It apoeared to even greater advantage. The Helebv and Kingsley Chapels were also tastefully decorated. The materials for the decorations had been supplied by the farmers and gentry in the neighbourhood, and several ladies and gentlemen who undertook the work of decoration. The service was full choral. The prayers were read ty the Rev. H. B. Bleu, 8.A., the leseons by the Revs. R. N. P. Butler and E. E. Charley. curates. Tanis responses were used. ' , The sermon was preached by the Rev. W. L. Paige Cox, M.A.., Vicar of St. Peter's, Rock Ferry. The anthem was by Sullivan, and was taken from the two last verses of the lix. Psalm. The Recessional Hymn was Number 381 of Hymns Ancient and Modern. Mr. Thomas Riley presided at the organ. A clllectien WAS made at the close of the service in aid of the funds of the Chester Infirmary, and amouhted to £l5 14s 7d.

THE FUSTIAN CUTTING TRADE. The fustian cutting trade of Warrington is at present in a very bad condition, several shops hav- ing been closed during the past few weeks. The inability of the small masters to provide work for their apprentices has caused great dissatisfaction, and at the Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, two young women made a statement to the magis- trates with the view of having their indentures cancelled. Mr. Chandley thought it was rather ob- jectionable to cancel indentures. Mr. Fairclough said the masters had no business to have so many apprentices if they could not find work for them. Mr. Chandley said he meant the masters should make some other arrangements. The Chief Con- stable said some of the shops had been closed, and the apprentices were not allowed to get work else- where; if they did they were liable to be called back to their old masters if trade happened to brighten up a little. The Magistrates' Clerk said the masters were bound to provide work for their apprentices. As the magistrates had already cancelled inden- tures, other apprentices would be encouraged to have their indentures cancelled also. In answer to the magistrates, one of the girls said when trade was good she could earn seven or eight shillings a week; but she had only earned little or nothing of late. Free summonses against their master to show cause why the indentures should not be cancelled were granted.—At the same Court, yesterday, Mr. Jno. Platt summoned three girls named Emma Ches- ter, Mary Ann Glynn, and Eunice Poyner for disobeying magisterial orders ,directing them to return to their work as fustian cutting apprentices. —Mr. Baines, from the establishment of Mr. Platt, said that not a single apprentice of theirs had been deprived of work in consequence of the slackness of trade. He thought perhaps the magistrates might think that, they had been placed in that pre-. dicament, but they gave the apprentices preference. —Captain Reynolds: We are glad to hear so. We had evidence a week ago that there were one or two young, women who seemed on the brink of starvation.—Mr. Baines said that if the journey hands had to go a little short the apprentice had always been provided with work—The girls were each sent to prison for seven days. Sarah Jane Starkey, for wilfully damaging a .piece of fustian at Mr. Platt's works, was sent to prison for a month, and orders were made for the following girls to re- turn to work :—Jane Ellison, Mary Ann Fynn, Ann Charnock, arid Elizabeth Rutter.

The second meeting of the Cabinet during the recess was held at noon on Friday. at the official residence of the First Lord of the Trea.ury. in Downing-street. CARDINAL NRIVIVAN.—On Friday the Roman Catholic body celebrated the 40th anniversary of Cardinal Newman's reception into their communion, which took place.at Oxford on the 9th of October. 1845. Mary Niels, aged 58,a spinster, was found drowned in the canal at Meccleatield on Friday morning. The deceased had been in a desponding state for some time, and it to be- . . .

_ liered that she has committed suicide. CHARGE OF WIFE MORDER.—John Young, coal agent. of Blairgowrie, was arrested on Friday, charged with wife murder. It is alleged that during a quarrel, on Thursday night, Young knocked his wife down, and she died soon after. . _

MURDER OF A LODGER. At Nottingham on Fri- day afternoon, George Bingham. an elderly man, win committed for trial on a charge of murdering James Moore. his lodger, by striking him repeatedly on the head with a poker. FRAUDS ON • BUILDING SOCIETY.—AI Exeter, on Fri- day, a stock and sharebroker and mining agent, named Har- ris. was committed for trial for defrauding a local building society to the extent of £3,500. The defalcatiGns were spread over a period of eight years, but bad escaped notice owing to the loose system et audit. DETERMINED SUICIDE—George Johnson, A married RVID,
, of Grafton, near Stratford-on-Avon, on Thursday night committed suicide in a very methodical manner. He went to the bank of the river Avon, took his clothes off, and,

carefully folding them up, placed them under a tree, with his hat on the top. lie then jumped into the deepest part of the river. The deceased, who was a johbing butcher, had remarked to a neighbour that he was tired of killing pigs. WAGES IN TILE Corrow TRADE.—The twelfth strike pay day was held at Oldham on Friday, when members of unions received their moneys. The total number of persons paid from the Spinners' Association funds is 10834, against 10,840 for the previous week. The adjourned meeting of the amalgamation is to be held in Manchester to-day to consider the masters' decision of ten per cent, for three months and five per cent, restored at the end of tbat time if trade improves to allow of that. BRAVERY AT THE CLIFTON HALL COLLIERY.—Fri- day night's Gazette states that the Queen has been ' graciously pleased to confer the Albert medal on the fol- lowing persons for conspicuous gallant-y displayed on the occasion of the explosion at Clifton Hall Colliery, in June last :—Albert medal of the firbt class to Thomas Worrall, underlooker, and John Creok, manager, Agecroft Colliery; the Albert medal of the second.class to Charles Parkinson, fireman George Higson, fireman, Aaron Manley, pit carpen- ter, and George Hindley, Blacksmith. OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.—The house of a farmer named Desmond, situated near Dunanncy. County Cork, was en- tered by a party of seven armed and disguised men, who demanded to see the rent book in order to ascertain whether Desmond had paid his rent. Having satisfied themselves that the rent was still unpaid, the captain of the gang pro- ' duced a small book, forced Desmond on his knees, and made ' him swear, under pain of death, to pay no rent until after theifiret sitting of the new parliament. The outrage has L caused men excitement in the district.
