WARRINGTON. FOWL STEALING.—On Sunday twelve fowls, of the value of £l, were stolen from a fowlhouse in the borough, in the neighbourhood of Latchford. The police are making every endeavour to bring the offender or offenders to justice. SUDDEN DEATH.—On Saturday morning, Mrs. Williams, wife of a broker and general dealer, carry- ing on business in Winwick-street, was seized with an apoplectic fit whilst carrying out her household duties, and immediately expired. She was under medical attendance, and an inquest was not thought

necessary. DEPA.UTITRE o TROOPS.—On Monday evening a draft of the South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, left Bank Quay station f Portsmouth, whence they will afterwards proceed to South Africa to join the main body of their re gi- ment. The draft, numbering 150non-commissicned officers and men, were played to the station by a
band from the barracks: CA.DISITEAD HARRIERS.—The above club held its

first annual race for captaincy and sub-captaincyl on Saturday afternoon, on the Broad Oak cinder path, Partington. The distance chosen was five miles, and the following is the order in which the members finished :-1, W. Jeffrey, captain; 2, J. R. Gatenby, sub-captain; 3, E. Hampson, sub-captain. Won easily; a yard between second and third. Time for the distance 27 minutes 48 seconds. ASSAULTING A MOTHEIL.-At the Borough Court, on Monday, a young man named Thomas Conway, who had been apprehended by warrant, was charged with assaulting his aged mother, who now appeared somewhat reluctant to give 'evidence against him, simply saying that he threw a loaf of bread at her face. It appeared, however, that prisoner had been in trouble before for assaulting his parents, and the Mayor said that that was the fourteenth time he had been charged with some outrage or another. He was sent to prison for two months, with hard

labour. PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.--The first debate of the session took place on Thursday. The subject was "Education,' and the discussion was opened by Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins in a very able manner, especial stress being laid on the question of free education, the recent proposals in reference to the subject being skilfully criticized by Mr. Jenkins, and either advocated or condemned by the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Arthur Ben- net, J. J. Nield, Theodore C. London, Charles Plins- ton, Thomas Corbett, Frederick Wright, and Frank Wrightson. The meeting was open to the public, and closed with an interesting reply by the essayist. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT THELWALL.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Saturday and Sunday at All Saints' Church, Thelwall, when there were good congregations. On Saturday the Rev. 11. P. Ramsden, 24. A., diocesan inspector of schools, preached an excellent sermon, making an appeal on behalf of the Society for the Propogation of the Gospel and the diocesan institutions. The Rev. H. P. Ramsden also preached on Sunday morning, and the Rev. B. B. Prescott, M.A., vicar of Christ Church, Latchford, occupied the pulpit in the afternoon. In the. evening the Rev. W. J. Stanton, 8.A., curate of Poynton, preached. The church was prettily deco- rated. .

Riorogs Yourus.—On Wednesday, at the County Petty Sessions, a young man named John Griffiths was charged under a warrant with being disorderly at Houghton on the 3rd of August. It was stated that on that day defendant and about twenty other young men hailing from Warrington assembled at a public-house at Houghton, where a lodge meeting was being held. Their conduct was so disgraceful that they were ejected from the house. At night they collected together and armed themselves with stones and palings of wood, and to disperse them the police had to draw their truncheons. Eleven If them were afterwards summoned before the magis- trates, but two of them, one being the defendant, did not appear. Defendant was ordered to find sureties for his good behaviour for six months, and to pay costs, or in default to go to prison for four- teen days. CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY LOCAL LECTURES.—The second of the series of lectures on" Physical Geog- raphy ," in connection with the Cambridge Univer- sity Extension Movement was delivered in the Co- operative Halt, on Monday evening, by Mr. W. W. Watts, M.A., F.G.S. There was a large attendance. Mr. T. G. Rylands, the president, said it was not customary for the chairman or president to say any- thing except on the occasion of the opening lecture, but he was sure they would excuse him if he told 6them that he stood there solely for the purpose of asking them to join with him in expressing their 'cordial thanks to the Co-operative Society for grant- ing the free use of that room for the course of leo- tures now commenced. (Applause.) They all knew the constitution of the Co-operative Society, and to his mind it reflected the highest honour upon them that they not only set apart a portion of their own profits for the pure and simple purposes of education, but that they, as in the case of the present lectures, which were ontside their own means and outside tho province of their own work, except as being a portion of the great work of pop- ular education, allowed the free use of that room. (Applause.)— A vote of thanks to the Co-operative Society was passed by acclamation.—Mr. Watts then proceeded with his lecture, the subject of which was "The atmosphere.". He first explained the composition of the atmosphere, and then in dealing with its temperature he gave an extremely. interest- ing and lucid description of the manner in which the temperature was guaged, and mapped out over the globe by means of isothermal lines. The lecture was most interesting throughout, and was atten- tively listened to.

div.head: LATE LORD SHAFTESBURY.
div.p: THE LATE LORD SHAFTESBURY.

Friday at noon was the hour fixed for the interment of the late Earl of Shaftesbury in the family tomb, at St. Giles' Church, near Wimborne. In accordance with the Implied wish of the late Etrl the funeral arrangement were of a simple character, and all who attended were connected merely with local bodies—magistrates, clergymen, and the tenantry of the surrounding towns and villages. The morning was fine and warm, and many drove long dis- tances by road. The tenantry. to the number of over 1,000, assembled before noon in the vicinity of the hall. Soon after 12 o'clock the coffin was borne in a plain hearse across the park to St. Giles' Church, preceded by eight clergymen bolding benefices under the late Earl, and fol- lowed by Lord Ashley and members of the family, after which came a walking procession of magistracy, country gentlemen, and tenantry. On reaching the church the funeral procession was met by the officiating clergy, the Revs. George Law Harkness, William Hubert Groome, and J. Morley Truman, and with the beneficed clergy preceded !the coffin. Each of the mourners following bore a wreath, which was laid on the coffin. After a simple service the . coffin was lowered into the vault on the north side of the church, where it will occapy a niche, adjoining the remains of the late Countess. The mourners, friends, and tenantry then slowly dispersed.

Tamersys. Samtrossa,2B.—Fightingbas taken place at Passandava Bay between the Hovas and the French troops, but without any decisive result. The French lost twenty- one killed and wounded. The loss cf the Hovas was two hundred killed and wounded. THE CHOLERA.

A Central News telegram, dated Ito-Ine, Friday, says : The daily official bulletin to-day states that 118 fresh cases of cholera and 59 deaths took place in Palermo yesterday. The cholera has also broken out in the province of Parma, where five persons have been attacked.

ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN —At the Pollee Court, on Monday, a labourer named Joseph Eaves, from Hiaton, was brought before Mr. T. P. Norris on a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Heatley, on the previous Sunday, and assaulting P.C. Buchanan at the same time and place. The assault was described as a severe one, and prisoner was remanded to the sessions to be held at Altrinchatn. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday anniversary ser- vices were held in connection with Lymrn Congregational. Sunday School, when two sermons were preached by the Hey. It C. Hutchings, of Nottingham. A special service was held in the afternoon, when the sacred cintatA, " Daniel," WAS rendered by a choir of thirty voices, amongst whom were several ladies and gentlemen connected with Wycliffe Chapel, Warrington. Mr. Albert Leather pre- sided at the harmonium. The congregations were large, and the collections realised £22.

WARRINGTON UoUNTY COURT. TRIIRSDAT.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. ADMINISTRATION ORDER. William 4avery, labourer, applied for an administration order. After hearing his statement and his answe-s to Questions asked him by credi- tors in Court. his Honour granted the application. A DISPUTED BARGAIN.—ThiII Was a jury case in which Mr. A. Browne appeared for Ike plaintiff, and Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defendant. Mr. Browne said the action was one originally brought in the High Court of Justice, and would, have been tried at Liverpool Assizes, but both parties agreed to leave the matter in the hands of that court ; and had, therefore, been remitted by consent. The action was for willows, or twigs, which were sold by Mr. Henry Cook, of Thelwall, to Mr. Daniel Johnson. basket and ham- per manufacturer, of Knutsford-road, Litchford. Mr. Cook was a grower of Willows, and offered a quantity that he wished to dispose of to the defendant. In November last year defendant went to Mr. Cook's place at Thal wall, and examined the willows then growing there. He might say at the outset that there were two kinds of willows, known in the trade as one-year-olds and two-year-olds. The farmer were considered more valuable than the latter. On the plaintiff's bed of willows tkere WAS a quantity of one-year olds and a larger quantity of two-year-olds. Mr. Johnson e:c mined them closely, and afterwards a bargain was made. ' It was, the plaintiff contended, that the willows, both sorts, should be sold for .-C2 17e 61 per ton. On the part of the defendant it would be urged that the bargain was for £3 3s per ton for the one-year olds, and 17+ GI seer ton for the I two-year olds. There was not much dispute about the weight. Thep!, was no one present when the bargain Was made, and the jury, after hearing evidenc, that would be called, would have to decide which of the two they would believe. The amount in dispute would he a little over £lO. —Witnesses were then examined at length.—Mr. Jenkins, for the defence, submitted that it was unreasonable to sup- pose that a man like Mr. Johnson, who had been engaged , the whole of his life in the purchase of willows, and the manmfacture of those articles for which willows are used, • should ever have dreamed of buying the willows at the price stated all-round. He contended that there was a distinct bargain to purchase the one-year old willows at £3 3s a ton, and the two-year old ones at £1 178 6d a too..—Evidence for ; the defence was being taken when the court rose. The hear. lug is to be continued at next Thursday's sitting of the • court.
On Thureday, the session of the C4ngregational Union. at Hanley, closed with the adoption of a resolution in favour of the closing of public houses on Sundays

Mn. EDWARD MILNER ON FREIj' EDUCATION.— Speaking at a meetint, at Wincham on Thurs lay in support of the candidature of Mr. J. T. Brunner, Mr. Edward Milner, J.P., of Warrington, said :—With regard to the education question, he, was very anxious to see carried a law providing for free education. He never could endure the idea of sending poor but respectable and intelligent people to the workhouse to seek relief in the way of school pence. (Cheers.) The reason he wished to see education free was that all suspicion of connect- ing education with pauperism might be entirely done away with. (Loud cheers.) And further, if they did away with ignorance, he believed that pauperism would not be long before it followed. (Cheers.) To achieve good results the one great thing was that the voice of the people should be clearly and unmistakeably heard in Parliament. To get the views of the people fully heard in Parlia- nient, they could not do better than send men like Mr. Brunner, who were thoroughly in earnest in wishing for the freedom and happiness of the whole community. (Cheers.)

EMMA NIIBL CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL BAND OF HOPE.—On Monday the first of a series of monthly entertainments was held in the schoolroom, Old- road, Mr. John Hall in the chair. The programme, consisting of songs, recitations, readings, 6:.c., was well rendered.

Tice Imi:immix CoildenT.—The annual work- ing-men's concert in aid of the Warrington Infir- mary is to be held on the 24th inst. An excellent programme will, we understand, be submitted, most of the artistes being professionals from Liverpool and Manchester. ' • WESLEYAN Bize.A.B.—We would remind our readers that a forest bazaar in aid of the building fund of the Sankey Bridges new Weslgyan ,Chapel will be opened by the Mayor of St. Helens (Alder- man T. Cook) in Bold-street Wesleyan Schools, on Wednesday next. STRBTPON Caunen.—The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the above church will be held to-morrow (Sunday.) The preacher in the morning will be the vicar, the Rev. Canon Dodd; in the afternoon the Rev C. Brown, curate of Holy Trinity, Warrington; and in the evening the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, vicar of Antrobns. GOLBORNE-STREBT BAPTIST eIIAPRL,-012 Sunday the Rev. E. Parker, D.D., president of the Manchester Baptist College, preached in the above church,on the occasion of the holding of the anniversary\ services, I Large congregationd listened to the rev. gentleman's discourses, the collections, in aid of the church ex- penses and the repair of the organ, amounting to .£ll. On Thursday evening the services were' con- tinued, the preacher being Mr. W. P. Lockhart, of Liverpool. COCKHEDOE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIRTY.—The first meeting' of the above society was held on Monday evening, when Mr. J. T. Blease read a paper on "Character," which was interesting and instructive. In the debate which followed, Messrs. Bridge, Garner, Roger, Hunt, Atherton, and Parry took part. The Rev. W. B. Parry, president of the society, occupied the chair. A considerable number have already been enrolled as members. TRANSFERS. The following transfers were granted by the borough justices on Monday, Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) offering no objection on the part of the police :—Golden Lion, St. James-street, from Richard Harding to William Whittaker; Kings Arms, Buttermarket-street, from Thomas Peacock to John Liddle; Ring o' Bells, Wilderspool-road, from Samuel Brookes to George Brooks; Rose Inn, Dial- steeet, from Edward Wright to Thomas Robertson; shopkgeper's license, Wmwick-road, from John Gibbs to Joseph Caldwell. Sr. PAUL'S TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—This society held a concert at Warburton on Thursday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr. T. Lawless presided, and spoke against the evils of the drink traffic, which, he said, was the cause of the ruin of so many. A programme consisting of singing, reci- tations, dialogues, stump and negro speeches, was then gone through. A stump speech, given by Mr. Massey, and a dialogue entitled "Unfortunate 1 lovers,' caused much amusement. Subsequently Mr. Smith (secretary) made a few remarks, in the course of which he said that the St. Paul's branch of the Temperance Society was doing good work. They had a Band of Hope which numbered from 400 to 500 members, and an adult branch with about 50 members He strongly urged those pre- sent to sign the pledge. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks. THE Ils.unrens.—The Warrington Harriers on Saturday had their first cross country run, twelve members taking part. The hares, J. Dumbell and T. Bandies, were despatched with the bags at 3-15, the pack following at 345. The trail lay down by the Poet-office, Slutcheis-lane, and across the fields to Walton Arches, then along the canal for about a mile. Here the hares crossed the canal, went through the fields, and on to the high road at Moore. Then they crossed the fields again to Dares- bury,went round by Hill Cliff water works, through Higher Walton, and on. the high road at Tom Payne's Bridge to Wilderspool Causeway. Here the word "go ' was given, and the race ended as fol- lows :—T. Locker, first; J. Massey (captain), second; lE. Sherlock, third; D. Walsh, fourth; Beswick, ; fifth. Distance about eight miles. James Green I acted as pace, and J. Massey whip. 1 ORFORD CI:MACH. —On " Sunday, the harvest thanksgiving services were held in, the above 'church. The building was profusely and tastefully decorated. In addition to the various wreaths, flovfers, &c., there were elaborately-worked texts in various parts, and Many bunches of grapes, &c. There were four services during the day, namely, Holy Communion at eight a.m., morning service at 10-30 a.m., with Holy Communion, Litany and children's service at three p.m., and evensong at 6-30. The preacher was the Rev: J. Phillips, of Orford. in the morning, and the Rev. J. F. Hoctor, of Maghull, in the evening. Special psalms were sung and special lessons read at each service. The grapes, &c., were afterwards sent to the Warrington Infirmary. The offertories were devoted to the various diocesan funds. The building was crowded at the evening service. • HARVEST FESTIVAL AT GREAT SANEEY.—On Sine- day harvest thanksgiving services were held at St. Mary's, when sermons were preached by the Vicar, Ithat in the morning from St. Luke, VIII. 11, "The. seed is the word; and in the evening Proverbs x. 5," He that gathereth in summer is a wise sou, but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame." There were large congregations at both services, but particularly at night, when the church was crowded to its utmost capacity. Large quan- tities of corn l fruit, vegetables, and flowers were contributed by members of the congregation and friends, and a beautiful collection of hothouse plants were lent by Mr. Bolton for the occasion. I Praise is due to the .Misses Bolton, Dignum, Grange, I Hatton Jeans Kerfoot Standish, Skelton, Tinsley, I and d ' ' Mrs. Wylde, for the manner in which the decorations were carried out. The offertories realized ..£l7 6s Oid. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARUINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Oct. 3rd, 1885.—The mean temperature was 48.2 Fehr., and therefore 2.3 degrees colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 59 Fahrenheit, was recorded 'on the Ist inst., and the minimum temperature. 32 Fahrenheit, on the 28th ult. The rainfall measured 0.79 in. The general directiqn of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 40th of the current year, 31 births and 16 deaths were registered. The death 'rate from all causes was equal to 18.3 per 1,000, against 19.4 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 15.4 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from diarrhcea, 1 from cancer, 1 from phthisis, 1 from old age, 3 from heart disease, 1 from brain disease, 2 from lung disease, and 3 from premature birth. Three cases of typhus fever, and 2 of whooping cough were reported under the require- ments of the Act of Parliament. Joust H. •GonsfALL. Medical Officer of Health. FUNERAL OF AN OLD ABSTAINER.—The remains of the late Mr. William Mee, ren., of Grappenhall, were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on Tues- day afternoon. Mr. Mee had -been a most active worker in the temperance cause in Warrington I from its very commencement, something like fifty ' years ago, until the time of his death which took place last Saturday morning. Notwithstanding the 1 unfavourable weather, a considerable number of ' temperance friends attended the funeral as a token of respect to the memory,of the deceased. Amongst those present were Mr. Robert Garnett, Alderman Parish, Chester; Mr. William Roberts, secretary, Warrington Temperance Union; Mr. Thomas Hall, Independent Order of Rechabites ; Mr. David Houghton, League of the Cross; Mr. J. W. Hall, the Good Templars ; Mr. Edward Plinston, War- rington Band of Hops Union; and numerous other friends. The , funeral ceremony was performed by Mr. William Wright, of the Friar's Green Chapel, in a most solemn and impressive manqer. Mr. Jas. Mounfield, of Buttermarket-street, was the under- taker. ' HOYLE-STREET MISSION.—This mission, which was opened a short time ago, and is connected with St. Paul's Church, is proving very successful. Last evening the first harvest thanksgiving service was held. There was a good congregation, and the mission-room was very prettily adorned with fruit, flowers, and cereals. The service was commenced by. hymn 382, " Come ye faithful people come," and prayer was then read by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's). Mr. William Smith read the first lesson, and hymn 381, "Praise, oh praise our God and King," was then sung. The second lesson was read by Mr. T. Lawless, and then hymn 383, "We plough the fields and scatter," was sung. The Rev. W. F. Lane, of Manchester, gave an address, in which he referred to that being the first harvest festival held in connection with the mission. He I also expressed the belief that such a mission, con- ducted by working people, was eminently calcu- lated to benefit the working classes whom they wished to influence. The decorations were carried out by Messrs. Smith and Richards, and Misses Mackenzie, Reynolds, Rogers, and Sauce. Mr. J. Richards officiated at the harmonium. It may be mentioned that Mr. Marsh, of Market-street, who presented a clock at the commencement of the mis- sion, has since given a handsome lamp.

GOLBORNE. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—SpeciaI sermons were preached in the Edge Green Primitive Methodist Chapel laq Sunda Y, by Mr. Lee, of Chester, to large congregations. Collection/I were made in aid of the chapel trust. FLOWER SROW.—An exhibition of fruit, vegetables, and flowers was opened at the New Inn, Golborne, on Saturds9 afternoon. Competition in most of the classes was keen. and a capital display was made. The judging was in the hands of Mr. West (Newton), and Mr. Kennesey, of ilindleY Hall. The principal prize winners were :—Messrs. r.' Debb, E. Last, T. Ashcroft, jour., W. H. Lowe, John Lowe, E. Ormiston, J. Leetherbarrow, J. Boardman, and Vl' Walmsley. A large number of persons visited the show 00 Saturday and Sunday. WESLEYAN MIiTHODIS3L-4t a special meeting held TO the Go'borne Wesleyan Cnapel, on Tuesday evening (Rev' James Kent in the chair), at was decided to postpone the bazaar to be held in aid of the new school fund until JulYt 1886, owing partially to the depressed state of trade in the locality. The committee are about to purchase .£6O worth of land behind the chapel, so that the school can be built st the end of the present structure. By this arrangement both buildings could be thrown into one, should additional chapel accommodation be required. A building committee was formed to act in conjunction with the trustees. We understand Mr. Joseph Howard, of Waterloo, late of Bank Heath Mill, Golberne, has promised .£:3O towards the scheme.

A STEAMER Huw DOWN ON THE ..Tmotas.-012 SaturdaY evening the river steamer Martin, which was on its 11811S1 trip from Limehoune to London Bridge, with fifty passer gers on board, wae ruc down by the Liverpool steamer Mary Hough. The latter had just entered the river from the Regent's Canal Dock. The Martin began to sink, I'osl a lamentable loss of life was only prevented by the teadr ness of tke cap•ain et a steamtug which Was towing barge past the dock. He immediately took the sinking steamer, in tow and drew her to the Surrey shore, where she settle' upon the mud. All the passengers, by clambering on board either the tug or the barges, escaped, although a few were immersc din the river. An explanation of the collision i 5 not forthcoming. The Mary Hough did not snstain aeY damage.

CAIRO, WEDNESBAY.—The hospital stern-wheel paddle steamer Alexandria, with 40 invalids on board, sank at three o'clock on Monday, white moored to the river bank, 20 miles south of Edfon. All on board were save& It is ex- pected that the vessel will become a total wreck. NEW ZEALAND. WELLINGTON, WEDNESDAY.—A new contract has been arranged or by the New Zealand Government with the Union Steamship Ccmpany for the renewal of the San Francisco service. The New South Wales and United States Government have agreed to join in a contribution to the subsidy. The Union .Company will run the new line between Sydney, Auckland, and Honolulu, connecting at the Ilatter place with the Oceanic Company's tine between Hono- lulu and San Francisco. AUSTRIA. VIENNA, WEENESDAT.—In to-day's sitting of the Lower House of the Reichsrath, the Government introduced a Bill for the prolongation of the law suspending trial by jury in Vienna. RUSSIA. , Sr. PETERSBURG, WSDNESDAY.---A decision of the Coun- cil of War, which was sanctioned by the Czar on the 17th ult., is published to-day, directing that two rifle battalions shall be 'formed for the Transcaspian territory, and the local forces raised for Merv,Sarakhs, ami Kachka. FATAL DUEL WITH SWORDS. An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris states: A French Officer and a Paris merchant, who quarrelled on some private matter, fought a duel with swords on Wednesday on the Belgian frontier. The officer ran his weapon through the heart of his adversary, who died in- stantly. ARREST OF AN ENGLISH MINISTER BY THE SPANISH. On Thursday morning, information was rereived in Liver. peel of the arrest at Fernando, West Africa, of the Rev. W. Melford, ref the‘Primitive Methodist Mission. The rev. gen- tleman is said to have been subjected to petty annovauces by the Spanish authorities of the island and then arrested, 'being confined on board A river hulk.
